Processing Information
Collection process by Judd Foundation Archives staff from 2021-2023 through a major project supported by a
grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities. Processing was led by Irene Lule and Caitlin Murray.

Lifetime and Post-Lifetime Materials
Following Judd’s death on February 12, 1994, the Donald Judd Estate was created to settle Judd’s activities at
the time of his death as well as any legal claims. Judd Foundation was legally established in 1996 by the
Trustees of the Donald Judd Estate. During the years of the Donald Judd Estate (1994-2000) and the early years
of Judd Foundation, staff intermixed records created by the Estate in the years immediately after Judd’s death
with records created by Judd and his studio. Throughout the Donald Judd Papers, there are post-lifetime
materials mixed with lifetime materials and files created after Judd’s death that contain lifetime documents.
These materials were reviewed on a case-by-case basis to determine their appropriate arrangement within the
Donald Judd Papers or possible movement to the Donald Judd Estate and Early Judd Foundation Records.
Areas that were heavily used by the Estate include financial records (Financial, Employee, and Legal Records
series) and materials related to properties (Architecture and Spaces subseries). If you are interested in any
material from 1992-1996, please carefully read the Scope and Content notes for each series and consult the
Archivist.

Processing Notes
Careful attention was paid to accessibility, use, and existing original order when present. Please read the Scope
and Content sections of each series for more detailed information. All original folders were photocopied, and
these photocopies were placed at the beginning of the new archival folders for context. Due to their size, only
folders with Judd handwriting and/or extensive handwriting by his staff were kept with the original material. Any
sticky notes found were photocopied on archival paper. Additionally, any sticky notes covering text or in fragile
condition were removed and rehoused in polyester sleeves.

Special Collections
Due to their fragility, rarity, and handling requirements, drawings created by Donald Judd, photographs, and
material samples found in the Donald Judd Papers have been replaced by photocopies. Drawings by Donald
Judd and photographs were moved to Special Collections; material samples were moved to Collections. Please
consult the Archivist to view Special Collections or Collections items.

Works consist of materials related to Donald Judd’s activities in art, architecture, furniture, and design. Materials
include correspondence, drawings, photographs, handwritten notes, blueprints, legal documents, financial
documents such as invoices and receipts, and printed material. The bulk of this material was created and
maintained by Judd’s studio. In some cases, original folders were created by Judd or the Donald Judd Estate.
The Works series includes four subseries: Artwork; Architecture and Spaces; Furniture; and Design.

Subseries A. Artwork, 1959-1999, undated

The Artwork subseries relates to the creation, commissioning, and sale of Judd’s work in painting and objects.
Records pertaining to paintings consist of one folder. The bulk of the records in this subseries document the
creation of objects, including fabricator, studio, and materials records.

Consisting of 13 boxes, Fabricator Records for Objects document the production of and payment for the
fabrication of Judd’s works in three dimensions. Created and maintained by the studio, these records are
arranged alphabetically by fabricator, then chronologically by year. Fabrication entities include businesses (e.g.,
Bernstein Brothers Inc., Lippincott, Inc.), individuals (e.g., Peter Ballantine, Celedonio Mediano), and cities or
entities that commissioned works (e.g., Münster). Materials in these folders often follow a standard arrangement:
purchase orders, invoices, correspondence, drawings, and restoration-related documents. Whereas purchase
orders were created by the studio to document the ordering of a work, invoices were typically generated by the
fabricator. Correspondence consists of handwritten notes created by studio assistants and correspondence
primarily between the studio and fabricator. Drawings largely consist of photocopies made by Judd’s studio
assistants of his original drawings or drawings by fabricators. Records documenting the restoration of works
consist primarily of photocopied invoices or purchase orders created for pieces undergoing restoration. For
these documents, please look for keywords that specify the form of remediation.

The Fabricator Records section includes records that had been left in situ in Judd’s Art Studio in Marfa. Due to
its unique arrangement, the found order was maintained. Original records were removed by the Archives staff in
2021 and replaced by surrogates. Additionally, the Fabricator Records subseries includes records that originated
from Lippincott, Inc. and were provided to Judd Foundation after Judd’s death. These records consist of
photocopies of drawings, invoices, correspondence, and notes created by the company.

Fabricator Records are closed until the completion of the Donald Judd Catalogue Raisonné Project. Please
consult the Archivist (archives@juddfoundation.org) for questions or additional information.

Studio Records for Objects consists of eight boxes of files created and maintained by Judd’s studio assistants
that pertain to the creation and tracking of artworks, including restoration files, records documenting various
types of works (unrealized, destroyed, canceled, fakes), and material files. The bulk consists of records created
by Dudley Del Balso (Judd’s assistant from 1968-1983), with additional records created by Ellie Meyer (Judd’s
assistant from 1983-1991). These files include correspondence, financial records, drawings, photographs, notes,
and printed material that was arranged topically. Of particular interest are research files that document updates

track fabrication.

Two categories on prints and works in edition, the Roy C. Judd Files and Studio Records for Prints and Works in
Edition, relate to the design, fabrication, sale, and loan of woodblocks, prints, and multiples made between 1963
and 1993. The material consists of correspondence, drawings, and handwritten notes with a small amount of
printed material. The bulk of these materials relates to prints, with a small quantity of files related to works in

The Roy C. Judd Files include correspondence between Roy and studio assistants Dudley Del Balso and Jamie
Dearing; Roy and staff at the National Gallery of Canada; and ledgers, drawings, and invoices. Roy C. Judd’s

These records document the number of prints he made from each block over time. Also included is a folder with
drawings by Roy C. Judd for woodblocks that were never produced. The bulk of these records date to 1978.

accessibility and use. These files include correspondence and notes from printers. Additional folders reflect
realized and unrealized projects, financial documents from accountant Rubin L. Gorewitz, and potential printers
and paper supplies/suppliers.

Subseries B. Architecture and Spaces, 1951, 1968-1999, undated

Architecture and Spaces pertains to architectural projects and spaces created by Judd, both on property he
owned or leased and commissioned projects for others. The term “spaces” has been used for this subseries title
rather than “properties” to reflect the term Judd used. Materials were arranged alphabetically by project or
space name. To improve accessibility, artificial folders were created for projects and spaces that had a small
quantity of materials that were previously dispersed across the records.

There are five boxes of materials related to the ownership and maintenance of 101 Spring Street, the first
building Judd purchased, in 1968 in New York. Titles, insurance, and mortgage information are gathered into two
folders. Approximately three boxes relate to the maintenance of 101 Spring Street, including materials for

New York departments (Fire, Buildings, Transportation, etc.) document inspections and violations. There are

in the maintenance of the building. Items found in these folders consist mainly of correspondence, receipts,
invoices, and handwritten notes. Note that additional records pertaining to the maintenance and upkeep of 101
Spring Street are in the Expenditures section of the Financial, Employee, and Legal Records series. Due to the
importance of early titles, insurance, and mortgage information, these two aforementioned folders were placed
at the beginning of the arrangement. All other materials pertaining to 101 Spring Street were grouped together
by topic in alphabetical order.

In 1989, Judd hired the firm of Sean West Sculley to begin restoration of 101 Spring Street. Materials pertaining

folders also include financial and legal documents. There is a single folder from Mike Howard, an early employee
of Judd who performed basic building maintenance from May to July 1970 with early photos of the interior of
101 Spring Street included.

Beginning in 1976, throughout the 1980s, and principally from 1989 to 1991, Judd purchased extensive areas of
ranch land south of Marfa, Texas. Records pertaining to Ayala de Chinati, the name Judd gave to his ranch,

accessibility and use, these materials were combined into single folders reflecting the purchase.

The three folders for La Mansana de Chinati/The Block, Judd’s main living and working complex in Marfa,
include titles, taxes, and files pertaining to the construction of the adobe walls that Judd added to the complex.
Along with La Mansana de Chinati/The Block, Judd purchased several buildings in Marfa, mainly in the late
1980s and early 1990s. These include the Marfa National Bank (which Judd converted into the Architecture
Studio), a former Safeway grocery store (Art Studio), a hotel (Print Building), and additional buildings downtown.
Most of the materials for these spaces are photocopies of financial and legal documents compiled for inventory
purposes after Judd’s death. As with materials from Ayala de Chinati, records were occasionally dispersed and
then combined by space.

Architectural projects with extensive documentation include the Bahnhof Ost Basel (Peter Merian Haus) in Basel,
Switzerland; Winterthur Fountains in Winterthur, Switzerland; and Eichholteren, Judd’s home and studio, in
Küssnacht am Rigi, Switzerland. These materials include blueprints, correspondence, photographs, drawings,
financial and project documents, and printed material. For Eichholteren, there are files created during Judd’s
lifetime and several created after his death by the Donald Judd Estate to identify and document Judd’s personal
effects.

This subseries also includes materials pertaining to projects Judd worked on with European museums. These
include the design of a floor for the Lange Voorhout Palace (The Hague, Netherlands) and a room redesign for
the Österreichisches Museum für Angewandte Kunst (MAK – Museum of Applied Arts, Vienna, Austria). For
additional correspondence and context on the project at the MAK, please refer to the corresponding MAK folder
in the Museums, Galleries, and Collectors series. For additional information on the Lange Voorhout Palace
project, please see the Adrian Jolles Papers and the Haags Gemeentemuseum (now Kunstmuseum Den Haag)
folders in the Museums, Galleries, and Collectors series.

A small quantity of general folders have been arranged in alphabetical order. These items include financial
documents, correspondence, photocopies of plans and sketches by Judd, maps, surveys, and commissions.

The Donald Judd Estate made heavy use of materials related to these spaces due to the financial and legal
obligations present after Judd’s death. Most of the material related to Ayala de Chinati and Marfa acquisitions

Subseries C. Dia Art Foundation Records, 1974-1990, 1994, undated

The Dia Art Foundation Records subseries relates to the conception and execution of large-scale, permanent
installations of artwork in Marfa. These installations, originally referred to as the Dia Marfa Project and later
known as the Art Museum of the Pecos, would eventually open to the public independently in 1986 as the
Chinati Foundation (see The Chinati Foundation subseries). These records document the institutional relationship
between Judd and Dia Art Foundation (formerly the Lone Star Foundation), based in New York and founded by
Heiner Friedrich, Philippa Pellizzi, and Helen Winkler.

Included in this subseries are documents related to installations of artwork by Judd, John Chamberlain, Dan
Flavin, and Barnett Newman; administrative memoranda between Dia Art Foundation offices in Marfa and New
York; correspondence between Judd, his assistants, Heiner Friedrich, and third parties; legal agreements and
correspondence between Judd and Dia Art Foundation; financial documents; printed material; and documents
related to the establishment of archives in Marfa. These records have been arranged into the following
categories: Works and Projects; Correspondence; Dia/Marfa Activity Reports; Donald Judd’s Working Records;
Legal Records; Financial Records; and Printed Material.

Subseries D. The Chinati Foundation/La Fundación Chinati, 1986-1994, undated

The Chinati Foundation/La Fundación Chinati subseries includes administrative records, correspondence,
financial records, insurance records, and printed material pertaining to the Chinati Foundation. Prior to 1986, this
initiative was also known as the Dia Marfa Project and Art Museum of the Pecos.

Administrative records consist of meeting agendas and notes, nonprofit paperwork, budgets, handwritten notes,
drafts of promotional material, and party invitation lists. Correspondence is composed of letters and faxes
regarding repairs, property purchases, artwork acquisitions, and event planning. Financial records consist of
account statements, tax documents, inventories, payroll, tax deposit coupon books, and receipts. Insurance
records include paperwork related to various insurance policies held by the foundation over the years. Printed
material includes postcards, invitations, posters, brochures, exhibition ephemera, and newspaper articles.

In addition to material concerning Judd, this subseries contains material relating to artists who exhibited at the
Chinati Foundation, including Josef Albers, Ingólfur Arnasson, John Chamberlain, El Lissitzky, Günther Förg,
Roni Horn, Richard Paul Lohse, Ilya Kabakov, Richard Long, Agnes Martin, Piet Mondrian, Barnett Newman,
Claes Oldenburg, Jan Schoonhoven, John Wesley, as well as artists-in-residence.

For more archival material related to the Chinati Foundation, please see the Chinati Foundation Archives:
https://chinati.org/research/archives/.

This series is organized into 2 subseries:

The Writings and Publications series contains handwritten and typed drafts and photocopies of reviews,

related to publications made by or associated with him. Additionally, correspondence, exhibition ephemera,
clippings, and photocopies appear throughout.

Subseries A. Writings, 1959-1993, undated

The Writings subseries is organized into five categories: Reviews, Essays and Letters, Notes, Journals, and
Photocopies. These categories were created and maintained by Judd and/or his studio and were maintained
here as such. Each category was originally organized in loose chronological order, which has been maintained
and clarified when possible. The bulk of the notes were organized by Judd by year, and occasionally into groups
of notes with varying dates. This is most common in the notes structured by inclusive dates.

The category Reviews reflects the period between 1959 and 1965 when Judd worked as an art critic. Reviews
listed as “unidentified” refer to those that did not correspond to published or known reviews. The Notes category
reflects writings composed as part of Judd’s semi-regular daily writing practice. The bulk of the notes were
unpublished during his lifetime. The Photocopies category documents the studio practice of making
photocopies of notes, essays, and letters so Judd could have them on hand in other locations, such as his ranch
houses south of Marfa and his homes and studios in Germany and Switzerland. The nomenclature system for
these folders, created by Judd and written in his hand, is often idiosyncratic.

The bulk of the Writings subseries was transcribed and published in Donald Judd Writings (Judd
Foundation/David Zwirner Books, 2016). There is unpublished material throughout this subseries.

Subseries C. Civic Activities, circa 1940s-1994, undated

One of the larger subseries, Civic Activities covers the broad range of organizations and causes Judd was
involved in starting in the 1960s.

The first category, Organizations, records Judd’s involvement with different civic, activist, and politically minded
groups. Files are arranged in alphabetical order by organization name. Much of Judd’s involvement was through
writing letters of support, donating money or artwork for benefit exhibitions, or, in the case of the War Resisters
League, hosting benefit exhibitions at 101 Spring Street. Some of the files contain only minor correspondence,
donation letters, and/or newsletters sent by the organization. Other files indicate Judd’s deep or prolonged
involvement through personal correspondence and reports and agendas for boards he served on, including the
Texas Advisory Board for the Environmental Defense Fund and the Board of Visitors for the McDonald
Observatory. One of the most extensive files is the Citizens for Local Democracy, Lower-Manhattan Township, in
which Judd and Julie Finch were highly involved. This includes meeting minutes and reports, extensive
manuscripts and drafts, and published versions of writings for the group’s publications, some with Julie Finch’s
handwritten drafts.

The second subset of Civic Activities, Political and Civic Involvement and Interests, relates to Judd’s interests in
local political issues in Marfa, New York, and national or general issues. These files document his support for
various political campaigns, including Commissioner Jim Hightower for Texas Department of Agriculture and
United States Senator Edward M. Kennedy. Marfa concerns include a file of complaints regarding air traffic over
Judd’s ranch and a legal file for noise complaints against Tom Horn and his ice-making truck neighboring La
Mansana de Chinati/The Block. Additional Marfa concerns primarily consist of news articles and notes on a
proposed prison in Marfa and the arrest of Presidio County Sheriff Richard Dee Thompson for drug smuggling.
General files reflect Judd’s peace and antiwar interests, political party support, labor and economic issues, water
rights, and artists’ rights. Extensive civic-related correspondence and donations can also be found in the
Incoming Judd Correspondence and the Expenditures section. There are also several files of political
publications related to socialism, Marxism, and communism and a wide assortment of printed material.

Series VII. Financial, Employee, and Legal Records, circa 1940s-1994, undated
(162 boxes, 5 oversize boxes)

This series is organized into 3 subseries:
•  Subseries A. Financials
•  Subseries B. Employee Files
•  Subseries C. Legal

Financial, Employee, and Legal Records, the largest series of the Donald Judd Papers, documents the
financial and legal obligations of Judd and his studio as well as the individuals working for Judd and, to a lesser
extent, the Chinati Foundation. The series contains receipts, bills, tax and insurance documents, accounting
records, personnel files, and legal files. These materials cover a large area of Judd’s work and personal life,
including art fabrication, Judd’s personal art collection, travel expenses, daily and studio activities, and property
purchases.

The Financials subseries is organized into four categories: Expenditures, Accounting, Taxes, and Insurance. The
Employee subseries is organized into two categories: Payroll and Personnel. The Legal subseries is organized
into three categories: Law Firms, Individual Issues, and La Junta de los Rios. Each category has a small section
of associated general files.

Subseries A. Financials, 1948-1994, undated

The Financials subseries is the largest of the three subseries and covers a wide range of Judd’s financial history
including expenditures incurred by Judd, his studio, and employees; studio accounting records; and insurance
files.

With 101 boxes reflecting payments made by Judd and his studio, Expenditures is the largest section of the
Donald Judd Papers. These records consist of receipts, invoices, bills paid, credit card statements, petty cash
vouchers, and reimbursements accrued by Judd, his children, and numerous staff. Often, items are notated with
the amount paid and check number. Given the number of people involved in managing Judd’s personal and
professional activities, original order varies greatly by year and decade. In some years, materials are grouped
together by year with a topical focus (e.g., 1981 invoices from Marfa Hardware Company). In later years,
expenditures were often grouped together and arranged in sequential order by check number. Later years are
also more organized, generally following chronological order and corresponding to the original folder title.

Of note is the difference between bills paid and receipts. Bills paid were typically received by the
office/accountant(s) from a business, while receipts were often accrued by staff while traveling or running
errands and were used to validate reimbursement or confirm petty cash spent. Additionally, receipts were
typically compiled in envelopes with handwritten notes regarding the total amount spent and coding them to a
particular accounting category, while bills paid were filed in a folder with the associated check number and
accounting category. Receipt envelopes have been compiled together under “Receipts” at the end of each
respective year, with the bulk from 1987-1994.

In August 2022, Judd Foundation received 11 boxes of financial material dating from 1967-1979 and 1983 from
the Chinati Foundation related to Judd’s personal life and studio. These materials are believed to have been
stored in the artillery sheds at Fort D. A. Russell and moved and re-stored a number of times. Their found order
in 2019 indicates materials were compiled together based on size into large plastic containers. During the
processing of the Chinati Foundation’s records between 2019-2021, Chinati’s archivists organized material in
loose chronological order with additional refinement by Judd Foundation staff. For accurate searches, careful
attention should be paid to folder dates. Additionally, when possible, Judd Archives added a topical title when
one was present; folders with only dates contain a variety of expenditures. A good indication of whether a folder
was originally arranged by the studio or came from the Chinati Foundation’s deposit is the presence of a

42

[PDF page 44]
photocopy at the front of the folder. Studio/accounting files often include a photocopy created during
processing of the original folder used by the studio. Materials that came from the Chinati Foundation’s deposit
do not have an original folder, due to the frequency with which that material was moved and re-housed.

Materials from the 1950s-1970s that were not part of the Chinati Foundation’s deposit are loosely arranged in
chronological order and often have a topical focus (clothing, trips, utilities, etc.). There are numerous folders that
contain a mixture of receipts; these have been labeled “General” in the container list. Due to a tax audit in 1975,
expenditures from 1974 are particularly well documented compared to other years in this period. These have
been further arranged by alphabetical order based on their original folder title. There are also four folders related
to travel from 1976 to 1977, including trips to Mexico and Australia. Key materials include American Express
statements and folders categorized as Receipts. As previously mentioned, receipts often reflect reimbursements
incurred by Judd and his staff, the bulk of which were compiled during trips.

Throughout the 1980s, Judd’s financial responsibilities grew, with multiple land and property purchases in
Presidio County, increased staff, and extensive travel. Beginning in 1981, due to the hire of Willie Null (Judd’s
bookkeeper for most of the 1980s), several IRS audits, and a series of accounting firms hired by Judd, a more
consistent order was created and maintained.

Due to the volume of files and varying recordkeeping practices, a summary for each year from 1969-1994 is
provided below.

A bulk of 1969-1979 [224.1-241.8] consists of materials transferred from the Chinati Foundation. These items
were loosely arranged in chronological order and are followed by topical focus folders in alphabetical order.
While many of these folders include items for several years, there is typically one year prominent. These files also
contain accounting, banking, and tax documents.

All 1974 files were arranged by Judd’s studio in chronological and topical order (alphabetically). These materials
were most likely arranged in great detail due to a tax audit in 1975.

1980 has a single file present. A number of expenditures dated 1980 are in the 1979 and 1981 files.

1981 files are arranged in alphabetical order by their original folder titles, which were primarily titled by business
name. In some cases, an additional description has been added by the Archives staff to increase discoverability
and provide better context for certain business names.

1982 files are arranged in a similar alphabetical order as in 1981. These materials were transferred from the
Chinati Foundation.

1983-1985 files are arranged by property. This new arrangement was most likely implemented by an accounting
firm due to an IRS audit. The bulk of the folders contain a general ledger sheet summarizing yearly expenses by
property.

1986 only contains three files: property taxes paid, a file with bills related to Judd’s ranches, and general
receipts accrued by the studio.

Beginning in 1987, the volume of bills, invoices, and receipts increased substantially. Additionally, the
arrangement reverts to an alphabetical order based on original folder titles, which were primarily titled by
business name. As with material from 1981, an occasional descriptor was added to unclear business names for
better context and clarity. Starting in 1987, the files demonstrate a more robust recordkeeping practice in which
employees directly maintained their receipts, primarily for travel (taxis, restaurants, hotels) or errands grocery
stores, gas, postage, and various bills paid with petty cash or by the employee’s personal funds and kept for
reimbursements). The bulk of the receipts in 1987 were organized chronologically, rather than topically, with
additional receipts organized by travel or by reimbursement by employee name. Studio and travel folders were
arranged in loose chronological order, while reimbursements were arranged in alphabetical order by last name.

43

[PDF page 45]
1988 files follow a similar pattern to 1987. Most of the folders are arranged in alphabetical order by original folder

*   Collectively weighing 18 ¾ tons and measuring one kilometer when laid end to end, the work mirrors De Maria’s _The Vertical Earth Kilometer_ (1977), a companion piece permanently installed in Kassel, Germany, consisting of a brass rod of identical diameter, total length, and weight, inserted vertically into the earth.  
  
De Maria deploys numerical sequencing as a compositional principle to achieve a semblance of regularity. The appearance of a rational grid is thus an optical illusion created by the slightly increasing intervals between the brass rods as they recede from the viewer. Working with architect Richard Gluckman and engineer Michael Kellough on the installation design and renovations to the space, De Maria devises this arrangement and the halide stadium lighting such that each rod is rendered visible into the far reaches of the gallery space. Initially exhibited from April 14 to June 30, 1979, as part of a series of single-artist presentations at 393 West Broadway, _The Broken Kilometer_ draws 5,225 attendees in its first month on view. On October 20, 1979, _The Broken Kilometer_ reopens as a permanent Dia site and has remained on long-term view to the public since then.

*   In 1981, Masjid al-Farah opens at 155 Mercer Street as a permanent venue for hosting Sufi ceremonies. *   Working closely with architect Richard Gluckman and Dia’s director of operations James Schaeufele, Flavin oversees the building’s renovation between 1981 and 1983, making key decisions to best accommodate his work and preserve the property’s multiple legacies. To memorialize the building’s former life as a volunteer fire department, the barn-style double doors from the firehouse entrance are refurbished and the newel post in the vestibule is painted fire-engine red. The church doors and frosted-glass windows are moved to the back room of the second floor, which hosts a display of memorabilia from the First Baptist Church, including a neon cross. In keeping with his practice of acknowledging friends, relatives, curators, or historical personages in the titles of his work, Flavin dedicates the building to Schaeufele.

*   Starting in 1987, independent curator Henry Geldzahler advises Dia on a series of monographic exhibitions featuring artists with ties to the East End of Long Island such as Louise Bourgeois, Alice Neel, Cy Twombly, and Andy Warhol. *   Within one year’s time, the building becomes a pillar of the downtown dance scene, fostering a community of artists. In 1986, Susan Osberg, artistic director of the Workwith Dancers Company, initiates the Salon Project, an annual fall event that features new work by choreographers. *   In preparation for Documenta, Beuys arranged in early 1982 for basalt to be brought into Kassel from a quarry outside the city, which was then amassed on the front lawn of the Fridericianum, Documenta’s primary exhibition building. *   Through extensive material support, Dia engages deeply with artists on its roster to realize their commissions and collect their work. In January 1979, having already commissioned and presented several permanent and long-term displays, Dia develops the concept of individual-artist institutes dedicated to the exhibition, production, and preservation of a single artist’s work. The locations chosen reflect the site-responsive nature of each artist’s practice, ranging from sites in the western U.S., to outer Long Island, rural Massachusetts, and coastal Connecticut, as well as several in New York. Understanding the aesthetic potential of industrial architecture, the foundation identifies, for purchase or lease, abandoned or defunct factories or commercial sites for the purpose of artist studios or permanent displays. *   Flavin’s relighting of the platforms engages the structural elements of the station, immersing passengers in a soft complimentary continuity of blue, intensified en route by pink and gold. The completed work comprises 152 modular fluorescent units made up of eight- and four-foot-long fixtures, facing downward and outward, respectively. The daylight (blued) whites stream together and the pink and gold spark out on either side as one stands slightly to the right or left of center. The modular units link together into a receding linear procession, introducing an intense perspectival direction into the dark tunnel beyond.

*   The artist first used the material in the mid-1960s in a series of small, geometric sculptures, and highly polished metals will be subsequently featured in several of his most recognizable works. At _The Lightning Field_, the vertical poles vary in height to compensate for the earth’s undulating surface, creating a level plane that could support a plate of glass. _The Lightning Field_ juxtaposes imperial and metric standards against the vast expanse of the American desert. Within this context, the hard edges of these empirical systems of observation dissolve against the seemingly boundless, wide-open space. Moreover, _The Lightning Field_ requires both movement and time to be fully experienced. In addition to the physical terrain that the project occupies, the work is animated by changing light conditions, which cause the poles to come in and out of focus throughout the day.

Photo: Jon Abbott, courtesy Dia Art Foundation Archives, Beacon, New York   
*   As “one painting,” _Shadows_’equally sized canvases hang edge to edge and low to the ground. While _Shadows_ is fixed by these physical terms, the number of visible panels and their arrangement vary according to the size of an exhibition space; the work in total contracts, expands, and recalibrates each time it is installed. _Shadows_ is one of Warhol’s most abstract works, with its repetitive screenprints offset and inflected by the loose, gestural mopping of paint onto each monochromatic canvas. Installation view, 393 West Broadway, New York. © Estate of Walter De Maria. Photo: Jon Abbott, courtesy Dia Art Foundation Archives, Beacon, New York   
*   Collectively weighing 18 ¾ tons and measuring one kilometer when laid end to end, the work mirrors De Maria’s _The Vertical Earth Kilometer_ (1977), a companion piece permanently installed in Kassel, Germany, consisting of a brass rod of identical diameter, total length, and weight, inserted vertically into the earth.  
  
De Maria deploys numerical sequencing as a compositional principle to achieve a semblance of regularity. The appearance of a rational grid is thus an optical illusion created by the slightly increasing intervals between the brass rods as they recede from the viewer. Working with architect Richard Gluckman and engineer Michael Kellough on the installation design and renovations to the space, De Maria devises this arrangement and the halide stadium lighting such that each rod is rendered visible into the far reaches of the gallery space. Initially exhibited from April 14 to June 30, 1979, as part of a series of single-artist presentations at 393 West Broadway, _The Broken Kilometer_ draws 5,225 attendees in its first month on view. On October 20, 1979, _The Broken Kilometer_ reopens as a permanent Dia site and has remained on long-term view to the public since then.

*   In 1979, Dia deepens its patronage with the purchase of a three-story building on West 19th Street in Chelsea, known as Whitman Projects, as a venue and archives for the production, presentation, and documentation of the artist’s work. The earliest performances at Whitman Projects are held in December of 1980, presenting revivals of _Prune Flat_ (1965) and _Light Touch_. In 1982, Whitman premieres _Raincover_, an extravagant production comprising multiple film projections, set pieces, and choreographed movements unfolding over an hour on a 30-foot-long proscenium stage. Between 1983 and 1984, Dia funds the Whitman Projects performances of the artist’s _Eclipse_(1983) and his wife Sylvia Palacios’s _Irregulars_(1983).  
  
During this time, Dia also supports Whitman’s interest in radical site-specificity, beginning in 1979 with a commission to create an environmental installation at the Hudson River Museum in Yonkers, New York. Inhabiting built and natural environments on either side of the Hudson River, _Palisade_ comprises a multimedia installation of projections within the museum gallery and an outdoor installation at the base of the New Jersey Palisades on the opposing riverbanks. In 1980, Dia presents Whitman’s _Stound_, an outdoor performance combining film, found objects, and neighboring ponds, open fields, and woods at the Snug Harbor Cultural Center in Staten Island. Then, in 1981, Whitman returns to the Undercliff section of the Palisades State Park with _A Walk in the Park_, a nocturnal performance with film elements that unfolds along the park’s byways.

*   In preparation for Documenta, Beuys arranged in early 1982 for basalt to be brought into Kassel from a quarry outside the city, which was then amassed on the front lawn of the Fridericianum, Documenta’s primary exhibition building. [![Image 11: She Said So | Press Announces Its Founding During Women’s History Month and the Inaugural Release of Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love Los Angeles, CA — March 2026 — In honor of Women’s History Month, author Regina Louise announces the founding of She Said So | Press, an independent literary imprint devoted to publishing mythopoetic, embodied, and transformational writing that restores dignity and selfhood to those historically spoken for. The press will debut its inaugural title, Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love, releasing May 2026. The collection is a poetic cartography of exile and return—an exploration of self-retrieval, dignity, and the reclamation of voice beyond inherited narratives of abandonment, gender, and belonging. Founded by Louise after decades of traditional publishing, national media appearances, and public teaching, She Said So Press represents a decisive shift toward creative sovereignty. The imprint exists to publish work that functions not only as literature, but as witness, companion, and living practice. “Unladylike is not written from the margins,” Louise said. “It is written from the moment one crosses beyond them. This press exists so that no one has to ask permission to name what they know.” The launch of She Said So Press during Women’s History Month marks a continuation of women claiming authorship over their bodies, language, and legacy. Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love will be available May 2026 through major retailers, independent bookstores, and library distributors. [![Image 11: She Said So | Press Announces Its Founding During Women’s History Month and the Inaugural Release of Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love Los Angeles, CA — March 2026 — In honor of Women’s History Month, author Regina Louise announces the founding of She Said So | Press, an independent literary imprint devoted to publishing mythopoetic, embodied, and transformational writing that restores dignity and selfhood to those historically spoken for. The press will debut its inaugural title, Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love, releasing May 2026. The collection is a poetic cartography of exile and return—an exploration of self-retrieval, dignity, and the reclamation of voice beyond inherited narratives of abandonment, gender, and belonging. Founded by Louise after decades of traditional publishing, national media appearances, and public teaching, She Said So Press represents a decisive shift toward creative sovereignty. The imprint exists to publish work that functions not only as literature, but as witness, companion, and living practice. “Unladylike is not written from the margins,” Louise said. “It is written from the moment one crosses beyond them. This press exists so that no one has to ask permission to name what they know.” The launch of She Said So Press during Women’s History Month marks a continuation of women claiming authorship over their bodies, language, and legacy. Unladylike: A Mythopoetic Reclamation of Love will be available May 2026 through major retailers, independent bookstores, and library distributors. # Rose Salseda

Assistant Professor

Ph.D., University of Texas at Austin

M.A., University of Texas at Austin

B.A., California State University, Fullerton

![Image 1](https://art.stanford.edu/sites/art/files/styles/hs_medium_square_360x360/public/media/image/school_of_humanities_and_sciences-portrait-rose_salesda-harrison_truongstanford_university_1_0.jpg.webp?h=5b7dd105&itok=E9DDWyWv)

Image caption:
Portrait of Prof. Salseda by Harrison Truong/Stanford University

Dr. Rose Salseda is an assistant professor in the Department of Art & Art History and a cofounder of the [US Latinx Art Forum](https://uslaf.org/ "US Latinx Art Froum") (USLAF). Specializing in the fields of African American and U.S. Latinx art, and with a research background in the art of the African Diaspora in Latin America and the Caribbean, Dr. Salseda’s research explores the politics of race, identity, and representation; the intersections of art with underground and popular music; and the aesthetic strategies of appropriation, abstraction, and minimalism. She consults art world and academic leaders on Latinx art and has spearheaded and implemented data collections and research initiatives on the field, tracking its growth, targeting areas for advocacy, and overseeing the development of resources for artists, scholars, and students.

Dr. Salseda's first book, [_Unrest: Art in the Aftermath of The 1992 Los Angeles Riots_](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/U/bo269415625.html)(University of Chicago Press, August 2026), foregrounds uprising as a response to the injustices of state violence.Closely reading works made by two generations of multimedia artists, she reveals how they have challenged racial polarization and underscored the complex intergenerational, cross-racial, and immigrant experiences of racism and xenophobia in the United States and abroad.

Her second book, _A Cry for Justice: Chicano Art and the Cultivation of Humanity at Stanford University_(in preparation)_,_ casts light on how artists, students, and staff used visual art to make meaningful contributions and changes to campus life, curriculum, and political movements across the world, reflecting a larger drive across the U.S. to transform institutions of higher learning as fair and inclusive global leaders.

As a first-generation college student and the fourth generation of her family to have been raised in South Los Angeles, Dr. Salseda's research and scholarship are inspired and influenced by her family and community in Southern California.

# Rose Salseda

Assistant Professor

Ph.D., University of Texas at Austin

M.A., University of Texas at Austin

B.A., California State University, Fullerton

![Image 1](https://art.stanford.edu/sites/art/files/styles/hs_medium_square_360x360/public/media/image/school_of_humanities_and_sciences-portrait-rose_salesda-harrison_truongstanford_university_1_0.jpg.webp?h=5b7dd105&itok=E9DDWyWv)

Image caption:
Portrait of Prof. Salseda by Harrison Truong/Stanford University

Dr. Rose Salseda is an assistant professor in the Department of Art & Art History and a cofounder of the [US Latinx Art Forum](https://uslaf.org/ "US Latinx Art Froum") (USLAF). Specializing in the fields of African American and U.S. Latinx art, and with a research background in the art of the African Diaspora in Latin America and the Caribbean, Dr. Salseda’s research explores the politics of race, identity, and representation; the intersections of art with underground and popular music; and the aesthetic strategies of appropriation, abstraction, and minimalism. She consults art world and academic leaders on Latinx art and has spearheaded and implemented data collections and research initiatives on the field, tracking its growth, targeting areas for advocacy, and overseeing the development of resources for artists, scholars, and students.

Dr. Salseda's first book, [_Unrest: Art in the Aftermath of The 1992 Los Angeles Riots_](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/U/bo269415625.html)(University of Chicago Press, August 2026), foregrounds uprising as a response to the injustices of state violence.Closely reading works made by two generations of multimedia artists, she reveals how they have challenged racial polarization and underscored the complex intergenerational, cross-racial, and immigrant experiences of racism and xenophobia in the United States and abroad.

Her second book, _A Cry for Justice: Chicano Art and the Cultivation of Humanity at Stanford University_(in preparation)_,_ casts light on how artists, students, and staff used visual art to make meaningful contributions and changes to campus life, curriculum, and political movements across the world, reflecting a larger drive across the U.S. to transform institutions of higher learning as fair and inclusive global leaders.

As a first-generation college student and the fourth generation of her family to have been raised in South Los Angeles, Dr. Salseda's research and scholarship are inspired and influenced by her family and community in Southern California.

# HBA Book Awards

The Historians of British Art annually awards prizes to outstanding books on the history of British art, architecture, and visual culture. We are pleased to announce that we will consider books in six categories: Pre-1600, 1600–1800, 1800-1960, contemporary, multi-authored volume, and exhibition catalogue.

The 2025 Book Award winners can be found [here](https://historiansofbritishart.org/hba-book-awards-2025/). Previous winners can be found in the drop-down menu above.

In 2026, we will be considering books published in 2024. The copyright date published in the first edition establishes year of eligibility. The committee accepts nominations and self-nominations, although these should include publisher contact details. There is no limit on the number of books from a single publisher that may be considered in each category. The deadline for submissions of books published in 2024 is**September 1, 2025.** Winners will be announced in January 2026, in advance of the annual meeting of the College Art Association in February, so that publishers can market prize-winners there. Feel free to contact Sam Rose, the committee chair, with any questions: [sper@st-andrews.ac.uk](mailto:sper@st-andrews.ac.uk). # Fellows in Focus: Shannah Rose

August 15, 2025

[Shannah Rose](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/shannah-rose "Shannah Rose") is the 2025 Samuel H. Kress Foundation | Marian and Andrew Heiskell Rome Prize Fellow in Renaissance and early modern studies and a PhD candidate in the history of art at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University. She specializes in the visual and material culture of colonial Latin America, early modern Italy, and the Iberian Peninsula. Her dissertation, _The Codex Ríos (Codex Vaticanus A) and the Reception of Mesoamerican Pictography in Early Modern Italy_, focuses on the production and translation of illustrated codices in sixteenth-century Mexico and their reception and reproduction in early modern Italy. Rose earned an MA in the history of art and Latin American studies at Tulane University and a BFA in printmaking and BA in the history of art, both from the University of Virginia.

**Your dissertation focuses on the Codex Ríos and its copies as sites of cultural negotiation and mediation in sixteenth-century Mexico and Italy. What makes this manuscript unique, and why is it central to understanding the reception of Mesoamerican religion and culture in early modern Italy?**

The Codex Ríos (Vat.lat.3738, also known as the Codex Vaticanus A.) is an endlessly fascinating document. Held in the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana since its arrival in Italy in the 1560s, it is the only surviving colonial Mexican pictorial manuscript to feature a comprehensive textual account in Italian of the religion, culture, and customs of the Nahua, commonly referred to as the Aztecs. Nahua _tlahcuilohque_ (painter-scribes) created the manuscript under the behest of Dominican friars in central Mexico (New Spain) in the mid-sixteenth century, and it contains texts and images on 101 folios of imported Fabriano paper. The _tlahcuilohque_ produced the Codex Ríos as an augmented reproduction and translation of an earlier colonial Mexican manuscript, the Codex Telleriano-Remensis, and the scribes intended the Codex Ríos to be a clean copy of its prototype for a non-Indigenous, Italian readership.

In the tradition of other colonial-era Mexican manuscripts, the Codex Ríos comprises multiple sections of images with accompanying textual commentary and glosses. These include the Indigenous _tonalamatl_ (divinatory almanac), _xiuhpohualli_ (solar calendar), and the pictorial year count characteristic of pre-Hispanic Aztec codices. Two new sections are unique to the Codex Ríos as they were not included in the manuscript’s model. One section depicts the cosmological and mythological traditions of ancient Mesoamerica; importantly, this cosmology contains the only known images of the Aztec celestial layers. The second section is a proto-ethnography that details sacrificial and mortuary customs with native figural types. These additions to the Codex Ríos serve as valuable records of the Italian reception of Aztec religion and culture roughly thirty years after the onset of European settler-colonialism in New Spain.

The manuscript’s location in the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana gave it special visibility, particularly among elite circles connected to the Vatican. This tightly knit intellectual circle added another intriguing chapter to the manuscript’s object biography: when it arrived in Italy in the 1560s, the codex operated within a unique social context that dictated its subsequent reception history, or what I refer to as the manuscript’s “reproductive afterlife.” Central to this story are the Roman antiquarians who reproduced the Codex Ríos’s images and texts in several printed books and hand-illustrated manuscripts. My Rome Prize allowed me to consult these documents firsthand and paint a more complete picture of how the system of Mesoamerican pictography—writing with images—was (mis)interpreted and translated in early modern Italy.

**The Codex Ríos contains illustrations and descriptions in Nahuatl and Italian of Indigenous cosmology and customs. What do these depictions and translations reveal about the ways Italians understood and reinterpreted Nahua culture?**

What drew me to this subject is a fascination with how people make sense of cultural difference through images and texts. At a very basic level, we do this today (often subconsciously) through comparison and heuristics. The early modern period was no different, particularly when it came to Europeans’ “discovery” of and interactions with communities and materials from the Indigenous Americas. The Codex Ríos’s two new sections—the cosmology and what I call the “proto-ethnography”—represent this confluence of worldviews through a combination of glyphs that are distinctly Indigenous and alphabetic texts that are distinctly European.

For now, I won’t reveal too much of my research on this topic; you can read more in two publications I finished while I was at the Academy. I have a chapter, “Reproducing Mesoamerican Cosmologies and Customs in the Codex Ríos (Codex Vaticanus A),” in a [forthcoming volume with Brill](https://brill.com/edcollbook/title/63230), in addition to several essays I contributed to the catalogue for the exhibition [_Barocco globale: Il mondo a Roma nel secolo di Bernini_,](https://www.electa.it/prodotto/barocco-globale-il-mondo-a-roma-nel-secolo-di-bernini/) which opened at the Scuderie del Quirinale while I was in Rome.

**Where have you conducted research, and what is your most surprising discovery?**

I had a lot of fun (and practiced a lot of patience) hunting down various rare books, manuscripts, and copies of the Codex Ríos during my fellowship. I am thankful for the professional relationships I cultivated over the year, which were key to accessing these precious documents. For example, at AAR’s [Barbara Goldsmith Rare Book Room](https://www.aarome.org/research/special-collections/rare-book-room "Barbara Goldsmith Rare Book Room and Chiaraviglio Rare Book Collection"), [Paolo Imperatori](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/paolo-imperatori "Paolo Imperatori") and [Sebastian Hierl](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/sebastian-hierl "Sebastian Hierl") generously allowed me to regularly consult several editions of Vincenzo Cartari and Lorenzo Pignoria’s mythological treatise _Imagini de gli dei delli antichi_. It was such a privilege to have these books just two flights of stairs away from my office. In Rome, I frequented the Biblioteca Angelica and the Biblioteca Casanatense for manuscripts. I also transcribed inventories and _avvisi_ at the Archivio di Stato and completed secondary research at the Bibliotheca Hertziana. Most importantly, with the help of Dr. Claudia Montuschi at the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, I studied the Codex Ríos with my own eyes on several occasions!

Beyond Rome, I consulted other Mexican manuscripts and related copies and documents at the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana in Venice, the Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, and the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. I cannot possibly pin down the most exciting discovery from my manuscript adventures—each day brought new insights and observations. As an art historian and trained printmaker, I know intuitively that digital reproductions and facsimiles mediate our somatic interactions with objects, obscuring our understanding of their materiality and facture. I suppose, then, I am surprised that before my time at the Academy, I had never fully considered how scale factors into my study of Mexican manuscripts and early modern reproductive technologies. For example, compared to their cognates in the Codex Ríos, the size of the printed images from Cartari and Pignoria and the watercolor images from the Biblioteca Angelica manuscripts tells me so much about the methods Roman antiquarians used to make their copies. One simply cannot make these observations and inferences with digitizations or facsimiles.

**How have your interactions with this year’s Fellows and Residents influenced your work or changed your perspective?**

Every single one of the 2024–25 Fellows, Fellow Travelers, and Residents challenged me to push the theoretical and disciplinary boundaries of my research. On a personal level, I cannot imagine my life without them, and I will always treasure the ten months we shared on the Gianicolo. It sounds cliché, but it’s true! For one year, I lived with and worked alongside passionate writers, visionary artists and musicians, and expert archaeologists, epigraphers, and historians—from PhD students to tenured faculty and Guggenheim and MacArthur Fellows. How did I get so lucky that my new colleagues are now lifelong best friends _and_ my most meticulous copyeditors? (I owe you, [Carol](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/carol-e-harrison "Carol E. Harrison"), [Lily](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/vassiliki-panoussi "Vassiliki Panoussi"), and [Crystal](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/crystal-rosenthal "Crystal Rosenthal")!) When I needed it most, the Academy reminded me that the world is full of brilliant artists and scholars who are also deeply compassionate, sometimes silly, and naturally generous people.

I recently realized why, during the past few years of graduate school, I filled my time with mentoring, teaching, and committee work: I was craving the collaborative spirit that was missing in the solitary thinking that dissertation writing demands. My cohort of Rome Prize Fellows reminded me that art history can and should be a collaborative and interdisciplinary field, one strengthened through diverse perspectives, politics, and specialties.

At AAR, I benefitted much from the Works in Progress roundtables that [Caroline Goodson](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/caroline-goodson "Caroline Goodson") spearheaded. It was refreshing to receive honest and critical feedback on publications and dissertation chapters in a format where hierarchies and power dynamics between dissertators and professors dissolved. Our artists and my fellow “paper person” [Katherine Beaty](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/katherine-l-beaty "Katherine L. Beaty") inspired me to revive my own printmaking practice, which I had neglected while working on my dissertation. Bringing my knowledge of relief and intaglio techniques back into the fold has introduced another dimension to my study of Mexican manuscripts and the art of copying in colonial Latin America.

Many of the most important conversations about the arts and humanities happened over long Saturday morning runs with the unofficial AAR run club I accidentally started in September while training for the Rome Marathon. Running with colleagues from Doria Pamphilj to the Tiber to Villa Ada was an unexpectedly productive space for intellectual and creative exchange. Followed, always, by a cappuccino!

**What is coming up for you in the next few months?**

Since leaving the Academy and returning to the United States, I have relocated to Chicago, where I am currently the Anne Jacobson Shutte Fellow in Early Modern Studies at the [Newberry Library](https://www.newberry.org/). During the 2025–26 academic year, I will hold a Fulbright-Hays DDRA Fellowship at the Instituto de Investigaciones Estéticas at the [Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México](https://www.unam.mx/) (UNAM) in Mexico City.

# Fellows in Focus: Shannah Rose

August 15, 2025

[Shannah Rose](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/shannah-rose "Shannah Rose") is the 2025 Samuel H. Kress Foundation | Marian and Andrew Heiskell Rome Prize Fellow in Renaissance and early modern studies and a PhD candidate in the history of art at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University. She specializes in the visual and material culture of colonial Latin America, early modern Italy, and the Iberian Peninsula. Her dissertation, _The Codex Ríos (Codex Vaticanus A) and the Reception of Mesoamerican Pictography in Early Modern Italy_, focuses on the production and translation of illustrated codices in sixteenth-century Mexico and their reception and reproduction in early modern Italy. Rose earned an MA in the history of art and Latin American studies at Tulane University and a BFA in printmaking and BA in the history of art, both from the University of Virginia.

**Your dissertation focuses on the Codex Ríos and its copies as sites of cultural negotiation and mediation in sixteenth-century Mexico and Italy. What makes this manuscript unique, and why is it central to understanding the reception of Mesoamerican religion and culture in early modern Italy?**

The Codex Ríos (Vat.lat.3738, also known as the Codex Vaticanus A.) is an endlessly fascinating document. Held in the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana since its arrival in Italy in the 1560s, it is the only surviving colonial Mexican pictorial manuscript to feature a comprehensive textual account in Italian of the religion, culture, and customs of the Nahua, commonly referred to as the Aztecs. Nahua _tlahcuilohque_ (painter-scribes) created the manuscript under the behest of Dominican friars in central Mexico (New Spain) in the mid-sixteenth century, and it contains texts and images on 101 folios of imported Fabriano paper. The _tlahcuilohque_ produced the Codex Ríos as an augmented reproduction and translation of an earlier colonial Mexican manuscript, the Codex Telleriano-Remensis, and the scribes intended the Codex Ríos to be a clean copy of its prototype for a non-Indigenous, Italian readership.

In the tradition of other colonial-era Mexican manuscripts, the Codex Ríos comprises multiple sections of images with accompanying textual commentary and glosses. These include the Indigenous _tonalamatl_ (divinatory almanac), _xiuhpohualli_ (solar calendar), and the pictorial year count characteristic of pre-Hispanic Aztec codices. Two new sections are unique to the Codex Ríos as they were not included in the manuscript’s model. One section depicts the cosmological and mythological traditions of ancient Mesoamerica; importantly, this cosmology contains the only known images of the Aztec celestial layers. The second section is a proto-ethnography that details sacrificial and mortuary customs with native figural types. These additions to the Codex Ríos serve as valuable records of the Italian reception of Aztec religion and culture roughly thirty years after the onset of European settler-colonialism in New Spain.

The manuscript’s location in the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana gave it special visibility, particularly among elite circles connected to the Vatican. This tightly knit intellectual circle added another intriguing chapter to the manuscript’s object biography: when it arrived in Italy in the 1560s, the codex operated within a unique social context that dictated its subsequent reception history, or what I refer to as the manuscript’s “reproductive afterlife.” Central to this story are the Roman antiquarians who reproduced the Codex Ríos’s images and texts in several printed books and hand-illustrated manuscripts. My Rome Prize allowed me to consult these documents firsthand and paint a more complete picture of how the system of Mesoamerican pictography—writing with images—was (mis)interpreted and translated in early modern Italy.

**The Codex Ríos contains illustrations and descriptions in Nahuatl and Italian of Indigenous cosmology and customs. What do these depictions and translations reveal about the ways Italians understood and reinterpreted Nahua culture?**

What drew me to this subject is a fascination with how people make sense of cultural difference through images and texts. At a very basic level, we do this today (often subconsciously) through comparison and heuristics. The early modern period was no different, particularly when it came to Europeans’ “discovery” of and interactions with communities and materials from the Indigenous Americas. The Codex Ríos’s two new sections—the cosmology and what I call the “proto-ethnography”—represent this confluence of worldviews through a combination of glyphs that are distinctly Indigenous and alphabetic texts that are distinctly European.

For now, I won’t reveal too much of my research on this topic; you can read more in two publications I finished while I was at the Academy. I have a chapter, “Reproducing Mesoamerican Cosmologies and Customs in the Codex Ríos (Codex Vaticanus A),” in a [forthcoming volume with Brill](https://brill.com/edcollbook/title/63230), in addition to several essays I contributed to the catalogue for the exhibition [_Barocco globale: Il mondo a Roma nel secolo di Bernini_,](https://www.electa.it/prodotto/barocco-globale-il-mondo-a-roma-nel-secolo-di-bernini/) which opened at the Scuderie del Quirinale while I was in Rome.

**Where have you conducted research, and what is your most surprising discovery?**

I had a lot of fun (and practiced a lot of patience) hunting down various rare books, manuscripts, and copies of the Codex Ríos during my fellowship. I am thankful for the professional relationships I cultivated over the year, which were key to accessing these precious documents. For example, at AAR’s [Barbara Goldsmith Rare Book Room](https://www.aarome.org/research/special-collections/rare-book-room "Barbara Goldsmith Rare Book Room and Chiaraviglio Rare Book Collection"), [Paolo Imperatori](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/paolo-imperatori "Paolo Imperatori") and [Sebastian Hierl](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/sebastian-hierl "Sebastian Hierl") generously allowed me to regularly consult several editions of Vincenzo Cartari and Lorenzo Pignoria’s mythological treatise _Imagini de gli dei delli antichi_. It was such a privilege to have these books just two flights of stairs away from my office. In Rome, I frequented the Biblioteca Angelica and the Biblioteca Casanatense for manuscripts. I also transcribed inventories and _avvisi_ at the Archivio di Stato and completed secondary research at the Bibliotheca Hertziana. Most importantly, with the help of Dr. Claudia Montuschi at the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, I studied the Codex Ríos with my own eyes on several occasions!

Beyond Rome, I consulted other Mexican manuscripts and related copies and documents at the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana in Venice, the Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, and the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. I cannot possibly pin down the most exciting discovery from my manuscript adventures—each day brought new insights and observations. As an art historian and trained printmaker, I know intuitively that digital reproductions and facsimiles mediate our somatic interactions with objects, obscuring our understanding of their materiality and facture. I suppose, then, I am surprised that before my time at the Academy, I had never fully considered how scale factors into my study of Mexican manuscripts and early modern reproductive technologies. For example, compared to their cognates in the Codex Ríos, the size of the printed images from Cartari and Pignoria and the watercolor images from the Biblioteca Angelica manuscripts tells me so much about the methods Roman antiquarians used to make their copies. One simply cannot make these observations and inferences with digitizations or facsimiles.

**How have your interactions with this year’s Fellows and Residents influenced your work or changed your perspective?**

Every single one of the 2024–25 Fellows, Fellow Travelers, and Residents challenged me to push the theoretical and disciplinary boundaries of my research. On a personal level, I cannot imagine my life without them, and I will always treasure the ten months we shared on the Gianicolo. It sounds cliché, but it’s true! For one year, I lived with and worked alongside passionate writers, visionary artists and musicians, and expert archaeologists, epigraphers, and historians—from PhD students to tenured faculty and Guggenheim and MacArthur Fellows. How did I get so lucky that my new colleagues are now lifelong best friends _and_ my most meticulous copyeditors? (I owe you, [Carol](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/carol-e-harrison "Carol E. Harrison"), [Lily](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/vassiliki-panoussi "Vassiliki Panoussi"), and [Crystal](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/crystal-rosenthal "Crystal Rosenthal")!) When I needed it most, the Academy reminded me that the world is full of brilliant artists and scholars who are also deeply compassionate, sometimes silly, and naturally generous people.

I recently realized why, during the past few years of graduate school, I filled my time with mentoring, teaching, and committee work: I was craving the collaborative spirit that was missing in the solitary thinking that dissertation writing demands. My cohort of Rome Prize Fellows reminded me that art history can and should be a collaborative and interdisciplinary field, one strengthened through diverse perspectives, politics, and specialties.

At AAR, I benefitted much from the Works in Progress roundtables that [Caroline Goodson](https://www.aarome.org/about/staff/caroline-goodson "Caroline Goodson") spearheaded. It was refreshing to receive honest and critical feedback on publications and dissertation chapters in a format where hierarchies and power dynamics between dissertators and professors dissolved. Our artists and my fellow “paper person” [Katherine Beaty](https://www.aarome.org/people/rome-prize-fellows/katherine-l-beaty "Katherine L. Beaty") inspired me to revive my own printmaking practice, which I had neglected while working on my dissertation. Bringing my knowledge of relief and intaglio techniques back into the fold has introduced another dimension to my study of Mexican manuscripts and the art of copying in colonial Latin America.

Many of the most important conversations about the arts and humanities happened over long Saturday morning runs with the unofficial AAR run club I accidentally started in September while training for the Rome Marathon. Running with colleagues from Doria Pamphilj to the Tiber to Villa Ada was an unexpectedly productive space for intellectual and creative exchange. Followed, always, by a cappuccino!

**What is coming up for you in the next few months?**

Since leaving the Academy and returning to the United States, I have relocated to Chicago, where I am currently the Anne Jacobson Shutte Fellow in Early Modern Studies at the [Newberry Library](https://www.newberry.org/). During the 2025–26 academic year, I will hold a Fulbright-Hays DDRA Fellowship at the Instituto de Investigaciones Estéticas at the [Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México](https://www.unam.mx/) (UNAM) in Mexico City.

# Jacques Barzun Prize in Cultural History

![Image 4: Darrin McMahon](https://www.amphilsoc.org/sites/default/files/styles/full/public/2025-10/2024_11_15_KM0581.jpg?h=b2774bcf&itok=-V0drI0p)

The Jacques Barzun Prize in Cultural History honors Jacques Barzun (November 30, 1907–October 25, 2012), the distinguished historian who helped establish the modern discipline of cultural history. Jacques Barzun was elected a Member of the American Philosophical Society in 1984. The prize was established and funded by Roger Williams, a former student of Professor Barzun. The prize is awarded annually to the author whose book exhibits distinguished work in American or European cultural history. Recipients of the Barzun Prize are awarded a prize of $5000 and a hand-illuminated certificate.

# Prize Guidelines

#### Eligibility

Authors must be citizens or permanent residents of the United States. Books must be written in English, and published in the United States between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2026. Books must be single-authored volumes, not collections of articles or edited texts. The subject must be American or European cultural history.

#### Deadline for submission

Authors and publishers are invited to submit entries for the 2027 prize between September 14, 2026 and January 31, 2027. There is strict a three-book limit per publisher, whether books are submitted by the publisher or directly by an author. If more than three books are submitted by a publisher, all of them will be dropped from consideration.

#### Submission

Send one copy of the book to each member of the prize committee (total of three copies):

American Philosophical Society

Philadelphia, PA 19106

# Jacques Barzun Prize in Cultural History

![Image 4: Darrin McMahon](https://www.amphilsoc.org/sites/default/files/styles/full/public/2025-10/2024_11_15_KM0581.jpg?h=b2774bcf&itok=-V0drI0p)

The Jacques Barzun Prize in Cultural History honors Jacques Barzun (November 30, 1907–October 25, 2012), the distinguished historian who helped establish the modern discipline of cultural history. Jacques Barzun was elected a Member of the American Philosophical Society in 1984. The prize was established and funded by Roger Williams, a former student of Professor Barzun. The prize is awarded annually to the author whose book exhibits distinguished work in American or European cultural history. Recipients of the Barzun Prize are awarded a prize of $5000 and a hand-illuminated certificate.

# Prize Guidelines

#### Eligibility

Authors must be citizens or permanent residents of the United States. Books must be written in English, and published in the United States between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2026. Books must be single-authored volumes, not collections of articles or edited texts. The subject must be American or European cultural history.

#### Deadline for submission

Authors and publishers are invited to submit entries for the 2027 prize between September 14, 2026 and January 31, 2027. There is strict a three-book limit per publisher, whether books are submitted by the publisher or directly by an author. If more than three books are submitted by a publisher, all of them will be dropped from consideration.

#### Submission

Send one copy of the book to each member of the prize committee (total of three copies):

Philadelphia, PA 19106

Norton**, professor and chair of German and Russian Languages and Literatures at the University of Notre Dame, in recognition of his book _Secret Germany: Stefan George and His Circle_, Cornell University Press.This book is a comprehensive and original study of the most influential, perhaps greatest, and in recent times most unappreciated poet of twentieth-century Germany. He "loved art as power," and he aspired indeed to turn poetry into reality in his imagined domain. He was a major presence as an author but even more as an arachnoid "master" and Führer of many poets, philosophers, artists, and historians of the Weimar Republic and, though his hubris kept him from participating in fascist politics before his death in 1933, as a cultural harbinger of the Third Reich.

and to

and to

Morgan**, Professor of History, College of William and Mary, and Editor of _The William and Mary Quarterly_, for _Slave Counterpoint_, University of North Carolina Press.The author combines cultural, social, and economic history to recreate the external and inner life of African American slaves in eighteenth-century America.

The subject is a group of devotional drawings made by a Benedictine nun around 1500 for other members of her community. The author shows what this type of art, often held in low esteem, can tell us about late medieval religious thought and spirituality.

and to

The subject is the international importance of Chicago in the transformation of Western culture at the end of the nineteenth century. The author studies the collision between old world assumptions and new world realities.

She analyzes the social and psychological motives of the collectors, the types of art they favored, and the impact they had on the British art world and British society.

**C. Stephen Jaeger**, Professor of Germanics and Comparative Literature, University of Washington, for _The Envy of Angels: Cathedral Schools and Social Ideals in Medieval Europe, 950-1200_, University of Pennsylvania Press. The author studies the cathedral schools of France and Germany in the tenth and eleventh centuries, both as centers of learning and as conveyors of a new standard of behavior for the aristocracy, before the rise of the universities in the twelfth century.

and to

**James H. Johnson**, Assistant Professor of History, Boston University, for _Listening in Paris_, University of California Press. The author examines the Parisian opera audiences of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, analyzing their reactions to the performances, both in the context of history of music and in that of the history of cultural change.

**1993**  
**Roger Chickering**, Professor of History, Georgetown University, for _Karl Lamprecht: A German Academic Life_, Humanities Press International. This is the first comprehensive intellectual biography of the most controversial historian of imperial Germany. Lamprecht's emphasis on scientific cultural history was long disparaged.

and to

**John O'Malley,** Distinguished Professor of Church History, Weston Jesuit School of Theology, for _The First Jesuits_, Harvard University Press/MIT Press. The author places the Jesuits in the cultural context of the sixteenth century. This new light shows the era in its own perspective and dispels long-held views about the Reformation, the Counter-Reformation, and the Jesuits.

# Jordan Rose![Image 2: rose](https://visarts.ucsd.edu/_images/faculty/rose-big.jpg)

### **Associate Professor**

[jmrose@ucsd.edu](mailto:jmrose@ucsd.edu)

**Biography**

Jordan Rose specializes in 19th- through early 20th-century European Art and is the author of _The Revolution Takes Form: Art and the Barricade in Nineteenth-Century France_ (Penn State University Press, 2024). He is now working on a second book project, provisionally titled _Figure/Ground_,which will examine the multiple, often contradictory ways in which 19th-century painters, sculptors, and printmakers envisioned the conditions of refugeedom and migration. Undergraduate courses he has taught include "Formations of Modern Art," "Art and the Age of Revolutions," "Art and Modernity," "Paris, Capital of the Nineteenth Century," "The Image of Work," and "The Production of Nature." At the graduate level, he has led seminars on Art and Value, Theories of the Comic, Theodor Adorno's _Aesthetic Theory_, Walter Benjamin's _Arcades Project_, Gershom Scholem's Philosophy of History and Language, and Mediation.

Prior to joining the faculty at UCSD, Rose taught at The University of Vermont and UC Berkeley. He received a Ph.D. in History of Art from UC Berkeley; a M.A. in History of Art from University College London; and a B.A. from UC Santa Cruz in History of Art and Visual Culture.

# Jordan Rose![Image 2: rose](https://visarts.ucsd.edu/_images/faculty/rose-big.jpg)

### **Associate Professor**

[jmrose@ucsd.edu](mailto:jmrose@ucsd.edu)

**Biography**

Jordan Rose specializes in 19th- through early 20th-century European Art and is the author of _The Revolution Takes Form: Art and the Barricade in Nineteenth-Century France_ (Penn State University Press, 2024). He is now working on a second book project, provisionally titled _Figure/Ground_,which will examine the multiple, often contradictory ways in which 19th-century painters, sculptors, and printmakers envisioned the conditions of refugeedom and migration. Undergraduate courses he has taught include "Formations of Modern Art," "Art and the Age of Revolutions," "Art and Modernity," "Paris, Capital of the Nineteenth Century," "The Image of Work," and "The Production of Nature." At the graduate level, he has led seminars on Art and Value, Theories of the Comic, Theodor Adorno's _Aesthetic Theory_, Walter Benjamin's _Arcades Project_, Gershom Scholem's Philosophy of History and Language, and Mediation.

Prior to joining the faculty at UCSD, Rose taught at The University of Vermont and UC Berkeley. He received a Ph.D. in History of Art from UC Berkeley; a M.A. in History of Art from University College London; and a B.A. from UC Santa Cruz in History of Art and Visual Culture.
