**Georges Pierre Seurat** ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English"): [/ˈ s ɜːr ɑː,-ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_SUR-ah, -⁠ə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"), [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/s ʊ ˈ r ɑː/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_suu-RAH_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-5)French:[[ʒɔʁʒ pjɛʁ sœʁa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French");[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-6) 2 December 1859 – 29 March 1891) was a French [post-Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionist "Post-Impressionist") artist. He devised the painting techniques known as [chromoluminarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromoluminarism "Chromoluminarism") and [pointillism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism "Pointillism") and used [conté crayon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cont%C3%A9_crayon "Conté crayon") for drawings on paper with a rough surface.

Seurat's artistic personality combined qualities that are usually thought of as opposed and incompatible: on the one hand, his extreme and delicate sensibility, on the other, a passion for logical abstraction and an almost mathematical precision of mind.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-7) His large-scale work _[A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Sunday\_Afternoon\_on\_the\_Island\_of\_La\_Grande\_Jatte "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte")_ (1884–1886) altered the direction of [modern art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art "Modern art") by initiating [Neo-Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Impressionism "Neo-Impressionism"), and is one of the icons of [late 19th-century painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_painting "History of painting").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-8)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Georges_Seurat%2C_1889-90%2C_Le_Chahut%2C_Kr%C3%B6ller-M%C3%BCller_Museum.jpg/250px-Georges_Seurat%2C_1889-90%2C_Le_Chahut%2C_Kr%C3%B6ller-M%C3%BCller_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Seurat,_1889-90,_Le_Chahut,_Kr%C3%B6ller-M%C3%BCller_Museum.jpg)

Georges Seurat, 1889–90, _[Le Chahut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Chahut "Le Chahut")_, oil on canvas, 170 x 141 cm, [Kröller-Müller Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kr%C3%B6ller-M%C3%BCller_Museum "Kröller-Müller Museum"), Otterlo

### Family and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Family and education")]

Seurat was born on 2 December 1859 in Paris, at 60 rue de Bondy (now rue René Boulanger). The Seurat family moved to 136 boulevard de Magenta (now 110 boulevard de Magenta) in 1862 or 1863.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmmbio-9) His father, Antoine Chrysostome Seurat, originally from [Champagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne,_France "Champagne, France"), was a former legal official who had become wealthy from speculating in property, and his mother, Ernestine Faivre, was from Paris.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%931891199111-10) Georges had a brother, Émile Augustin, and a sister, Marie-Berthe, both older. His father lived in [Le Raincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Raincy "Le Raincy") and visited his wife and children once a week at boulevard de Magenta.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Seurat:_p._17-11)

Georges Seurat first studied art at the École Municipale de Sculpture et Dessin, near his family's home in the boulevard Magenta, which was run by the sculptor Justin Lequien.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-techbull-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%931891199112-13) In 1878, he moved on to the [École des Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_des_Beaux-Arts "École des Beaux-Arts") where he was taught by [Henri Lehmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Lehmann "Henri Lehmann"), and followed a conventional academic training, drawing from casts of antique sculpture and copying drawings by old masters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-techbull-12) Seurat's studies resulted in a well-considered and fertile theory of contrasts: a theory to which all his work was thereafter subjected.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-14) His formal artistic education came to an end in November 1879, when he left the École des Beaux-Arts for a year of military service.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%931891199112-13)

After a year of infantry training with the 19th Line Regiment, stationed at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"), north-western France,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991400-16) he returned to Paris where he shared a studio with his friend [Aman-Jean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Aman-Jean "Edmond Aman-Jean"), while also renting a small apartment at 16 rue de Chabrol.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%931891199111-10) For the next two years, he worked at mastering the art of monochrome drawing. His first exhibited work, shown at the [Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_de_Paris "Salon de Paris"), of 1883, was a Conté crayon drawing of Aman-Jean.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%931891199148-17) He also studied the works of [Eugène Delacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix "Eugène Delacroix") carefully, making notes on his use of color.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-techbull-12)

### _Bathers at Asnières_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Bathers at Asnières")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Baigneurs_a_Asnieres.jpg/330px-Baigneurs_a_Asnieres.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baigneurs_a_Asnieres.jpg)

_[Bathers at Asnières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathers\_at\_Asni%C3%A8res "Bathers at Asnières")_, 1884, oil on canvas, 201 × 301 cm, [National Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery "National Gallery"), London

He spent 1883 working on his first major painting–a large canvas titled _[Bathers at Asnières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathers\_at\_Asni%C3%A8res "Bathers at Asnières")_,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991148-18) a monumental work showing young men relaxing by the Seine in a working-class suburb of Paris.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991150-19) Although influenced in its use of color and light tone by Impressionism, the painting with its smooth, simplified textures and carefully outlined, rather sculptural figures, shows the continuing impact of his neoclassical training; the critic [Paul Alexis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Alexis "Paul Alexis") described it as a "faux [Puvis de Chavannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puvis_de_Chavannes "Puvis de Chavannes")".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991147%E2%80%9348-20) Seurat also departed from the Impressionist ideal by preparing for the work with a number of drawings and oil sketches before starting on the canvas in his studio.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991147%E2%80%9348-20)

_Bathers at Asnières_ was rejected by the Paris Salon, and instead he showed it at the Groupe des Artistes Indépendants in May 1884. Soon, however, disillusioned by the poor organization of the Indépendants, Seurat and some other artists he had met through the group – including [Charles Angrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Angrand "Charles Angrand"), [Henri-Edmond Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross"), [Albert Dubois-Pillet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Dubois-Pillet "Albert Dubois-Pillet") and [Paul Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac") – set up a new organization, the [Société des Artistes Indépendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_des_Artistes_Ind%C3%A9pendants "Société des Artistes Indépendants").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991148-18) Seurat's new ideas on [pointillism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointillism "Pointillism") were to have an especially strong influence on Signac, who subsequently painted in the same idiom.

### _A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/A_Sunday_on_La_Grande_Jatte%2C_Georges_Seurat%2C_1884.png/330px-A_Sunday_on_La_Grande_Jatte%2C_Georges_Seurat%2C_1884.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Sunday_on_La_Grande_Jatte,_Georges_Seurat,_1884.png)

_[A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Sunday\_Afternoon\_on\_the\_Island\_of\_La\_Grande\_Jatte "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte")_, 1884–1886, oil on canvas, 207.5 × 308.1 cm, [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago")

In summer 1884, Seurat began work on _[A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Sunday\_Afternoon\_on\_the\_Island\_of\_La\_Grande\_Jatte "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte")_.

The painting shows members of each of the social classes participating in various park activities. The tiny juxtaposed dots of multi-colored paint allow the viewer's eye to blend colors optically, rather than having the colors physically blended on the canvas. It took Seurat two years to complete this 10-foot-wide (3.0 m) painting, much of which he spent in the park sketching in preparation for the work. There are about 60 studies for the large painting, including a smaller version, _Study for A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte_ (1884–1885), which is now in the collection of The [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago"). The full work is also part of the permanent collection of the Art Institute of Chicago.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-21)

The painting was the inspiration for [James Lapine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lapine "James Lapine") and [Stephen Sondheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Sondheim "Stephen Sondheim")'s musical _[Sunday in the Park with George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_in\_the\_Park\_with\_George "Sunday in the Park with George")_[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-24) and played a significant symbolic role in [John Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hughes_(filmmaker) "John Hughes (filmmaker)")' _[Ferris Bueller's Day Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferris\_Bueller's\_Day\_Off "Ferris Bueller's Day Off")_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-25)

### Later career and personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later career and personal life")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Georges_Seurat%2C_1889-90%2C_Jeune_femme_se_poudrant_%28Young_Woman_Powdering_Herself%29%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_95.5_x_79.5_cm%2C_Courtauld_Institute_of_Art.jpg/250px-Georges_Seurat%2C_1889-90%2C_Jeune_femme_se_poudrant_%28Young_Woman_Powdering_Herself%29%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_95.5_x_79.5_cm%2C_Courtauld_Institute_of_Art.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Seurat,_1889-90,_Jeune_femme_se_poudrant_(Young_Woman_Powdering_Herself),_oil_on_canvas,_95.5_x_79.5_cm,_Courtauld_Institute_of_Art.jpg)

_[Jeune femme se poudrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Woman\_Powdering\_Herself\_(Seurat) "Young Woman Powdering Herself (Seurat)")_ (_Young Woman Powdering Herself_), 1888–1890, oil on canvas, 95.5 x 79.5 cm, [Courtauld Institute of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtauld_Institute_of_Art "Courtauld Institute of Art")

Seurat concealed his relationship with Madeleine Knobloch (or Madeleine Knoblock, 1868–1903), an artist's model whom he portrayed in his painting _[Jeune femme se poudrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Woman\_Powdering\_Herself\_(Seurat) "Young Woman Powdering Herself (Seurat)")_. In 1889, she moved in with Seurat in his studio on the seventh floor of 128 bis [Boulevard de Clichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulevard_de_Clichy "Boulevard de Clichy").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmm1822-26)

When Madeleine became pregnant, the couple moved to a studio at 39 passage de l'Élysée-des-Beaux-Arts (now rue André Antoine). There she gave birth to their son, who was named Pierre-Georges, on 16 February 1890.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmm1822-26)

Seurat spent the summer of 1890 on the coast at [Gravelines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravelines "Gravelines"), where he painted four canvases including _[The Channel of Gravelines, Petit Fort Philippe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Channel\_of\_Gravelines,\_Petit\_Fort\_Philippe "The Channel of Gravelines, Petit Fort Philippe")_, as well as eight oil panels, and made a few drawings.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorges_Seurat,_1859%E2%80%9318911991360-27)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

Seurat died in Paris in his parents' home on 29 March 1891 at the age of 31.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmmbio-9) The cause of his death is uncertain, and has been variously attributed to a form of [meningitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meningitis "Meningitis"), [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia"), infectious angina, and [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria"). His son died two weeks later from the same disease.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-28) His last ambitious work, _[The Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Circus\_(Seurat\_painting) "The Circus (Seurat painting)")_, was left unfinished at the time of his death.

On 30 March 1891 a funeral Mass was held in the [Church of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Vincent-de-Paul,_Paris "Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, Paris").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmmbio-9) Seurat was interred 31 March 1891 at [Cimetière du Père-Lachaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimeti%C3%A8re_du_P%C3%A8re-Lachaise "Cimetière du Père-Lachaise").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Seurat:_p._17-11)

At the time of Seurat's death, Madeleine was pregnant with a second child who died during or shortly after birth.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-29)

## Colour theory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Colour theory")]

### Contemporary ideas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Contemporary ideas")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg/250px-Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seurat-La_Parade_detail.jpg)

Detail from _[Circus Sideshow (Parade de Cirque)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade\_de\_cirque "Parade de cirque")_ (1889) showing pointillism and color theory

During the 19th century, scientist-writers such as [Michel Eugène Chevreul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Eug%C3%A8ne_Chevreul "Michel Eugène Chevreul"), [Ogden Rood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden_Rood "Ogden Rood") and David Sutter wrote treatises on colour, [optical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical "Optical") effects and [perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perception "Perception"). They adapted the scientific research of [Hermann von Helmholtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_von_Helmholtz "Hermann von Helmholtz") and [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton") into a form accessible to laypeople.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30) Artists followed new discoveries in perception with great interest.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

Chevreul was perhaps the most important influence on artists at the time; his great contribution was producing a colour wheel of primary and intermediary hues. Chevreul was a French [chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist "Chemist") who restored [tapestries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapestries "Tapestries"). During his restorations he noticed that the only way to restore a section properly was to take into account the influence of the colours around the missing [wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool "Wool"); he could not produce the right hue unless he recognized the surrounding [dyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dye "Dye"). Chevreul discovered that two colours juxtaposed, slightly overlapping or very close together, would have the effect of another colour when seen from a distance. The discovery of this phenomenon became the basis for the pointillist technique of the Neo-Impressionist painters.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

Chevreul also realized that the "halo" that one sees after looking at a colour is the opposing colour (also known as [complementary color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complementary_color "Complementary color")). For example: After looking at a red object, one may see a cyan echo/halo of the original object. This complementary colour (as an example, cyan for red) is due to [retinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina "Retina") persistence. Neo-Impressionist painters interested in the interplay of colours made extensive use of complementary colors in their paintings. In his works, Chevreul advised artists to think and paint not just the colour of the central object, but to add colours and make appropriate adjustments to achieve a harmony among colours. It seems that the harmony Chevreul wrote about is what Seurat came to call "emotion".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

It is not clear whether Seurat read all of Chevreul's book on colour contrast, published in 1859, but he did copy out several paragraphs from the chapter on painting, and he had read [Charles Blanc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Blanc "Charles Blanc")'s _Grammaire des arts du dessin_ (1867),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-techbull-12) which cites Chevreul's work. Blanc's book was directed at artists and art connoisseurs. Because of colour's emotional significance to him, he made explicit recommendations that were close to the theories later adopted by the Neo-Impressionists. He said that colour should not be based on the "judgment of taste", but rather it should be close to what we experience in reality. Blanc did not want artists to use equal intensities of colour, but to consciously plan and understand the role of each hue in creating a whole.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

While Chevreul based his theories on Newton's thoughts on the mixing of light, Ogden Rood based his writings on the work of Helmholtz. He analyzed the effects of mixing and juxtaposing material pigments. Rood valued as [primary colors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_colors "Primary colors") red, green and blue-violet. Like Chevreul, he said that if two colours are placed next to each other, from a distance they look like a third distinctive colour. He also pointed out that the juxtaposition of primary hues next to each other would create a far more intense and pleasing colour, when perceived by the eye and mind, than the corresponding color made simply by mixing paint. Rood advised artists to be aware of the difference between additive and subtractive qualities of colour, since material pigments and optical pigments (light) do not mix in the same way:

*   Material pigments: Red + Yellow + Blue = Black ([Magenta, Yellow and Cyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMY_color_model "CMY color model") give a true black when mixed; Red, Yellow and Blue generally do not)
*   Optical / Light: Red + Green + Blue = White

Seurat was also influenced by Sutter's _Phenomena of Vision_ (1880), in which he wrote that "the laws of harmony can be learned as one learns the laws of harmony and music".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-31) He heard lectures in the 1880s by the mathematician [Charles Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Henry_(librarian) "Charles Henry (librarian)") at the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris"), who discussed the [emotional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion "Emotion") properties and symbolic meaning of lines and colour. There remains controversy over the extent to which Henry's ideas were adopted by Seurat.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

### Language of colour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Language of colour")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Georges_Seurat_019.jpg/250px-Georges_Seurat_019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Seurat_019.jpg)

_[The Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Circus\_(Seurat\_painting) "The Circus (Seurat painting)")_, 1891, [Musée d'Orsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_d'Orsay "Musée d'Orsay"), Paris

Seurat took to heart the colour theorists' notion of a scientific approach to painting. He believed that a painter could use colour to create harmony and emotion in art in the same way that a musician uses [counterpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpoint "Counterpoint") and variation to create harmony in music. He theorized that the scientific application of colour was like any other natural law, and he was driven to prove this conjecture. He thought that the knowledge of perception and optical laws could be used to create a new language of art based on its own set of [heuristics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heuristic "Heuristic") and he set out to show this language using lines, colour intensity and colour schema. Seurat called this language [Chromoluminarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromoluminarism "Chromoluminarism").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

In a letter to the writer Maurice Beaubourg in 1890 he wrote: "Art is Harmony. Harmony is the analogy of the contrary and of similar elements of tone, of colour and of line. In tone, lighter against darker. In colour, the complementary, red-green, orange-blue, yellow-violet. In line, those that form a right-angle. The frame is in a harmony that opposes those of the tones, colours and lines of the picture, these aspects are considered according to their dominance and under the influence of light, in gay, calm or sad combinations".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-33)

Seurat's theories can be summarized as follows: The emotion of gaiety can be achieved by the domination of luminous hues, by the predominance of warm colours, and by the use of lines directed upward. Calm is achieved through an equivalence/balance of the use of the light and the dark, by the balance of warm and cold colours, and by lines that are horizontal. Sadness is achieved by using dark and cold colours and by lines pointing downward.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

## Influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Influence")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Georges_Seurat_066.jpg/330px-Georges_Seurat_066.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Seurat_066.jpg)

_[Circus Sideshow (Parade de Cirque)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade\_de\_cirque "Parade de cirque")_, 1887–88, [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), New York

Where the dialectic nature of [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne")'s work had been greatly influential during the highly expressionistic phase of [proto-Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Cubism "Proto-Cubism"), between 1908 and 1910, the work of Seurat, with its flatter, more linear structures, would capture the attention of the [Cubists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubists "Cubists") from 1911.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Mittelmann-34) Seurat in his few years of activity, was able, with his observations on irradiation and the effects of contrast, to create afresh without any guiding tradition, to complete an esthetic system with a new technical method perfectly adapted to its expression.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-35)

"With the advent of monochromatic Cubism in 1910–1911," writes art historian Robert Herbert, "questions of form displaced color in the artists' attention, and for these Seurat was more relevant. Thanks to several exhibitions, his paintings and drawings were easily seen in Paris, and reproductions of his major compositions circulated widely among the Cubists. _[The Chahut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Chahut "Le Chahut")_ [Rijksmuseum Kröller-Müller, Otterlo] was called by André Salmon 'one of the great icons of the new devotion', and both it and the _[Cirque (Circus)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Circus\_(Seurat\_painting) "The Circus (Seurat painting)")_, Musée d'Orsay, Paris, according to [Guillaume Apollinaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Apollinaire "Guillaume Apollinaire"), 'almost belong to Synthetic Cubism'."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Robert_Herbert-30)

The concept was well established among the French artists that painting could be expressed mathematically, in terms of both color and form; and this mathematical expression resulted in an independent and compelling "objective truth", perhaps more so than the objective truth of the object represented.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Mittelmann-34)

Indeed, the Neo-Impressionists had succeeded in establishing an objective scientific basis in the domain of color (Seurat addresses both problems in _Circus_ and _Dancers_). Soon, the Cubists were to do so in both the domain of form and dynamics; [Orphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orphism_(art) "Orphism (art)") would do so with color too.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-Mittelmann-34)

On 2 December 2021, Google honored Seurat with a [Google Doodle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Doodle "Google Doodle") on his 162nd birthday.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-GoogleDoodle-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-38)

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Georges_Seurat&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Portrait_d%27Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_Seurat.jpg/250px-Portrait_d%27Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_Seurat.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_d'Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_Seurat.jpg)

Portrait of [Edmond Aman-Jean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Aman-Jean "Edmond Aman-Jean"), shown at the 1883 Salon

From 1883 until his death, Seurat exhibited his work at the [Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_(Paris) "Salon (Paris)"), the [Salon des Indépendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_des_Ind%C3%A9pendants "Salon des Indépendants"), [Les XX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_XX "Les XX") in Brussels, the eighth Impressionist exhibition, and other exhibitions in France and abroad.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-kmmexh-39)

*   Salon, Paris, 1 May–20 June 1883  
The Salon showed Seurat's drawing of [Edmond Aman-Jean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Aman-Jean "Edmond Aman-Jean").
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 15 May–30 June 1884  
Seurat showed _[Une Baignade, Asnières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Une\_Baignade,\_Asni%C3%A8res "Une Baignade, Asnières")_, after the official Salon had rejected it. Seurat's debut as a painter.
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 10 December 1884 – 17 January 1885
*   _Works in Oil and Pastel by the Impressionists of Paris_, [American Art Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Art_Association "American Art Association"), New York, April and May 1886.  
Organised by [Paul Durand-Ruel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Durand-Ruel "Paul Durand-Ruel").
*   Impressionist exhibition, Paris, 15 May–15 June 1886  
_[Un dimanche après-midi à l'Île de la Grande Jatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un\_dimanche\_apr%C3%A8s-midi\_%C3%A0\_l'%C3%8Ele\_de\_la\_Grande\_Jatte "Un dimanche après-midi à l'Île de la Grande Jatte")_ shown for the first time.
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 21 August–21 September 1886
*   _Les impressionnistes_, Palais du Cours Saint-André, Nantes, 10 October 1886 – 15 January 1887
*   Galerie Martinet, Paris, December 1886 – January 1887
*   Les XX, Brussels, February 1887
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 26 March–3 May 1887
*   [Théâtre Libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Libre "Théâtre Libre"), Paris, November 1887 – January 1888  
Works by Seurat, Signac and van Gogh.
*   _Exposition de Janvier_, La Revue indépendante, Paris, January 1888
*   _Exposition de Février_, La Revue indépendante, Paris, February 1888
*   Hôtel Drouot, Paris, 1–3 March 1888 (sales exhibition)
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 22 March–3 May 1888
*   Tweede Jaarlijksche Tentoonstelling der Nederlandsche Etsclub, [Arti et Amicitiae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arti_et_Amicitiae "Arti et Amicitiae"), Amsterdam, June 1888  
Drawing _Au café concert_, lent by [Theo van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_van_Gogh_(art_dealer) "Theo van Gogh (art dealer)").
*   Les XX, Brussels, February 1889
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 3 September–4 October 1889
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 20 March–27 April 1890  
Showed _Le Chahut_, _Jeune femme se poudrant_ and 9 other works.
*   Les XX, Brussels, 7 February–8 March 1891  
Showed _Le Chahut_ and 6 other paintings.
*   Salon des Indépendants, Paris, 20 March–27 April 1891  
Showed _Le Cirque_ and four paintings from Gravelines.

Posthumous exhibitions:

*   Solomon R. Guggenheim Collection of Non-Objective Paintings, South Carolina, 1938, Gibbes Memorial Art Gallery[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-40)
*   _Seurat’s Circus Sideshow_, 2017, Metropolitan Museum of Art[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-41)
*   _Seurat and the Sea_, 2026, Courtauld Gallery[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat#cite_note-42)

# Actor Ed Asner, TV’s blustery Lou Grant, dies at 91

[](mailto:?subject=Actor%20Ed%20Asner,%20TV%E2%80%99s%20blustery%20Lou%20Grant,%20dies%20at%2091&body=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.threads.com/intent/post?url=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)

By MARCELA ISAZA (Associated Press)

LOS ANGELES Aug. 29, 2021 6:35 p.m.

## Actor Ed Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died

![Image 3: FILE - In this Feb. 8, 2016 file photo, actor Ed Asner arrives at the 15th Annual Movies for Grownups Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died. He was 91. Asner's representative confirmed the death in an email Sunday, Aug. 29, 2021, to The Associated Press.](https://cloudfront-us-east-1.images.arcpublishing.com/opb/MH64B7EAMBGVJJVTPA6VCXAGGY.jpg)

FILE - In this Feb. 8, 2016 file photo, actor Ed Asner arrives at the 15th Annual Movies for Grownups Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died. He was 91. Asner's representative confirmed the death in an email Sunday, Aug. 29, 2021, to The Associated Press.

_Rich Fury / AP_

Ed Asner, the burly and prolific character actor who became a star in middle age as the gruff but lovable newsman Lou Grant, first in the hit comedy “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and later in the drama “Lou Grant,” died Sunday. He was 91.

THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:

[Become a Sponsor](https://www.opb.org/sponsorship/)

Asner's representative confirmed the actor's death in an email to The Associated Press. Asner's official [Twitter account included a note](https://twitter.com/theonlyedasner/status/1432034864384000007?s=21) from his children: "We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head- Goodnight dad. We love you."

Built like the football lineman he once was, the balding Asner was a journeyman actor in films and TV when he was hired in 1970 to play Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show.” For seven seasons he was the rumpled boss to Moore’s ebullient Mary Richards (He called her “Mary,” she called him “Mr. Grant”) at the fictional Minneapolis TV newsroom where both worked. Later, he would play the role for five years on “Lou Grant.”

The part brought Asner three best supporting actor Emmys on “Mary Tyler Moore” and two best actor awards on “Lou Grant.” He also won Emmys for his roles in the miniseries “Rich Man, Poor Man” (1975-1976) and “Roots” (1976-1977).

He had more than 300 acting credits and remained active throughout his 70s and 80s in a variety of film and TV roles. In 2003, he played Santa Claus in Will Ferrell’s hit film “Elf.” He was John Goodman’s father in the short-lived 2004 CBS comedy “Center of the Universe” and the voice of the elderly hero in the hit 2009 Pixar release, “Up.” More recently, he was in such TV series as “Forgive Me” and “Dead to Me.”

Nonetheless, Asner told The Associated Press in 2009 that interesting roles were hard to come by.

“I never get enough work,” he said. “It’s the history of my career. There just isn’t anything to turn down, let me put it that way.”

“I’d say most people are probably in that same boat, old people, and it’s a shame,” he said.

As Screen Actors Guild president, the liberal Asner was caught up in a political controversy in 1982 when he spoke out against U.S. involvement with repressive governments in Latin America. “Lou Grant” was canceled during the furor that followed and he did not run for a third SAG term in 1985.

Asner discussed his politicization in a 2002 interview, noting he had begun his career during the McCarthy era and for years had been afraid to speak out for fear of being blacklisted.

Then he saw a nun’s film depicting the cruelties inflicted by El Salvador’s government on that country’s citizens.

“I stepped out to complain about our country’s constant arming and fortifying of the military in El Salvador, who were oppressing their people,” he said.

Former SAG President Charlton Heston and others accused him of making un-American statements and of misusing his position as head of their actors union.

“We even had bomb threats at the time. I had armed guards,” Asner recalled.

The actor blamed the controversy for ending the five-year run of “Lou Grant," although CBS insisted declining ratings were the reason the show was canceled.

Asner’s character had caught on from the first episode of “Mary Tyler Moore,” when he told Mary in their initial meeting, “You’ve got spunk. ... I hate spunk!” The inspired cast included Ted Knight as Ted Baxter, the dimwitted news anchor; Gavin MacLeod as Murray Slaughter, the sarcastic news writer; and Betty White as the manipulative, sex-obsessed home show hostess Sue Ann Nivens. Valerie Harper and Cloris Leachman, playing Mary’s neighbors, both saw their characters spun off into their own shows.

“Mary Tyler Moore” was still a hit when the star decided to pursue other interests, and so it was brought to an end in the seventh season with a hilarious finale in which all of the principals were fired except for the bumbling Baxter.

Asner went immediately into “Lou Grant,” his character moving from Minneapolis to Los Angeles to become city editor of the Tribune, a crusading newspaper under the firm hand of Publisher Margaret Pynchon, memorably played by Nancy Marchand.

Although the show had its light moments, its scripts touched on a variety of darker social issues that most series wouldn’t touch at the time, including alcoholism and homelessness. Asner remained politically active for the rest of his life and in 2017 published the book “The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs.”

Asner, born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1929, almost became a newsman in real life. He studied journalism at the University of Chicago until a professor told him there was little money to be made in the profession.

He quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred Thomas Becket in a campus production of T.S. Eliot’s “Murder in the Cathedral.”

He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver and other jobs before being drafted in 1951. He served with the Army Signal Corps in France.

Returning to Chicago after military service, he appeared at the Playwrights Theatre Club and Second City, the famed satire troupe that launched the careers of dozens of top comedians.

Later, in New York, he joined the long-running “The Threepenny Opera” and appeared opposite Jack Lemmon in “Face of a Hero.”

Arriving in Hollywood in 1961 for an episode of television’s “Naked City,” Asner decided to stay and appeared in numerous movies and TV shows, including the film “El Dorado,” opposite John Wayne; and the Elvis Presley vehicles “Kid Galahad” and “Change of Habit.” He was a regular in the 1960s political drama series “Slattery’s People.”

He was married twice, to Nancy Lou Sykes and Cindy Gilmore, and had four children, Matthew, Liza, Kate and Charles.

# Actor Ed Asner, TV’s blustery Lou Grant, dies at 91

[](mailto:?subject=Actor%20Ed%20Asner,%20TV%E2%80%99s%20blustery%20Lou%20Grant,%20dies%20at%2091&body=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)[](https://www.threads.com/intent/post?url=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/08/29/actor-ed-asner-tv-s-blustery-lou-grant-dies-at-91/)

By MARCELA ISAZA (Associated Press)

LOS ANGELES Aug. 29, 2021 6:35 p.m.

## Actor Ed Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died

![Image 3: FILE - In this Feb. 8, 2016 file photo, actor Ed Asner arrives at the 15th Annual Movies for Grownups Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died. He was 91. Asner's representative confirmed the death in an email Sunday, Aug. 29, 2021, to The Associated Press.](https://cloudfront-us-east-1.images.arcpublishing.com/opb/MH64B7EAMBGVJJVTPA6VCXAGGY.jpg)

FILE - In this Feb. 8, 2016 file photo, actor Ed Asner arrives at the 15th Annual Movies for Grownups Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, has died. He was 91. Asner's representative confirmed the death in an email Sunday, Aug. 29, 2021, to The Associated Press.

_Rich Fury / AP_

Ed Asner, the burly and prolific character actor who became a star in middle age as the gruff but lovable newsman Lou Grant, first in the hit comedy “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and later in the drama “Lou Grant,” died Sunday. He was 91.

THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:

[Become a Sponsor](https://www.opb.org/sponsorship/)

Asner's representative confirmed the actor's death in an email to The Associated Press. Asner's official [Twitter account included a note](https://twitter.com/theonlyedasner/status/1432034864384000007?s=21) from his children: "We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head- Goodnight dad. We love you."

Built like the football lineman he once was, the balding Asner was a journeyman actor in films and TV when he was hired in 1970 to play Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show.” For seven seasons he was the rumpled boss to Moore’s ebullient Mary Richards (He called her “Mary,” she called him “Mr. Grant”) at the fictional Minneapolis TV newsroom where both worked. Later, he would play the role for five years on “Lou Grant.”

The part brought Asner three best supporting actor Emmys on “Mary Tyler Moore” and two best actor awards on “Lou Grant.” He also won Emmys for his roles in the miniseries “Rich Man, Poor Man” (1975-1976) and “Roots” (1976-1977).

He had more than 300 acting credits and remained active throughout his 70s and 80s in a variety of film and TV roles. In 2003, he played Santa Claus in Will Ferrell’s hit film “Elf.” He was John Goodman’s father in the short-lived 2004 CBS comedy “Center of the Universe” and the voice of the elderly hero in the hit 2009 Pixar release, “Up.” More recently, he was in such TV series as “Forgive Me” and “Dead to Me.”

Nonetheless, Asner told The Associated Press in 2009 that interesting roles were hard to come by.

“I never get enough work,” he said. “It’s the history of my career. There just isn’t anything to turn down, let me put it that way.”

“I’d say most people are probably in that same boat, old people, and it’s a shame,” he said.

As Screen Actors Guild president, the liberal Asner was caught up in a political controversy in 1982 when he spoke out against U.S. involvement with repressive governments in Latin America. “Lou Grant” was canceled during the furor that followed and he did not run for a third SAG term in 1985.

Asner discussed his politicization in a 2002 interview, noting he had begun his career during the McCarthy era and for years had been afraid to speak out for fear of being blacklisted.

Then he saw a nun’s film depicting the cruelties inflicted by El Salvador’s government on that country’s citizens.

“I stepped out to complain about our country’s constant arming and fortifying of the military in El Salvador, who were oppressing their people,” he said.

THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:

[Become a Sponsor](https://www.opb.org/sponsorship/)

Former SAG President Charlton Heston and others accused him of making un-American statements and of misusing his position as head of their actors union.

“We even had bomb threats at the time. I had armed guards,” Asner recalled.

The actor blamed the controversy for ending the five-year run of “Lou Grant," although CBS insisted declining ratings were the reason the show was canceled.

Asner’s character had caught on from the first episode of “Mary Tyler Moore,” when he told Mary in their initial meeting, “You’ve got spunk. ... I hate spunk!” The inspired cast included Ted Knight as Ted Baxter, the dimwitted news anchor; Gavin MacLeod as Murray Slaughter, the sarcastic news writer; and Betty White as the manipulative, sex-obsessed home show hostess Sue Ann Nivens. Valerie Harper and Cloris Leachman, playing Mary’s neighbors, both saw their characters spun off into their own shows.

“Mary Tyler Moore” was still a hit when the star decided to pursue other interests, and so it was brought to an end in the seventh season with a hilarious finale in which all of the principals were fired except for the bumbling Baxter.

Asner went immediately into “Lou Grant,” his character moving from Minneapolis to Los Angeles to become city editor of the Tribune, a crusading newspaper under the firm hand of Publisher Margaret Pynchon, memorably played by Nancy Marchand.

Although the show had its light moments, its scripts touched on a variety of darker social issues that most series wouldn’t touch at the time, including alcoholism and homelessness. Asner remained politically active for the rest of his life and in 2017 published the book “The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs.”

Asner, born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1929, almost became a newsman in real life. He studied journalism at the University of Chicago until a professor told him there was little money to be made in the profession.

He quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred Thomas Becket in a campus production of T.S. Eliot’s “Murder in the Cathedral.”

He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver and other jobs before being drafted in 1951. He served with the Army Signal Corps in France.

Returning to Chicago after military service, he appeared at the Playwrights Theatre Club and Second City, the famed satire troupe that launched the careers of dozens of top comedians.

Later, in New York, he joined the long-running “The Threepenny Opera” and appeared opposite Jack Lemmon in “Face of a Hero.”

Arriving in Hollywood in 1961 for an episode of television’s “Naked City,” Asner decided to stay and appeared in numerous movies and TV shows, including the film “El Dorado,” opposite John Wayne; and the Elvis Presley vehicles “Kid Galahad” and “Change of Habit.” He was a regular in the 1960s political drama series “Slattery’s People.”

He was married twice, to Nancy Lou Sykes and Cindy Gilmore, and had four children, Matthew, Liza, Kate and Charles.

___

Late Associated Press writer Bob Thomas contributed biographical information to this report.

# Actor Ed Asner, TV's blustery Lou Grant, dies at 91

[](https://artscanvas.org/)[Arts](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts) Aug 29, 2021 3:26 PM EDT 

LOS ANGELES — Ed Asner, the burly and prolific character actor who became a star in middle age as the gruff but lovable newsman Lou Grant, first in the hit comedy "The Mary Tyler Moore Show" and later in the drama "Lou Grant," died Sunday. He was 91.

Asner's representative confirmed the actor's death in an email to The Associated Press. Asner's official[Twitter account included a note](https://twitter.com/theonlyedasner/status/1432034864384000007?s=21)from his children: "We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head- Goodnight dad. We love you."

Built like the football lineman he once was, the balding Asner was a journeyman actor in films and TV when he was hired in 1970 to play Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." For seven seasons he was the rumpled boss to Moore's ebullient Mary Richards (He called her "Mary," she called him "Mr. Grant") at the fictional Minneapolis TV newsroom where both worked. Later, he would play the role for five years on "Lou Grant."

Asner's character had caught on from the first episode of "Mary Tyler Moore," when he told Mary in their initial meeting, "You've got spunk. ... I hate spunk!" The inspired cast included Ted Knight as Ted Baxter, the dimwitted news anchor; Gavin MacLeod as Murray Slaughter, the sarcastic news writer; and Betty White as the manipulative, sex-obsessed home show hostess Sue Ann Nivens. Valerie Harper and Cloris Leachman, playing Mary's neighbors, both saw their characters spun off into their own shows.

Asner is the third "Mary Tyler Moore" alum to die in recent months.[Leachman died in January](https://apnews.com/article/cloris-leachman-dead-7b9eb2aa8de5a62e8502ca94cff89e83)and[MacLeod died in May.](https://apnews.com/article/gavin-macleod-entertainment-arts-and-entertainment-6313dfd801244eeeea2be2ddeac1cdbb)

The 99-year-old White is the lone surviving main cast member from "Mary Tyler Moore."

"Mary Tyler Moore" was still a hit when the star decided to pursue other interests, and so it was brought to an end in the seventh season with a hilarious finale in which all of the principals were fired except for the bumbling Baxter.

Asner went immediately into "Lou Grant," his character moving from Minneapolis to Los Angeles to become city editor of the Tribune, a crusading newspaper under the firm hand of Publisher Margaret Pynchon, memorably played by Nancy Marchand.

Asner won three best supporting actor Emmys on "Mary Tyler Moore" and two best actor awards on "Lou Grant." He also won Emmys for his roles in the miniseries "Rich Man, Poor Man" (1975-1976) and "Roots" (1976-1977).

He had more than 300 acting credits and remained active throughout his 70s and 80s in a variety of film and TV roles. In 2003, he played Santa Claus in Will Ferrell's hit film "Elf." He was John Goodman's father in the short-lived 2004 CBS comedy "Center of the Universe" and the voice of the elderly hero in the hit 2009 Pixar release, "Up." More recently, he was in such TV series as "Forgive Me" and "Dead to Me."

Nonetheless, Asner told The Associated Press in 2009 that interesting roles were hard to come by.

"I never get enough work," he said. "It's the history of my career. There just isn't anything to turn down, let me put it that way."

"I'd say most people are probably in that same boat, old people, and it's a shame," he said.

As Screen Actors Guild president, the liberal Asner was caught up in a political controversy in 1982 when he spoke out against U.S. involvement with repressive governments in Latin America. "Lou Grant" was canceled during the furor that followed and he did not run for a third SAG term in 1985.

Asner discussed his politicization in a 2002 interview, noting he had begun his career during the McCarthy era and for years had been afraid to speak out for fear of being blacklisted.

Then he saw a nun's film depicting the cruelties inflicted by El Salvador's government on that country's citizens.

"I stepped out to complain about our country's constant arming and fortifying of the military in El Salvador, who were oppressing their people," he said.

Former SAG President Charlton Heston and others accused him of making un-American statements and of misusing his position as head of their actors union.

"We even had bomb threats at the time. I had armed guards," Asner recalled.

The actor blamed the controversy for ending the five-year run of "Lou Grant," although CBS insisted declining ratings were the reason the show was canceled.

Although the show had its light moments, its scripts touched on a variety of darker social issues that most series wouldn't touch at the time, including alcoholism and homelessness. Asner remained politically active for the rest of his life and in 2017 published the book "The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs."

Asner, born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1929, almost became a newsman in real life. He studied journalism at the University of Chicago until a professor told him there was little money to be made in the profession.

He quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred Thomas Becket in a campus production of T.S. Eliot's "Murder in the Cathedral."

He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver and other jobs before being drafted in 1951. He served with the Army Signal Corps in France.

Returning to Chicago after military service, he appeared at the Playwrights Theatre Club and Second City, the famed satire troupe that launched the careers of dozens of top comedians.

Later, in New York, he joined the long-running "The Threepenny Opera" and appeared opposite Jack Lemmon in "Face of a Hero."

Arriving in Hollywood in 1961 for an episode of television's "Naked City," Asner decided to stay and appeared in numerous movies and TV shows, including the film "El Dorado," opposite John Wayne; and the Elvis Presley vehicles "Kid Galahad" and "Change of Habit." He was a regular in the 1960s political drama series "Slattery's People."

He was married twice, to Nancy Lou Sykes and Cindy Gilmore, and had four children, Matthew, Liza, Kate and Charles.

# Actor Ed Asner, TV's blustery Lou Grant, dies at 91

[](https://artscanvas.org/)[Arts](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts) Aug 29, 2021 3:26 PM EDT 

LOS ANGELES — Ed Asner, the burly and prolific character actor who became a star in middle age as the gruff but lovable newsman Lou Grant, first in the hit comedy "The Mary Tyler Moore Show" and later in the drama "Lou Grant," died Sunday. He was 91.

Asner's representative confirmed the actor's death in an email to The Associated Press. Asner's official[Twitter account included a note](https://twitter.com/theonlyedasner/status/1432034864384000007?s=21)from his children: "We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head- Goodnight dad. We love you."

Built like the football lineman he once was, the balding Asner was a journeyman actor in films and TV when he was hired in 1970 to play Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." For seven seasons he was the rumpled boss to Moore's ebullient Mary Richards (He called her "Mary," she called him "Mr. Grant") at the fictional Minneapolis TV newsroom where both worked. Later, he would play the role for five years on "Lou Grant."

Asner's character had caught on from the first episode of "Mary Tyler Moore," when he told Mary in their initial meeting, "You've got spunk. ... I hate spunk!" The inspired cast included Ted Knight as Ted Baxter, the dimwitted news anchor; Gavin MacLeod as Murray Slaughter, the sarcastic news writer; and Betty White as the manipulative, sex-obsessed home show hostess Sue Ann Nivens. Valerie Harper and Cloris Leachman, playing Mary's neighbors, both saw their characters spun off into their own shows.

Asner is the third "Mary Tyler Moore" alum to die in recent months.[Leachman died in January](https://apnews.com/article/cloris-leachman-dead-7b9eb2aa8de5a62e8502ca94cff89e83)and[MacLeod died in May.](https://apnews.com/article/gavin-macleod-entertainment-arts-and-entertainment-6313dfd801244eeeea2be2ddeac1cdbb)

The 99-year-old White is the lone surviving main cast member from "Mary Tyler Moore."

"Mary Tyler Moore" was still a hit when the star decided to pursue other interests, and so it was brought to an end in the seventh season with a hilarious finale in which all of the principals were fired except for the bumbling Baxter.

Asner went immediately into "Lou Grant," his character moving from Minneapolis to Los Angeles to become city editor of the Tribune, a crusading newspaper under the firm hand of Publisher Margaret Pynchon, memorably played by Nancy Marchand.

Asner won three best supporting actor Emmys on "Mary Tyler Moore" and two best actor awards on "Lou Grant." He also won Emmys for his roles in the miniseries "Rich Man, Poor Man" (1975-1976) and "Roots" (1976-1977).

He had more than 300 acting credits and remained active throughout his 70s and 80s in a variety of film and TV roles. In 2003, he played Santa Claus in Will Ferrell's hit film "Elf." He was John Goodman's father in the short-lived 2004 CBS comedy "Center of the Universe" and the voice of the elderly hero in the hit 2009 Pixar release, "Up." More recently, he was in such TV series as "Forgive Me" and "Dead to Me."

Nonetheless, Asner told The Associated Press in 2009 that interesting roles were hard to come by.

"I never get enough work," he said. "It's the history of my career. There just isn't anything to turn down, let me put it that way."

"I'd say most people are probably in that same boat, old people, and it's a shame," he said.

As Screen Actors Guild president, the liberal Asner was caught up in a political controversy in 1982 when he spoke out against U.S. involvement with repressive governments in Latin America. "Lou Grant" was canceled during the furor that followed and he did not run for a third SAG term in 1985.

Asner discussed his politicization in a 2002 interview, noting he had begun his career during the McCarthy era and for years had been afraid to speak out for fear of being blacklisted.

Then he saw a nun's film depicting the cruelties inflicted by El Salvador's government on that country's citizens.

"I stepped out to complain about our country's constant arming and fortifying of the military in El Salvador, who were oppressing their people," he said.

Former SAG President Charlton Heston and others accused him of making un-American statements and of misusing his position as head of their actors union.

"We even had bomb threats at the time. I had armed guards," Asner recalled.

The actor blamed the controversy for ending the five-year run of "Lou Grant," although CBS insisted declining ratings were the reason the show was canceled.

Although the show had its light moments, its scripts touched on a variety of darker social issues that most series wouldn't touch at the time, including alcoholism and homelessness. Asner remained politically active for the rest of his life and in 2017 published the book "The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs."

Asner, born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1929, almost became a newsman in real life. He studied journalism at the University of Chicago until a professor told him there was little money to be made in the profession.

He quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred Thomas Becket in a campus production of T.S. Eliot's "Murder in the Cathedral."

He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver and other jobs before being drafted in 1951. He served with the Army Signal Corps in France.

Returning to Chicago after military service, he appeared at the Playwrights Theatre Club and Second City, the famed satire troupe that launched the careers of dozens of top comedians.

Later, in New York, he joined the long-running "The Threepenny Opera" and appeared opposite Jack Lemmon in "Face of a Hero."

Arriving in Hollywood in 1961 for an episode of television's "Naked City," Asner decided to stay and appeared in numerous movies and TV shows, including the film "El Dorado," opposite John Wayne; and the Elvis Presley vehicles "Kid Galahad" and "Change of Habit." He was a regular in the 1960s political drama series "Slattery's People."

He was married twice, to Nancy Lou Sykes and Cindy Gilmore, and had four children, Matthew, Liza, Kate and Charles.

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000799/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

Edward Asner was born of Russian Jewish parentage in Kansas City, to Morris David Asner (founder and owner of the Kansas City-based Asner Iron & Metal Company) and his wife Elizabeth "Lizzie" (Seliger). After attending college, Ed worked various jobs, including in a steel mill, as a door-to-door salesman and on an assembly line for General Motors. Between 1947 and 1949, he attended the University of Chicago. The onset of the Korean War saw him drafted into the U.S. Army Signals Corps and posted to France where he was primarily assigned clerical tasks. Upon demobilization, Asner joined the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago but soon progressed to New York. In 1955, he appeared off-Broadway in the leading role of the beggar king Jonathan Peachum in Brecht's Threepenny Opera. Five years later, he made his debut on the Great White Way in the courtroom drama Face of a Hero, co-starring alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000493/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He also began regular TV work in anthology drama.  
  
From the early '60s, Asner, now based in California, earned his living as a busy supporting actor. His many noted guest appearances included turns in [Route 66 (1960)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0053534/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Untouchables (1959)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0052522/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Fugitive (1963)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0056757/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (1964)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0057798/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (sinister dictator-in-exile Brynov), [The Invaders (1967)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0061265/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (twice -- as aliens) and [How the Ghosts Stole Christmas (1998)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0751138/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (one of a couple of ghostly residents in a haunted mansion). Heavy-set and distinctively gravelly-voiced, Asner established his reputation as tough, robust and uncompromising (though, on occasion, good-hearted) authority figures. Excellent at conveying menace, he was memorably cast as the brutish patriarch Axel Jordache in [Rich Man, Poor Man (1976)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0074048/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and as the slave ship's morally conflicted master, Captain Thomas Davies, in [Roots (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075572/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), which earned him a Primetime Emmy Award in 1977. The immensely prolific Asner (417 IMDB screen credits!) would receive seven Emmys in total (from 21 nominations), all Primetime, and become the only actor to win in both the comedy and drama category for the same role. That was also the part which made Asner a household name: the gruff, snarky newspaper editor [Lou Grant (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075528/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Grant began as a mainstay on [The Mary Tyler Moore Show (1970)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0065314/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), a 30-minute sitcom.  
  
When the character was promoted to West Coast editor of The Los Angeles Tribune, Asner went on to star in his own much acclaimed drama series. Despite consistently high ratings, the show was axed after five seasons amid rumours of disharmony between the star and producers, possibly due to the former's outspoken political views. Indeed, Asner has been a controversial figure as an activist and campaigner, engaged in a variety of humanitarian and political issues. A self-proclaimed liberal Democrat, he published a book in 2017, amusingly titled "The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs."  
  
Between 1981 and 1985, Asner served twice as President of the Screen Actors Guild, during which time he was critical of former SAG President [Ronald Reagan](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001654/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) -- then the president of a greater concern -- for his Central American policy. In 1996, he was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame and in 2002 received the Screen Actors Guild's Life Achievement Award. In addition to appearing on screen and stage, he performed extensive work for radio, video games and animated TV series. He voiced the lead character Carl Fredricksen in Pixar's Oscar-winning production of [Up (2009)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1049413/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), starred as Santa in [Elf (2003)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0319343/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), and played Nicholas Drago in [The Games Maker (2014)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2766268/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Ed passed away in Los Angeles at the age of 91 on August 29, 2021.

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000799/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

Edward Asner was born of Russian Jewish parentage in Kansas City, to Morris David Asner (founder and owner of the Kansas City-based Asner Iron & Metal Company) and his wife Elizabeth "Lizzie" (Seliger). After attending college, Ed worked various jobs, including in a steel mill, as a door-to-door salesman and on an assembly line for General Motors. Between 1947 and 1949, he attended the University of Chicago. The onset of the Korean War saw him drafted into the U.S. Army Signals Corps and posted to France where he was primarily assigned clerical tasks. Upon demobilization, Asner joined the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago but soon progressed to New York. In 1955, he appeared off-Broadway in the leading role of the beggar king Jonathan Peachum in Brecht's Threepenny Opera. Five years later, he made his debut on the Great White Way in the courtroom drama Face of a Hero, co-starring alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000493/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He also began regular TV work in anthology drama.  
  
From the early '60s, Asner, now based in California, earned his living as a busy supporting actor. His many noted guest appearances included turns in [Route 66 (1960)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0053534/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Untouchables (1959)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0052522/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Fugitive (1963)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0056757/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (1964)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0057798/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (sinister dictator-in-exile Brynov), [The Invaders (1967)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0061265/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (twice -- as aliens) and [How the Ghosts Stole Christmas (1998)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0751138/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) (one of a couple of ghostly residents in a haunted mansion). Heavy-set and distinctively gravelly-voiced, Asner established his reputation as tough, robust and uncompromising (though, on occasion, good-hearted) authority figures. Excellent at conveying menace, he was memorably cast as the brutish patriarch Axel Jordache in [Rich Man, Poor Man (1976)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0074048/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and as the slave ship's morally conflicted master, Captain Thomas Davies, in [Roots (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075572/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), which earned him a Primetime Emmy Award in 1977. The immensely prolific Asner (417 IMDB screen credits!) would receive seven Emmys in total (from 21 nominations), all Primetime, and become the only actor to win in both the comedy and drama category for the same role. That was also the part which made Asner a household name: the gruff, snarky newspaper editor [Lou Grant (1977)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0075528/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Grant began as a mainstay on [The Mary Tyler Moore Show (1970)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0065314/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), a 30-minute sitcom.  
  
When the character was promoted to West Coast editor of The Los Angeles Tribune, Asner went on to star in his own much acclaimed drama series. Despite consistently high ratings, the show was axed after five seasons amid rumours of disharmony between the star and producers, possibly due to the former's outspoken political views. Indeed, Asner has been a controversial figure as an activist and campaigner, engaged in a variety of humanitarian and political issues. A self-proclaimed liberal Democrat, he published a book in 2017, amusingly titled "The Grouchy Historian: An Old-Time Lefty Defends Our Constitution Against Right-Wing Hypocrites and Nutjobs."  
  
Between 1981 and 1985, Asner served twice as President of the Screen Actors Guild, during which time he was critical of former SAG President [Ronald Reagan](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001654/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) -- then the president of a greater concern -- for his Central American policy. In 1996, he was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame and in 2002 received the Screen Actors Guild's Life Achievement Award. In addition to appearing on screen and stage, he performed extensive work for radio, video games and animated TV series. He voiced the lead character Carl Fredricksen in Pixar's Oscar-winning production of [Up (2009)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1049413/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), starred as Santa in [Elf (2003)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0319343/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), and played Nicholas Drago in [The Games Maker (2014)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2766268/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). Ed passed away in Los Angeles at the age of 91 on August 29, 2021.

[Obituaries](https://playbill.com/category/obituaries "Obituaries")Emmy Winner Ed Asner, Star of _Lou Grant_ and _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, Dies at 91 The character actor was last seen on Broadway in the 2012 play _Grace._

By Talaura Harms 

August 30, 2021

*   [](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=760188134086076&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fplaybill.com%2Farticle%2Femmy-winner-ed-asner-star-of-lou-grant-and-the-mary-tyler-moore-show-dies-at-91&caption=&description=&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fplaybill.com%2Farticle%2Femmy-winner-ed-asner-star-of-lou-grant-and-the-mary-tyler-moore-show-dies-at-91&picture=https%3A%2F%2Fbsp-static.playbill.com%2Fd0%2Fec%2F2be3030d4cd7930c20c51b109863%2FLin-Manuel-Miranda.1438116575.jpg "Share on facebook")

*   [](mailto:?Subject=Emmy%20Winner%20Ed%20Asner%2C%20Star%20of%20Lou%20Grant%20%20and%20The%20Mary%20Tyler%20Moore%20Show%2C%20Dies%20at%2091&Body=%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fplaybill.com%2Farticle%2Femmy-winner-ed-asner-star-of-lou-grant-and-the-mary-tyler-moore-show-dies-at-91 "Share on email")

![Image 7](https://assets.playbill.com/editorial/_articleLeadImage/43b8891fdb17b88751635cc7039ed7b5-ed-asner-obit-graphic.jpg)

 Ed Asner 

Actor [Ed Asner](https://playbill.com/person/ed-asner-vault-0000076605), best known for his 12 years of television work as the character Lou Grant, died August 29 at the age of 91. His family confirmed the death [via Twitter](https://twitter.com/TheOnlyEdAsner/status/1432034864384000007).

Born November 15, 1929, in Kansas City, Missouri, Mr. Asner began his professional theatrical career in the Chicago comedy scene in 1953, following two years of military service. He co-founded Playwrights Theatre Company, who later regrouped as Compass Players, the predecessor of The Second City. He returned for several guest appearances with the famed comedy troupe.

A move to New York found him in the long-running 1955 Off-Broadway revival of _The Threepenny Opera_ at Theatre de Lys in Greenwich Village. He made his Broadway debut in the short-lived play _Face of Hero,_ starring Jack Lemmon.

![Image 8: //assets.playbill.com/editorial/dda0347e419dab090e48cdc74387fdbe-shutterstock-476260018.jpg](https://assets.playbill.com/editorial/_enhancementPortrait/dda0347e419dab090e48cdc74387fdbe-shutterstock-476260018.jpg)

 Ed Asner Featureflash Photo Agency/Shutterstock.com

However, it was his 1961 move to Los Angeles where the character actor really started to find success in the business, appearing in several television and film projects before he landed the role that would win him five Emmy awards. The character of Lou Grant was introduced to TV audiences in 1970 on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, the title character's endearing crank of a boss at the Minneapolis news station. The show ran from 1970–1977, and Mr. Asner was nominated for an Emmy Award for Best Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series every year, winning three times. He won the Emmy twice again in the Best Actor category for _Lou Grant_, the drama series spin-off based on his sitcom character. _Lou Grant_ aired from 1977–1982.

Mr. Asner won two more Emmys for his TV work in the 1976 mini-series _Rich Man, Poor Man_ and in the 1977 mini-series _Roots._

He returned to Broadway in 1989, starring as Harry Brock opposite Madeline Kahn's Billie Dawn in a revival of _Born Yesterday._ His final Broadway appearance was in the 2012 play _Grace_ with Paul Rudd and Michael Shannon.

A new generation of audiences met Mr. Asner, again playing a lovable curmudgeon, in the 2009 animated movie _Up._ He also took a turn as Santa Claus in the hit holiday film _Elf_ in 2003. Other film credits include _Fort Apache, the Bronx_ and _JFK_. In more recent years he had been seen on the small screen with guest appearances in _Dead to Me, Cobra Kai, The Good Wife, Grace and Frankie_, and _Hot in Cleveland_, among many others.

The always-working performer was scheduled to appear in a staged reading of _Two Jews, Talking_ with fellow TV veteran Jamie Farr at a North Carolina theatre in September.

Ed Asner is survived by four children and 10 grandchildren.

By Talaura Harms 

August 30, 2021

 Ed Asner 

Actor [Ed Asner](https://playbill.com/person/ed-asner-vault-0000076605), best known for his 12 years of television work as the character Lou Grant, died August 29 at the age of 91. His family confirmed the death [via Twitter](https://twitter.com/TheOnlyEdAsner/status/1432034864384000007).

Born November 15, 1929, in Kansas City, Missouri, Mr. Asner began his professional theatrical career in the Chicago comedy scene in 1953, following two years of military service. He co-founded Playwrights Theatre Company, who later regrouped as Compass Players, the predecessor of The Second City. He returned for several guest appearances with the famed comedy troupe.

A move to New York found him in the long-running 1955 Off-Broadway revival of _The Threepenny Opera_ at Theatre de Lys in Greenwich Village. He made his Broadway debut in the short-lived play _Face of Hero,_ starring Jack Lemmon.

![Image 8: //assets.playbill.com/editorial/dda0347e419dab090e48cdc74387fdbe-shutterstock-476260018.jpg](https://assets.playbill.com/editorial/_enhancementPortrait/dda0347e419dab090e48cdc74387fdbe-shutterstock-476260018.jpg)

 Ed Asner Featureflash Photo Agency/Shutterstock.com

However, it was his 1961 move to Los Angeles where the character actor really started to find success in the business, appearing in several television and film projects before he landed the role that would win him five Emmy awards. The character of Lou Grant was introduced to TV audiences in 1970 on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, the title character's endearing crank of a boss at the Minneapolis news station. The show ran from 1970–1977, and Mr. Asner was nominated for an Emmy Award for Best Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series every year, winning three times. He won the Emmy twice again in the Best Actor category for _Lou Grant_, the drama series spin-off based on his sitcom character. _Lou Grant_ aired from 1977–1982.

Mr. Asner won two more Emmys for his TV work in the 1976 mini-series _Rich Man, Poor Man_ and in the 1977 mini-series _Roots._

He returned to Broadway in 1989, starring as Harry Brock opposite Madeline Kahn's Billie Dawn in a revival of _Born Yesterday._ His final Broadway appearance was in the 2012 play _Grace_ with Paul Rudd and Michael Shannon.

A new generation of audiences met Mr. Asner, again playing a lovable curmudgeon, in the 2009 animated movie _Up._ He also took a turn as Santa Claus in the hit holiday film _Elf_ in 2003. Other film credits include _Fort Apache, the Bronx_ and _JFK_. In more recent years he had been seen on the small screen with guest appearances in _Dead to Me, Cobra Kai, The Good Wife, Grace and Frankie_, and _Hot in Cleveland_, among many others.

The always-working performer was scheduled to appear in a staged reading of _Two Jews, Talking_ with fellow TV veteran Jamie Farr at a North Carolina theatre in September.

Ed Asner is survived by four children and 10 grandchildren.

# Ed Asner, Award-Winning Actor Who Played Lou Grant, Dies At 91

NPR | By Deepa Shivaram

 Published August 29, 2021 at 2:51 PM CDT
