Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, died at 91.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c0c18d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2740x2054+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap21241656148986-7809d0c6a750c8595d9f6d1e54085fe0c80e3fa2.jpg)

Matt Sayles

/

AP

Ed Asner arrives during the 82nd Academy Awards in the Hollywood section of Los Angeles on March 7, 2010. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, died at 91.

Ed Asner, the legendary actor known for his role as the crusty, loveable boss Lou Grant on _The Mary Tyler Moore_ _Show_, has [died](https://twitter.com/TheOnlyEdAsner/status/1432034864384000007?s=20) at the age of 91.

More recently, he was featured in _Elf_ as Santa Claus and in the movie _Up_ as the equally crusty, lovable voice of Carl Fredricksen.

"We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head — Goodnight dad. We love you," his family wrote on Twitter.

Asner won seven Emmys, five of them playing Lou Grant, and the other two as a German immigrant in _Rich Man, Poor Man,_ and as the sea captain in _Roots_.

His character of Mary Tyler Moore's boss was so popular that Asner played the same role in a spinoff show titled _Lou Grant_-- two of his Emmys came from the show in 1978 and 1980.

![Image 4: Lindsay Wagner, left, Ed Asner, center, and Nancy Marchand pose at the 30th annual Primetime Emmy Awards at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, in Pasadena, Calif., in 1978. Asner won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for <em>Lou Grant.</em>](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e96ef13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2768x2076+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap21241665514041-65db592c00c681559e65c32bd24271d3a6ce5183.jpg)

 / AP

/

AP

Lindsay Wagner, left, Ed Asner, center, and Nancy Marchand pose at the 30th annual Primetime Emmy Awards at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, in Pasadena, Calif., in 1978. Asner won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for _Lou Grant._

On looking back at his time with the _Mary Tyler Moore Show_, Asner told [_The Hollywood Reporter_](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-features/thr-icon-ed-asnwer-golden-age-live-tv-date-mary-tyler-moore-1235002217/), "There's nothing more fun than hearing rip-roaring laughter from an audience."

In addition to his acting career, Asner was the president of the Screen Actors Guild for two terms from 1981-1985.

Outspoken about politics and a self-described "[old-time lefty](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Grouchy-Historian/Ed-Asner/9781501166037)," Asner was critical of President Ronald Reagan's administration in the 1980s, particularly on America's involvement in El Salvador's civil war, and continued to [speak out](https://www.thedailybeast.com/ed-asner-sounds-off-on-republicans-they-want-to-destroy-the-middle-class) about progressive causes during the Trump administration.

![Image 5: Actors Ed Asner, left and Dennis Weaver stand on a picket line in Los Angeles on Dec. 19, 1978 as some 70,000 actors and announcers who make radio and television commercials went on strike. Asner served as president of the union for two terms.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/52920a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2644x1983+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap8409260596-44cd3934bdf418a3d514ead37cf698264e816a45.jpg)

Joanie / AP

/

AP

Actors Ed Asner, left and Dennis Weaver stand on a picket line in Los Angeles on Dec. 19, 1978 as some 70,000 actors and announcers who make radio and television commercials went on strike. Asner served as president of the union for two terms.

Asner was born in Kansas City, Mo. and briefly attended the University of Chicago before being drafted into the Army in 1951, serving in France. After his service ended, he acted in [several plays](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/ed-asner-dead-lou-grant-1235004802/) in Chicago and New York, including the Broadway play _Threepenny Opera._

Shortly before his death, Asner did an interview with [_The Hollywood Reporter_](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-features/thr-icon-ed-asnwer-golden-age-live-tv-date-mary-tyler-moore-1235002217/)in which he discussed his acting career, the COVID-19 pandemic and even his views on the Biden administration.

When asked what remained on his bucket list, Asner had his family in mind.

"I haven't climbed Suribachi! No, I think just ensuring that I've left enough for the family."

# Ed Asner, Award-Winning Actor Who Played Lou Grant, Dies At 91

NPR | By Deepa Shivaram

 Published August 29, 2021 at 2:51 PM CDT

Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, died at 91.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c0c18d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2740x2054+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap21241656148986-7809d0c6a750c8595d9f6d1e54085fe0c80e3fa2.jpg)

Matt Sayles

/

AP

Ed Asner arrives during the 82nd Academy Awards in the Hollywood section of Los Angeles on March 7, 2010. Asner, the blustery but lovable Lou Grant in two successful television series, died at 91.

Ed Asner, the legendary actor known for his role as the crusty, loveable boss Lou Grant on _The Mary Tyler Moore_ _Show_, has [died](https://twitter.com/TheOnlyEdAsner/status/1432034864384000007?s=20) at the age of 91.

More recently, he was featured in _Elf_ as Santa Claus and in the movie _Up_ as the equally crusty, lovable voice of Carl Fredricksen.

"We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head — Goodnight dad. We love you," his family wrote on Twitter.

Asner won seven Emmys, five of them playing Lou Grant, and the other two as a German immigrant in _Rich Man, Poor Man,_ and as the sea captain in _Roots_.

His character of Mary Tyler Moore's boss was so popular that Asner played the same role in a spinoff show titled _Lou Grant_-- two of his Emmys came from the show in 1978 and 1980.

![Image 4: Lindsay Wagner, left, Ed Asner, center, and Nancy Marchand pose at the 30th annual Primetime Emmy Awards at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, in Pasadena, Calif., in 1978. Asner won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for <em>Lou Grant.</em>](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e96ef13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2768x2076+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap21241665514041-65db592c00c681559e65c32bd24271d3a6ce5183.jpg)

 / AP

/

AP

Lindsay Wagner, left, Ed Asner, center, and Nancy Marchand pose at the 30th annual Primetime Emmy Awards at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, in Pasadena, Calif., in 1978. Asner won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for _Lou Grant._

On looking back at his time with the _Mary Tyler Moore Show_, Asner told [_The Hollywood Reporter_](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-features/thr-icon-ed-asnwer-golden-age-live-tv-date-mary-tyler-moore-1235002217/), "There's nothing more fun than hearing rip-roaring laughter from an audience."

In addition to his acting career, Asner was the president of the Screen Actors Guild for two terms from 1981-1985.

Outspoken about politics and a self-described "[old-time lefty](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Grouchy-Historian/Ed-Asner/9781501166037)," Asner was critical of President Ronald Reagan's administration in the 1980s, particularly on America's involvement in El Salvador's civil war, and continued to [speak out](https://www.thedailybeast.com/ed-asner-sounds-off-on-republicans-they-want-to-destroy-the-middle-class) about progressive causes during the Trump administration.

![Image 5: Actors Ed Asner, left and Dennis Weaver stand on a picket line in Los Angeles on Dec. 19, 1978 as some 70,000 actors and announcers who make radio and television commercials went on strike. Asner served as president of the union for two terms.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/52920a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2644x1983+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fassets%2Fimg%2F2021%2F08%2F29%2Fap8409260596-44cd3934bdf418a3d514ead37cf698264e816a45.jpg)

Joanie / AP

/

AP

Actors Ed Asner, left and Dennis Weaver stand on a picket line in Los Angeles on Dec. 19, 1978 as some 70,000 actors and announcers who make radio and television commercials went on strike. Asner served as president of the union for two terms.

Asner was born in Kansas City, Mo. and briefly attended the University of Chicago before being drafted into the Army in 1951, serving in France. After his service ended, he acted in [several plays](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/ed-asner-dead-lou-grant-1235004802/) in Chicago and New York, including the Broadway play _Threepenny Opera._

Shortly before his death, Asner did an interview with [_The Hollywood Reporter_](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-features/thr-icon-ed-asnwer-golden-age-live-tv-date-mary-tyler-moore-1235002217/)in which he discussed his acting career, the COVID-19 pandemic and even his views on the Biden administration.

When asked what remained on his bucket list, Asner had his family in mind.

"I haven't climbed Suribachi! No, I think just ensuring that I've left enough for the family."

The seven-time Emmy winner was funny on 'The Mary Tyler Moore Show' and serious on his own newspaper drama, then delighted movie audiences with 'Up.'

Ed Asner CBS/PHOTOFEST

Ed Asner, the tough guy with the soft side who starred as the irascible newsroom boss Lou Grant on the legendary sitcom The Mary Tyler Moore Show and on his own hard-hitting TV drama, died Sunday. He was 91.

Said his family on Twitter: “We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head — Goodnight dad. We love you.”

Publicist Charles Sherman said Asner died of natural causes at his home in Tarzana.

The actor received three of his record seven Emmy Awards (in 1971, ’72 and ’75) for playing the news director/producer of the WJM-TV evening news on CBS’ The Mary Tyler Moore Show, then reeled in two more trophies (1978, ’80) after his out-of-work character was hired as city editor of the Los Angeles Tribune newspaper on CBS’ Lou Grant.

He’s one of only two actors (Uzo Aduba is the other) to win a comedy and drama Emmy for the same role on different shows.

Asner also received Emmys for his performances on two renowned ABC miniseries: 1976’s Rich Man, Poor Man, in which he played an embittered German immigrant, and 1977’s Roots, as the sea captain who brought Kunta Kinte to America.

Asner then attracted a new generation of fans when he voiced Carl Fredricksen, a 78-year-old widower who ties thousands of balloons to his house to fulfill a dream of seeing South America, in the Oscar best picture nominee Up (2009).

An avowed liberal, Asner also served two terms as president of the Screen Actors Guild from 1981-85 and sparred often with Charlton Heston, a noted conservative who preceded him as head of the guild. He received the SAG Life Achievement Award in 2002.

After he was named a THR Icon, he reflected on his long life and career with THR‘s Scott Feinberg on Aug. 16 in his final interview.

Asked by Feinberg how “old he felt,” Asner replied: “If it weren’t for my bad left leg, I would feel younger. I’ve got many parts that need to be bolstered and refurbished. And I haven’t got time to undergo all those changes.”

And what was left on his bucket list? “I haven’t climbed Suribachi! No, I think just ensuring that I’ve left enough for the family,” he said.

Asner’s portrayal of a ill-tempered, comedic police chief in the 1971 Erle Stanley Gardner NBC telefilm They Call It Murder led to the role that changed his life. MTM Enterprises head Grant Tinker saw Asner’s work in the dailies and recommended him for the role of the gruff Grant on the new Mary Tyler Moore Show, starring Tinker’s wife.

(Gavin MacLeod also had read for the part of Grant but told producers he was probably better suited to play newswriter Murray Slaughter.)

“It was such a gorgeous character, such a gorgeous script,” Asner recalled in a 1973 interview with The New York Times. “I began licking my lips over the project. I couldn’t believe a situation comedy was affecting me this way. I had never regarded myself as a comedian, and I’d deliberately stayed away from comedy parts.”

Asner played Grant — who famously had a low tolerance for “spunk” — on The Mary Tyler Moore Show for seven seasons, from September 1970 until the series shut its doors in March 1977.

Six months later, Asner was still on the air, and still playing Grant, but now he was in an hourlong drama. The radical idea for the segue came from James L. Brooks and Allan Burns, the creators of The Mary Tyler Moore show, who originally had written that Grant had been a newspaper guy before he joined Minneapolis’ WJM.

They also believed they could have a hit in the wake of the success of the journalism film All the President’s Men.

But Lou Grant was a one-camera drama that emphasized journalism and serious, topical issues, not a three-camera comedy taped in front of a live audience — a much different animal than The Mary Tyler Moore Show.

“I was told [by the producers], ‘It’s up to you to maintain the flame of Lou Grant, remember who the character is,’ ” he said during a 1999 interview with the Archive of American Television. “I got down on that floor with the single camera and the new crew and began slogging through the first shows, and nobody’s laughing. I’m so busy gesticulating and grimacing to punch whatever I’m finding funny to make sure the audience knows that there’s a laugh here. I was becoming a nervous wreck.

“After the show opened, I went in for a session [with his therapist] and said, ‘What do you think [about the series]?’ He said, ‘Why are you grimacing so much?’ That’s all he said. I’m trying to get those laughs, knowing that the guys told me to remember who Lou was. I said, ‘I’m going to forget about comedy.’ … I was relieved.”

Even TV Guide listed Lou Grant as a comedy at first. “People were expecting to turn on a show that was a continuation of the old comedic routine,” Asner told Sam Tweedle in a 2010 interview. “They certainly weren’t prepared to see issues and events discussed in depth as Lou Grant presented them, so the ratings were terrible.”

Lou Grant, however, went on to capture the Emmy for best drama series in 1979 and ’80 — after The Mary Tyler Moore Show had closed with the best comedy statuette in 1975, ’76 and ’77 — and lasted five seasons.

The series could have lasted longer. The outspoken Asner often said that his public opposition of the U.S.-backed military dictatorship in El Salvador led to CBS canceling Lou Grant.

Edward Asner was born on Nov. 15, 1929, in Kansas City, Missouri, the youngest of five children (the family lived across the state line in Kansas City, Kansas). His father, Morris, owned a junkyard.

A few months ago, a student asked me, “If I study Interior Design, does that mean I'll spend my career choosing wall colors and furniture?”

I smiled because that question comes up far more often than you would think.

The truth is that Interior Design today is less about decoration and more about creating spaces that solve problems. Think about your favorite café, a retail store where you ended up spending more time than planned, or an office that simply feels comfortable to work in. None of that happens by accident. Designers basically shape how people move through, interact with, and experience different spaces.

That's why whenever students ask me what comes after a B.Des in Interior Design, I always tell them to look way past just residential homes. Depending on what they like, they can branch into furniture design, retail and commercial spots, exhibition setups, or even corporate workspaces.

While exploring various programs that actually prepare students for these diverse career tracks, a recent review of the Jindal School of Design and Architecture really stood out to me. Their B.Des Interior Design program gives you genuine, hands-on experience with materials, while allowing you to dive into sustainability, master digital tools, and experiment directly in studios. The whole focus is on learning by doing.

I also really like the sheer variety of projects the students tackle. From standard home and office layouts to community projects, stage sets, furniture concepts, and lighting installations, the work perfectly highlights the endless paths an interior design career can take.

Since you're wondering what comes after a B.Des in Interior Design, trust me, you won't just design rooms; you will design experiences. That's where the most exciting opportunities begin.

The seven-time Emmy winner was funny on 'The Mary Tyler Moore Show' and serious on his own newspaper drama, then delighted movie audiences with 'Up.'

Ed Asner CBS/PHOTOFEST

Ed Asner, the tough guy with the soft side who starred as the irascible newsroom boss Lou Grant on the legendary sitcom The Mary Tyler Moore Show and on his own hard-hitting TV drama, died Sunday. He was 91.

Said his family on Twitter: “We are sorry to say that our beloved patriarch passed away this morning peacefully. Words cannot express the sadness we feel. With a kiss on your head — Goodnight dad. We love you.”

Publicist Charles Sherman said Asner died of natural causes at his home in Tarzana.

The actor received three of his record seven Emmy Awards (in 1971, ’72 and ’75) for playing the news director/producer of the WJM-TV evening news on CBS’ The Mary Tyler Moore Show, then reeled in two more trophies (1978, ’80) after his out-of-work character was hired as city editor of the Los Angeles Tribune newspaper on CBS’ Lou Grant.

He’s one of only two actors (Uzo Aduba is the other) to win a comedy and drama Emmy for the same role on different shows.

Asner also received Emmys for his performances on two renowned ABC miniseries: 1976’s Rich Man, Poor Man, in which he played an embittered German immigrant, and 1977’s Roots, as the sea captain who brought Kunta Kinte to America.

Asner then attracted a new generation of fans when he voiced Carl Fredricksen, a 78-year-old widower who ties thousands of balloons to his house to fulfill a dream of seeing South America, in the Oscar best picture nominee Up (2009).

An avowed liberal, Asner also served two terms as president of the Screen Actors Guild from 1981-85 and sparred often with Charlton Heston, a noted conservative who preceded him as head of the guild. He received the SAG Life Achievement Award in 2002.

After he was named a THR Icon, he reflected on his long life and career with THR‘s Scott Feinberg on Aug. 16 in his final interview.

Asked by Feinberg how “old he felt,” Asner replied: “If it weren’t for my bad left leg, I would feel younger. I’ve got many parts that need to be bolstered and refurbished. And I haven’t got time to undergo all those changes.”

And what was left on his bucket list? “I haven’t climbed Suribachi! No, I think just ensuring that I’ve left enough for the family,” he said.

Asner’s portrayal of a ill-tempered, comedic police chief in the 1971 Erle Stanley Gardner NBC telefilm They Call It Murder led to the role that changed his life. MTM Enterprises head Grant Tinker saw Asner’s work in the dailies and recommended him for the role of the gruff Grant on the new Mary Tyler Moore Show, starring Tinker’s wife.

(Gavin MacLeod also had read for the part of Grant but told producers he was probably better suited to play newswriter Murray Slaughter.)

“It was such a gorgeous character, such a gorgeous script,” Asner recalled in a 1973 interview with The New York Times. “I began licking my lips over the project. I couldn’t believe a situation comedy was affecting me this way. I had never regarded myself as a comedian, and I’d deliberately stayed away from comedy parts.”

Asner played Grant — who famously had a low tolerance for “spunk” — on The Mary Tyler Moore Show for seven seasons, from September 1970 until the series shut its doors in March 1977.

Six months later, Asner was still on the air, and still playing Grant, but now he was in an hourlong drama. The radical idea for the segue came from James L. Brooks and Allan Burns, the creators of The Mary Tyler Moore show, who originally had written that Grant had been a newspaper guy before he joined Minneapolis’ WJM.

They also believed they could have a hit in the wake of the success of the journalism film All the President’s Men.

But Lou Grant was a one-camera drama that emphasized journalism and serious, topical issues, not a three-camera comedy taped in front of a live audience — a much different animal than The Mary Tyler Moore Show.

“I was told [by the producers], ‘It’s up to you to maintain the flame of Lou Grant, remember who the character is,’ ” he said during a 1999 interview with the Archive of American Television. “I got down on that floor with the single camera and the new crew and began slogging through the first shows, and nobody’s laughing. I’m so busy gesticulating and grimacing to punch whatever I’m finding funny to make sure the audience knows that there’s a laugh here. I was becoming a nervous wreck.

“After the show opened, I went in for a session [with his therapist] and said, ‘What do you think [about the series]?’ He said, ‘Why are you grimacing so much?’ That’s all he said. I’m trying to get those laughs, knowing that the guys told me to remember who Lou was. I said, ‘I’m going to forget about comedy.’ … I was relieved.”

Even TV Guide listed Lou Grant as a comedy at first. “People were expecting to turn on a show that was a continuation of the old comedic routine,” Asner told Sam Tweedle in a 2010 interview. “They certainly weren’t prepared to see issues and events discussed in depth as Lou Grant presented them, so the ratings were terrible.”

Lou Grant, however, went on to capture the Emmy for best drama series in 1979 and ’80 — after The Mary Tyler Moore Show had closed with the best comedy statuette in 1975, ’76 and ’77 — and lasted five seasons.

The series could have lasted longer. The outspoken Asner often said that his public opposition of the U.S.-backed military dictatorship in El Salvador led to CBS canceling Lou Grant.

Edward Asner was born on Nov. 15, 1929, in Kansas City, Missouri, the youngest of five children (the family lived across the state line in Kansas City, Kansas). His father, Morris, owned a junkyard.

A few months ago, a student asked me, “If I study Interior Design, does that mean I'll spend my career choosing wall colors and furniture?”

I smiled because that question comes up far more often than you would think.

The truth is that Interior Design today is less about decoration and more about creating spaces that solve problems. Think about your favorite café, a retail store where you ended up spending more time than planned, or an office that simply feels comfortable to work in. None of that happens by accident. Designers basically shape how people move through, interact with, and experience different spaces.

That's why whenever students ask me what comes after a B.Des in Interior Design, I always tell them to look way past just residential homes. Depending on what they like, they can branch into furniture design, retail and commercial spots, exhibition setups, or even corporate workspaces.

While exploring various programs that actually prepare students for these diverse career tracks, a recent review of the Jindal School of Design and Architecture really stood out to me. Their B.Des Interior Design program gives you genuine, hands-on experience with materials, while allowing you to dive into sustainability, master digital tools, and experiment directly in studios. The whole focus is on learning by doing.

I also really like the sheer variety of projects the students tackle. From standard home and office layouts to community projects, stage sets, furniture concepts, and lighting installations, the work perfectly highlights the endless paths an interior design career can take.

Since you're wondering what comes after a B.Des in Interior Design, trust me, you won't just design rooms; you will design experiences. That's where the most exciting opportunities begin.

**Eddie Asner**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Tname-1) ([/ˈ æ z n ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); November 15, 1929 – August 29, 2021) was an American actor. He is most notable for portraying [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant") on the sitcom _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ (1970–1977) and drama _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–1982), making him one of the few television actors to portray the same character in both a comedy and a drama.

Asner won seven [Primetime Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards"), the most of any male performer. Five were for portraying Lou Grant: three as [Supporting Actor in a Comedy Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Supporting_Actor_in_a_Comedy_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series") on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and two as [Lead Actor in a Dramatic Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series") on the spin-off _Lou Grant_. The other two were for performances in the miniseries _[Rich Man, Poor Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich\_Man,\_Poor\_Man\_(miniseries) "Rich Man, Poor Man (miniseries)")_ (1976) and _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(1977\_miniseries) "Roots (1977 miniseries)")_ (1977).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Asner acted in the films _[El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Dorado\_(1966\_film) "El Dorado (1966 film)")_ (1966), _[They Call Me Mister Tibbs!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Call\_Me\_Mister\_Tibbs! "They Call Me Mister Tibbs!")_ (1970), _[Fort Apache, The Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort\_Apache,\_The\_Bronx "Fort Apache, The Bronx")_ (1981), _[JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK\_(film) "JFK (film)")_ (1991), and _[Too Big to Fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too\_Big\_to\_Fail\_(film) "Too Big to Fail (film)")_ (2011). He also played [Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") in several films and voiced [Carl Fredricksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Fredricksen "Carl Fredricksen") in the [Pixar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixar "Pixar") animated film _[Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_(2009\_film) "Up (2009 film)")_ (2009).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-3)

Asner starred in the [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") sitcom _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_ (1994–1995), and _[Michael: Every Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael:\_Every\_Day "Michael: Every Day")_ (2011–2017). He also acted extensively in numerous television series such as _[The Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Practice "The Practice")_, _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_, _[The Good Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Good\_Wife "The Good Wife")_, _[Cobra Kai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra\_Kai "Cobra Kai")_, _[Briarpatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Briarpatch\_(TV\_series) "Briarpatch (TV series)")_, _[Working Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working\_Class\_(TV\_series) "Working Class (TV series)")_, and _[Dead to Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_to\_Me\_(TV\_series) "Dead to Me (TV series)")_. He also voiced [J. Jonah Jameson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Jonah_Jameson "J. Jonah Jameson") in _[Spider-Man: The Animated Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:\_The\_Animated\_Series "Spider-Man: The Animated Series")_ (1994–1998), Hudson in _[Gargoyles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyles\_(TV\_series) "Gargoyles (TV series)")_ (1994–1997), and Ed Wuncler Sr. in _[The Boondocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boondocks\_(TV\_series) "The Boondocks (TV series)")_ (2005–2014).

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Asner was born November 15, 1929,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-4) in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), and grew up in [Kansas City, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Kansas "Kansas City, Kansas").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His parents, Lizzie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Seliger; 1885–1967), a housewife, and Morris David Asner (1879–1957),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-6) were [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jewish "Ashkenazi Jewish") immigrants from [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") who ran a [second-hand shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand_shop "Second-hand shop") and junkyard.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His four older siblings were Ben J. Asner (1915–1986), Eve Asner (1916–2014), Esther Edelman (1919–2014) and Labe Asner (1923–2017).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7) He was raised in an [Orthodox Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Jewish "Orthodox Jewish") family and given the [Hebrew name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_name "Hebrew name") Yitzhak (יִצְחָק).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Asner-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-9)

Asner attended [Wyandotte High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandotte_High_School "Wyandotte High School") in Kansas City, Kansas, and the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"). He studied journalism in Chicago until a professor advised him there was little money to be made in the profession. He had been working in a steel mill,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Palast-10) but he quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred [Thomas Becket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Becket "Thomas Becket") in a campus production of [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot")'s _[Murder in the Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder\_in\_the\_Cathedral "Murder in the Cathedral")_. He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver, worked on the assembly line for [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors"), and other odd jobs before being drafted in the military in 1951.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-11)

Asner served with the [United States Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps") from 1951 to 1953 during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and appeared in plays that toured army bases in Europe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-12)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7)

### 1955–1969: Early work and television roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1955–1969: Early work and television roles")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg)

Cast of _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970, with Asner in center rear

Following his military service, Asner helped found the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago, but left for [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") before members of that company regrouped as the [Compass Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_Players "Compass Players") in the mid-1950s.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-eb-13) He later made frequent guest appearances with the successor to Compass, [The Second City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_City "The Second City").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-14) In New York City, [Off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") roles included Jonathan Jeremiah Peachum in the revival of _[Threepenny Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Threepenny\_Opera "The Threepenny Opera")_ and in Otway's [Venice Preserv'd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Preserv'd "Venice Preserv'd") in late 1955.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-15) Asner scored his first [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") role in _Face of a Hero_ alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lemmon "Jack Lemmon") in 1960, and began to make inroads as a television actor, having made his TV debut in 1957 on _[Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse\_Studio\_One "Westinghouse Studio One")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2) In two notable performances on television, Asner played Detective Sgt. Thomas Siroleo in the 1963 episode of _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_ titled "[It Crawled Out of the Woodwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Crawled_Out_of_the_Woodwork "It Crawled Out of the Woodwork")" and the reprehensible ex-premier Brynov in the 1965 _[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyage\_to\_the\_Bottom\_of\_the\_Sea\_(TV\_series) "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)")_ episode "The Exile". He made his film debut in 1962, in the [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") vehicle _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad "Kid Galahad")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Before landing his role with [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show"), Asner guest-starred in television series including four episodes of _[The Untouchables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Untouchables\_(1959\_TV\_series) "The Untouchables (1959 TV series)")_ starring [Robert Stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stack "Robert Stack"), the [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_syndication "Television syndication")[crime drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_drama "Crime drama")_[Decoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoy\_(TV\_series) "Decoy (TV series)")_, starring [Beverly Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Garland "Beverly Garland"), two episodes of _[Naked City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked\_City\_(TV\_series) "Naked City (TV series)")_ in 1961, and _[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route\_66\_(TV\_series) "Route 66 (TV series)")_ in 1962 (the episode titled "Welcome to the Wedding") as Custody Officer Lincoln Peers. He was cast on [Jack Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lord "Jack Lord")'s [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") drama series _[Stoney Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoney\_Burke\_(TV\_series) "Stoney Burke (TV series)")_ and in the series finale of [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS")'s _[The Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Reporter\_(TV\_series) "The Reporter (TV series)")_, starring [Harry Guardino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Guardino "Harry Guardino"). He also appeared on _[Mr. Novak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Novak "Mr. Novak")_, _[Ben Casey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben\_Casey "Ben Casey")_, _[Gunsmoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke "Gunsmoke")_, _[Mission: Impossible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission:\_Impossible\_(1966\_TV\_series) "Mission: Impossible (1966 TV series)")_, _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_, _[The Fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fugitive\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Fugitive (1963 TV series)")_, and _[The Invaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Invaders "The Invaders")_. In 1963, Asner appeared as George Johnson on _[The Virginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Virginian\_(TV\_series) "The Virginian (TV series)")_ in the episode "Echo of Another Day".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-16) In 1968 he was the villain Furman Crotty in the Wild Wild West episode "The Night of the Amnesiac".

### 1970–1982: _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and _Lou Grant_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1970–1982: The Mary Tyler Moore Show and Lou Grant")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg)

Publicity photo of the cast of [The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show") in 1977. From left standing: [Ted Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Knight "Ted Knight") (Ted Baxter), [Gavin McLeod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McLeod "Gavin McLeod") (Murray Slaughter), Ed Asner (Lou Grant). Seated: [Betty White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_White "Betty White") (Sue Ann Nivens), [Georgia Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Engel "Georgia Engel") (Georgette Baxter), [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Tyler_Moore "Mary Tyler Moore") (Mary Richards).

Asner was best known for his character [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant"), who was first introduced on _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970. In 1977, after Moore's series ended, Asner's character was given his own show, _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–82). In contrast to the _Mary Tyler Moore_ series, a thirty-minute award-winning comedy about television journalism, the _Lou Grant_ series was an hour-long award-winning drama about newspaper journalism. For his role as Grant, Asner was one of only two actors to win an Emmy Award for a sitcom and a drama for the same role (the second being [Uzo Aduba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzo_Aduba "Uzo Aduba")). In addition he made appearances as Lou Grant on two other shows: _[Rhoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhoda "Rhoda")_ and _[Roseanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne "Roseanne")_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-17) Other television series starring Asner in regular roles include _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_, _[The Bronx Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bronx\_Zoo\_(TV\_series) "The Bronx Zoo (TV series)")_, and _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_. He also starred in one episode of the [Western series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerns_on_television "Westerns on television")_[Dead Man's Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Man's\_Gun "Dead Man's Gun")_ (1997), as well as portraying art smuggler August March in an episode of the original _[Hawaii Five-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-O\_(1968\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)")_ (1975) and reprised the role in the _[Hawaii Five-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-0\_(2010\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-0 (2010 TV series)")_ (2012) remake.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-18) He also appeared as a streetwise veteran police officer in an episode of the 1973 version of _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1973\_TV\_series) "Police Story (1973 TV series)")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-19)

### 2021–present: Posthumous releases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2021–present: Posthumous releases")]

Asner had completed several roles in a number of TV series and films at the time of his death in August 2021, including three of his final productions released posthumously on the [Disney+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") streaming service. He returned to reprise his voice role as Carl Fredricksen from the [Pixar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixar "Pixar") film _[Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_(2009\_film) "Up (2009 film)")_ in the Disney+ animated miniseries of shorts _[Dug Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dug\_Days "Dug Days")_ (2021), which premiered three days after his death. Asner's cameo appearance as the Ghost of Claude in the Halloween special _[Muppets Haunted Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muppets\_Haunted\_Mansion "Muppets Haunted Mansion")_ (2021) was posthumous, and he provided the voice of Grandpa Heffley in the Disney+ animated film adaptation _[Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary\_of\_a\_Wimpy\_Kid:\_Rodrick\_Rules\_(2022\_film) "Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules (2022 film)")_ (2022), released over a year after his death. The final short film in the _Dug Days_ series, _[Carl's Date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl's\_Date "Carl's Date")_, which includes Asner's recorded voice-over performance as Carl Fredricksen, did not premiere on Disney+, but it was released separately in theaters along with the Pixar animated feature film _[Elemental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elemental\_(2023\_film) "Elemental (2023 film)")_ on June 16, 2023, nearly two years after his death and also served as the finale of the _Up_ franchise. These were Asner's last acting works overall for Disney and were all dedicated to his memory.

Asner also appeared posthumously in _Deadly Draw_ (2023), _A Fargo Christmas Story_ (2023), and _[Altered Reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered\_Reality "Altered Reality")_ (2024). At least two other projects, which would include Asner's final film roles, have yet to announce release dates: _Scarlett_ (a television drama film)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-54) and _Unplugged_ (an animated film).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-55)

## Activism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Activism")]

### Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Politics")]

He played a prominent role in the [1980 SAG strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_and_Emmy_Awards_boycott_of_1980 "Strike and Emmy Awards boycott of 1980").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-museo-56) He was also active in a variety of other causes, such as the movement to free [Mumia Abu-Jamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumia_Abu-Jamal "Mumia Abu-Jamal") and the movement to establish California One Care, [single-payer health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_health_care "Single-payer health care") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), for which he created a television advertisement. He endorsed [Dennis Kucinich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Kucinich "Dennis Kucinich") in the [2004 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election "2004 United States presidential election"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-57) and [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") during the [2008 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election"). He was formerly a member of the [Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialist_Organizing_Committee "Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee") (DSOC),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-58) as well as a member of DSOC's successor, the [Democratic Socialists of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialists_of_America "Democratic Socialists of America").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

The sudden cancellation of _Lou Grant_ in 1982 was the subject of much controversy. The show had high ratings, being in the [ACNielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACNielsen "ACNielsen") top ten throughout its final month on the air. However, the CBS television network declined to renew it. Asner believed that his [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") political views, as well as the publicity surrounding them, were the actual root causes for the show's cancellation.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-museo-56) In 2011, Asner endorsed [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") candidate Marcy Winograd who finished 4th in the 16-candidate primary behind eventual winner [Janice Hahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janice_Hahn "Janice Hahn"), in [California's 36th congressional district special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_California's_36th_congressional_district_special_election "2011 California's 36th congressional district special election").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-59) From 2011 to 2015, Asner worked with filmmaker Nicole Zwiren on the feature-length documentary _Behind the Fear_, which addressed [HIV/AIDS denialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS_denialism "HIV/AIDS denialism"). The film was released in 2016 with Asner as the narrator.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-60)

Asner endorsed [9/11 conspiracy theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_conspiracy_theories "9/11 conspiracy theories"), including voicing qualified support for the [9/11 truth movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_truth_movement "9/11 truth movement"). In 2004, he signed a statement released by the group [9/11 Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_Truth_movement#9/11_Truth "9/11 Truth movement") that included a call for a new investigation into some elements of the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") that he questioned.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-StephanieMiller-61) Asner confirmed his support for the statement in 2009.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-salon-petition-62) In April 2004, Asner wrote an open letter to "peace and justice leaders" encouraging them to demand "full 9–11 truth" through the organization _9-11 Visibility Project_.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-63) In 2011, Asner hosted the [Architects & Engineers for 9/11 Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architects_&_Engineers_for_9/11_Truth "Architects & Engineers for 9/11 Truth") documentary on the collapse of [7 World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_World_Trade_Center_(1987%E2%80%932001) "7 World Trade Center (1987–2001)"), which endorses the theory that the building was taken down by controlled [demolition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition "Demolition").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-65) Asner also narrated the documentary film _The Oil Factor: Behind the War on Terror_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-66)

### Nonprofit organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Nonprofit organizations")]

Asner was on the Entertainment Board of Directors for The Survivor Mitzvah Project, a nonprofit organization dedicated to providing direct emergency aid to elderly and impoverished [Holocaust survivors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors "Holocaust survivors") in [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-67) Asner was a member of the [Comic Book Legal Defense Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_Book_Legal_Defense_Fund "Comic Book Legal Defense Fund"), a free speech organization that is dedicated to protecting comic book creators and retailers from prosecutions based on content. He served as an advisor to the [Rosenberg Fund for Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosenberg_Fund_for_Children "Rosenberg Fund for Children"), an organization founded by the children of [Julius and Ethel Rosenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_and_Ethel_Rosenberg "Julius and Ethel Rosenberg"), which provides benefits for the children of political activists, and was a board member for the wildlife conservation organization [Defenders of Wildlife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenders_of_Wildlife "Defenders of Wildlife"). Asner also sat on the advisory board of [Exceptional Minds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exceptional_Minds "Exceptional Minds"), a nonprofit school and computer animation studio for young adults on the [autism spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism_spectrum "Autism spectrum").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-sesame-68)

Asner was a supporter of Humane Borders, an organization based in [Tucson, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucson,_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona"), which maintains water stations in the [Sonoran Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonoran_Desert "Sonoran Desert") for use by undocumented migrants, with the goal of preventing deaths by dehydration and exposure. He was the master of ceremonies at that organization's volunteer dinner in fall 2017.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-69)

In November 2017, the Ed Asner Family Center was founded by Asner's son, Matt, and daughter-in-law, Navah Paskowitz. The Center provides arts and vocational enrichment, counseling services, support groups, and camps for individuals with special needs and their families.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-70)

### SAG involvement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: SAG involvement")]

Asner served two terms as president of the [Screen Actors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild "Screen Actors Guild"), in which capacity during the 1980s he opposed United States policy in [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), working closely with the Alliance for Survival.

On March 30, 2012, the [Screen Actors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild "Screen Actors Guild") (SAG) and the [American Federation of Television and Radio Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Federation_of_Television_and_Radio_Artists "American Federation of Television and Radio Artists") (AFTRA) completed a merger of equals, forming a new union [SAG-AFTRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAG-AFTRA "SAG-AFTRA"). Asner was adamantly opposed to the merger, arguing that it would destroy the SAG's health plan and disempower actors.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-71) Asner and a group of fellow actors and voice-actors, such as [Michael Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bell_(actor) "Michael Bell (actor)"), [Clancy Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clancy_Brown "Clancy Brown"), [Wendy Schaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Schaal "Wendy Schaal"), her former stepmother [Valerie Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerie_Harper "Valerie Harper"), [Martin Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Sheen "Martin Sheen"), [Ed Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Harris "Ed Harris"), and [Nancy Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Sinatra "Nancy Sinatra"), filed and later dropped a lawsuit[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-73) against SAG president [Ken Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Howard "Ken Howard") and several SAG vice presidents, seeking to have the merger overturned and to have the two unions separated to their pre-merger organizations.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-74)

### Community theater

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Community theater")]

In 2021, Asner traveled to [Monte Rio, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Rio,_California "Monte Rio, California"), to support the reopening, revitalization, and shifted focus of the local Monte Rio Theater.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-76)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Asner was married to Nancy Lou Sykes from 1959 to 1988. They had three children, twins Matthew and Liza, and Kate. In 1987, he had a son named Charles with Carol Jean Vogelman.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-78) Asner was a parent and a grandparent to [autistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism "Autism") children and was involved with the [501(c)(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)(3)_organization "501(c)(3) organization")[nonprofit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization")[Autism Speaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism_Speaks "Autism Speaks").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-79) He also served as a [board member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") and adviser for Aspiritech, a nonprofit organization that trains high-functioning autistic persons to test software and perform [quality-assurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_assurance "Quality assurance") services for companies.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-81)

Asner became engaged to producer Cindy Gilmore in 1991. They married on August 2, 1998. Gilmore filed for [legal separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_separation "Legal separation") on November 7, 2007.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-82) Asner filed for [divorce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divorce "Divorce") in 2015.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-83)

Asner died of natural causes at his home in the [Tarzana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarzana,_Los_Angeles "Tarzana, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on August 29, 2021, at the age of 91.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-85) He was buried at Sheffield Cemetery in Kansas City, Missouri, on September 12.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-86) Several publications, including _The New York Times_, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ and _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, included a full name of "Edward David Asner" in articles about his death.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-89)

**Eddie Asner**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Tname-1) ([/ˈ æ z n ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); November 15, 1929 – August 29, 2021) was an American actor. He is most notable for portraying [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant") on the sitcom _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ (1970–1977) and drama _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–1982), making him one of the few television actors to portray the same character in both a comedy and a drama.

Asner won seven [Primetime Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards"), the most of any male performer. Five were for portraying Lou Grant: three as [Supporting Actor in a Comedy Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Supporting_Actor_in_a_Comedy_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series") on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and two as [Lead Actor in a Dramatic Television Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actor_in_a_Drama_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series") on the spin-off _Lou Grant_. The other two were for performances in the miniseries _[Rich Man, Poor Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich\_Man,\_Poor\_Man\_(miniseries) "Rich Man, Poor Man (miniseries)")_ (1976) and _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(1977\_miniseries) "Roots (1977 miniseries)")_ (1977).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Asner acted in the films _[El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Dorado\_(1966\_film) "El Dorado (1966 film)")_ (1966), _[They Call Me Mister Tibbs!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Call\_Me\_Mister\_Tibbs! "They Call Me Mister Tibbs!")_ (1970), _[Fort Apache, The Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort\_Apache,\_The\_Bronx "Fort Apache, The Bronx")_ (1981), _[JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK\_(film) "JFK (film)")_ (1991), and _[Too Big to Fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too\_Big\_to\_Fail\_(film) "Too Big to Fail (film)")_ (2011). He also played [Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") in several films and voiced [Carl Fredricksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Fredricksen "Carl Fredricksen") in the [Pixar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixar "Pixar") animated film _[Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_(2009\_film) "Up (2009 film)")_ (2009).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-3)

Asner starred in the [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") sitcom _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_ (1994–1995), and _[Michael: Every Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael:\_Every\_Day "Michael: Every Day")_ (2011–2017). He also acted extensively in numerous television series such as _[The Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Practice "The Practice")_, _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_, _[The Good Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Good\_Wife "The Good Wife")_, _[Cobra Kai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra\_Kai "Cobra Kai")_, _[Briarpatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Briarpatch\_(TV\_series) "Briarpatch (TV series)")_, _[Working Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working\_Class\_(TV\_series) "Working Class (TV series)")_, and _[Dead to Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_to\_Me\_(TV\_series) "Dead to Me (TV series)")_. He also voiced [J. Jonah Jameson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Jonah_Jameson "J. Jonah Jameson") in _[Spider-Man: The Animated Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:\_The\_Animated\_Series "Spider-Man: The Animated Series")_ (1994–1998), Hudson in _[Gargoyles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyles\_(TV\_series) "Gargoyles (TV series)")_ (1994–1997), and Ed Wuncler Sr. in _[The Boondocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boondocks\_(TV\_series) "The Boondocks (TV series)")_ (2005–2014).

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Asner was born November 15, 1929,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-4) in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), and grew up in [Kansas City, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Kansas "Kansas City, Kansas").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His parents, Lizzie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Seliger; 1885–1967), a housewife, and Morris David Asner (1879–1957),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-6) were [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jewish "Ashkenazi Jewish") immigrants from [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") who ran a [second-hand shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand_shop "Second-hand shop") and junkyard.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-birthplace-5) His four older siblings were Ben J. Asner (1915–1986), Eve Asner (1916–2014), Esther Edelman (1919–2014) and Labe Asner (1923–2017).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7) He was raised in an [Orthodox Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Jewish "Orthodox Jewish") family and given the [Hebrew name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_name "Hebrew name") Yitzhak (יִצְחָק).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Asner-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-9)

Asner attended [Wyandotte High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandotte_High_School "Wyandotte High School") in Kansas City, Kansas, and the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"). He studied journalism in Chicago until a professor advised him there was little money to be made in the profession. He had been working in a steel mill,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-Palast-10) but he quickly switched to drama, debuting as the martyred [Thomas Becket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Becket "Thomas Becket") in a campus production of [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot")'s _[Murder in the Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder\_in\_the\_Cathedral "Murder in the Cathedral")_. He eventually dropped out of school, going to work as a taxi driver, worked on the assembly line for [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors"), and other odd jobs before being drafted in the military in 1951.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-11)

Asner served with the [United States Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps") from 1951 to 1953 during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and appeared in plays that toured army bases in Europe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-12)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-NYT-7)

### 1955–1969: Early work and television roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1955–1969: Early work and television roles")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1970.jpg)

Cast of _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970, with Asner in center rear

Following his military service, Asner helped found the Playwrights Theatre Company in Chicago, but left for [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") before members of that company regrouped as the [Compass Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_Players "Compass Players") in the mid-1950s.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-eb-13) He later made frequent guest appearances with the successor to Compass, [The Second City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_City "The Second City").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-14) In New York City, [Off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") roles included Jonathan Jeremiah Peachum in the revival of _[Threepenny Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Threepenny\_Opera "The Threepenny Opera")_ and in Otway's [Venice Preserv'd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Preserv'd "Venice Preserv'd") in late 1955.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-15) Asner scored his first [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") role in _Face of a Hero_ alongside [Jack Lemmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lemmon "Jack Lemmon") in 1960, and began to make inroads as a television actor, having made his TV debut in 1957 on _[Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse\_Studio\_One "Westinghouse Studio One")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2) In two notable performances on television, Asner played Detective Sgt. Thomas Siroleo in the 1963 episode of _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_ titled "[It Crawled Out of the Woodwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Crawled_Out_of_the_Woodwork "It Crawled Out of the Woodwork")" and the reprehensible ex-premier Brynov in the 1965 _[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyage\_to\_the\_Bottom\_of\_the\_Sea\_(TV\_series) "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)")_ episode "The Exile". He made his film debut in 1962, in the [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") vehicle _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad "Kid Galahad")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-cnn-2)

Before landing his role with [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show"), Asner guest-starred in television series including four episodes of _[The Untouchables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Untouchables\_(1959\_TV\_series) "The Untouchables (1959 TV series)")_ starring [Robert Stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stack "Robert Stack"), the [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_syndication "Television syndication")[crime drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_drama "Crime drama")_[Decoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoy\_(TV\_series) "Decoy (TV series)")_, starring [Beverly Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Garland "Beverly Garland"), two episodes of _[Naked City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked\_City\_(TV\_series) "Naked City (TV series)")_ in 1961, and _[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route\_66\_(TV\_series) "Route 66 (TV series)")_ in 1962 (the episode titled "Welcome to the Wedding") as Custody Officer Lincoln Peers. He was cast on [Jack Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lord "Jack Lord")'s [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") drama series _[Stoney Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoney\_Burke\_(TV\_series) "Stoney Burke (TV series)")_ and in the series finale of [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS")'s _[The Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Reporter\_(TV\_series) "The Reporter (TV series)")_, starring [Harry Guardino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Guardino "Harry Guardino"). He also appeared on _[Mr. Novak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Novak "Mr. Novak")_, _[Ben Casey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben\_Casey "Ben Casey")_, _[Gunsmoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke "Gunsmoke")_, _[Mission: Impossible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission:\_Impossible\_(1966\_TV\_series) "Mission: Impossible (1966 TV series)")_, _[The Outer Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outer\_Limits\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)")_, _[The Fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fugitive\_(1963\_TV\_series) "The Fugitive (1963 TV series)")_, and _[The Invaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Invaders "The Invaders")_. In 1963, Asner appeared as George Johnson on _[The Virginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Virginian\_(TV\_series) "The Virginian (TV series)")_ in the episode "Echo of Another Day".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-16) In 1968 he was the villain Furman Crotty in the Wild Wild West episode "The Night of the Amnesiac".

### 1970–1982: _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ and _Lou Grant_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ed_Asner&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1970–1982: The Mary Tyler Moore Show and Lou Grant")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg/250px-Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Tyler_Moore_cast_1977.jpg)

Publicity photo of the cast of [The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show") in 1977. From left standing: [Ted Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Knight "Ted Knight") (Ted Baxter), [Gavin McLeod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_McLeod "Gavin McLeod") (Murray Slaughter), Ed Asner (Lou Grant). Seated: [Betty White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_White "Betty White") (Sue Ann Nivens), [Georgia Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Engel "Georgia Engel") (Georgette Baxter), [Mary Tyler Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Tyler_Moore "Mary Tyler Moore") (Mary Richards).

Asner was best known for his character [Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Grant "Lou Grant"), who was first introduced on _[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mary\_Tyler\_Moore\_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")_ in 1970. In 1977, after Moore's series ended, Asner's character was given his own show, _[Lou Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou\_Grant\_(TV\_series) "Lou Grant (TV series)")_ (1977–82). In contrast to the _Mary Tyler Moore_ series, a thirty-minute award-winning comedy about television journalism, the _Lou Grant_ series was an hour-long award-winning drama about newspaper journalism. For his role as Grant, Asner was one of only two actors to win an Emmy Award for a sitcom and a drama for the same role (the second being [Uzo Aduba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzo_Aduba "Uzo Aduba")). In addition he made appearances as Lou Grant on two other shows: _[Rhoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhoda "Rhoda")_ and _[Roseanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne "Roseanne")_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-17) Other television series starring Asner in regular roles include _[Thunder Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder\_Alley\_(TV\_series) "Thunder Alley (TV series)")_, _[The Bronx Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bronx\_Zoo\_(TV\_series) "The Bronx Zoo (TV series)")_, and _[Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio\_60\_on\_the\_Sunset\_Strip "Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip")_. He also starred in one episode of the [Western series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerns_on_television "Westerns on television")_[Dead Man's Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Man's\_Gun "Dead Man's Gun")_ (1997), as well as portraying art smuggler August March in an episode of the original _[Hawaii Five-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-O\_(1968\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)")_ (1975) and reprised the role in the _[Hawaii Five-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii\_Five-0\_(2010\_TV\_series) "Hawaii Five-0 (2010 TV series)")_ (2012) remake.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-18) He also appeared as a streetwise veteran police officer in an episode of the 1973 version of _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1973\_TV\_series) "Police Story (1973 TV series)")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Asner#cite_note-19)

Asner was acclaimed for his role in the ABC miniseries _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(1977\_miniseries) "Roots (1977 miniseries)")_, as Captain Davies, the morally conflicted captain of the _Lord Ligonier_, the slave ship that brought [Kunta Kinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunta_Kinte "Kunta Kinte") to America.
