The site of the fatal fire is now occupied the large high-rise Marriott Philadelphia Downtown hotel. There is no memorial marker at the site.

Commentary:

The tragic fire at the Hunt, Wilkinson & Company furniture factory remains the deadliest fire in the history of the City of Philadelphia. The blaze started in the basement of the building and involved flammable solvents and lacquers. The uncontrolled fire roared up an open elevator shaft trapping dozens of workers on the upper floors. The unsprinklered brick and joist structure was equipped on the back side of the building with early style iron fire escapes that featured vertical ladders between the balconies. Many victims were trapped on the balconies as the vertical ladders slowed the descent of workers attempting to flee the burning structure. Shortly after the fire, the city recognized the inadequacies of these types of fire escapes and they were prohibited in new construction, yet many existing buildings equipped with them remained. It wasn’t until several more years that this type of dangerous fire escape was finally outlawed in the city.

This large loss of life fire has been generally overlooked by many fire historians and has largely been overshadowed by another factory fire that occurred ten years later in New York City at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company that killed 146 garment factory workers in 1911: [[https://www.facebook.com/.../permalink/938730834464485/](https://www.facebook.com/groups/192218352449074/permalink/938730834464485/?__cft__[0]=AZjP95yTjWpY7K4GBiHqXvBVG9MDzodxEfeQxvvUoBhnNSBD2QgP4o8YRU_SDYwN8JCJJUYfSOR9fjNLAeSgbCKnEHCszaRPpgZFxBhyPjGTKNu01ghCvVHmKqvSuSKKaCJwSRWtUm6y0jumvH-dYnr2Jm70R6L1ujDKYTTptLjWSimNCdVd44vWTDb0RbfI0V9i&__tn__=-UK-R)](https://www.facebook.com/groups/192218352449074/permalink/938730834464485/?__cft__[0]=AZjP95yTjWpY7K4GBiHqXvBVG9MDzodxEfeQxvvUoBhnNSBD2QgP4o8YRU_SDYwN8JCJJUYfSOR9fjNLAeSgbCKnEHCszaRPpgZFxBhyPjGTKNu01ghCvVHmKqvSuSKKaCJwSRWtUm6y0jumvH-dYnr2Jm70R6L1ujDKYTTptLjWSimNCdVd44vWTDb0RbfI0V9i&__tn__=-UK-R)

**22 Workers Killed and Dozens Injured During Furniture Factory Fire - The Hunt, Wilkinson & Company Fire - 1219-1221 Market Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania - October 25, 1901**

Dozens of trapped workers were killed and injured in a fast-moving fire located in a furniture factory in Center City Philadelphia on October 25, 1901. The fire was reported to have started in the basement and involved flammable varnishes and lacquers. The flames raced up an open elevator shaft and quickly spread to the upper floors. Panicked employees frantically attempted to escape the thick black smoke and flames by using the fire escapes but were trapped by the advancing fire. Many were forced to jump to their deaths while a large crowd watched in horror. City firefighters, many of whom were injured themselves, were almost powerless to stop the fire or rescue the threatened.

The structure involved in the incident was a seven-story with basement Type III Ordinary construction double mercantile loft building located midblock at 1219-1221 Market Street between North Twelfth and North Thirteenth Streets in Center City Philadelphia. The building was occupied by the Hunt, Wilkinson & Company Furniture Factory and was part of a row of mercantile shops and factories that lined the street near the center of the city. The structure measured about 40 feet wide and 170 feet deep. An open shaft elevator and stairway served all the floors. Iron fire escapes were attached to the building on Side Charlie. The roof was flat with a large skylight at the center of the roof near Side Delta and a seven-foot-high parapet wall was along the roof edge on Side Alpha which faced 100-foot-wide Market Street. On Exposure Bravo was a seven-story with basement mercantile loft building. On Side Charlie was narrow 20-foot-wide Commerce Street that separated the factory building from several brick and wood joist dwellings. On Exposure Delta was a three-and-one-half story brick and wood joist mercantile building with a store on the first floor and dwellings above. The building was not equipped with a fire alarm system or an automatic fire sprinkler system. A fire hydrant was located across Market Street from the fire building. Fire alarm call boxes were located at each end of the block.

A description of the fire follows from an article published in Fire Engineering magazine on November 2, 1901:

Philadelphia’s Awful Fire

Never in the history of Philadelphia was known such a disastrous fire attended with so great a loss of life and injury as that of Friday, October 25, which destroyed the building at 1219 -1221 Market Street, occupied by Hunt, Wilkinson & Co., upholsterers and furniture dealers and three three-story buildings occupied by small merchants. The big furniture building extended back a half block to Commerce Street. The origin of the fire is variously put down to an explosion of naphtha or gasoline, “spontaneous combustion,” and the communication of flame from a lantern used by an elevator constructor in the basement to some of the gaseous liquids stored there.

Whatever it was, the flames spread with a rapidity never known before in any other fire in the city, up the elevator shaft, bursting through to the stairways and through each entrance from the elevator into each floor, as they were sucked up the shaft (which served as a flue) to the roof of the building, which before the fire department appeared on the scene (and it was as quick as usual in turning out) was alight from basement to attic. Each separate floor was filled full of furniture, draperies, and the like, besides which naphtha, gasoline, varnish, excelsior, chips of wood, and other combustible and inflammable matter lay all round. These fed the blaze, which was already being fanned with intolerable fierceness by the draught created by the fire within and the very high wind that was blowing outside. By 11:20 am, one hour after the fire had broken out, the fearful loss of life had taken place, and something like half a million dollars’ worth of property had been destroyed.

The scene from the street was something awful. Men and women died a lingering, agonizing death in the presence of thousands of spectators, who were unable to lift a hand to their assistance. The rear of Hunt, Wilkinson & Co.’s building is in Commerce Street, a small thoroughfare. On the fire escapes at the end of the building two men and one woman were slowly roasted to death, while the horror-stricken throng in the street below turned sick at the sight. In the front, in Market Street, a woman, driven to desperation, leaped, her garments on fire, from a window on the top floor and was dashed to death on the pavement. These are only a few of the heartrending scenes attending the conflagration. Firemen say they saw men and women, unable to reach the windows or fire escapes, burned to death in the interior of the building.

The firm employed 100 persons; besides these were on the premises outside workmen and some customers. Of the employees more than one-half were on the upper five floors, and it was among these (chiefly women, on the sixth floor, employed in sewing) that the most deaths took place. They were at work in the rear of the building, close to the fire escapes, which were of the ordinary Jacob’s ladder type and exposed to the flames as they burst through the windows and became confused by the great quantity of smoke that rushed out through the building. It was reported that goods were stored against the windows, which prevented the women from getting out on the fire escapes. On the seventh floor there were twenty upholsterers at work, and, thanks to the great presence of mind of the foreman of the floor, who is an official of the volunteer fire department at Mount Holly, New Jersey, all escaped unhurt. As soon as he learned of the fire, he marshaled his men and led them through the thick smoke down the stairway and safely into the street.

There were eleven employees and a number of outside workmen on the eighth floor. A ladder reached from this floor to the roof, which would have enabled those on that floor to reach the roof of an adjoining eight-story building; but in the excitement this means of escape was forgotten. Several made the terrible leap to the sidewalk and were crushed, while the others ran the gauntlet of smoke and fire down the rear fire escapes. With the possible exception of the engineer, who perished, but not before he had warned those in the basement to escape for their lives, all persons on the first three floors got out of the building safely. The members of the firm had their offices on the third floor, and their familiarity with the exits is all that saved them from suffocation. Mr. Wilkinson said that the smoke came up the stairway and elevator shaft in such great volumes that he and Mr. Hunt had much difficulty in reaching the street.

For an hour, the roaring flames threatened the lives of all who were compelled to work at fighting the fire or protecting the surrounding property, and every minute of time threatened many other thousands of dollars’ worth of property on all sides of the principal building in which the blaze started. It looked for a time as if the entire block would become a prey to the flames; but the falling of the walls of the burning building prevented the spread of the fire. Adjoining the Hunt, Wilkinson & Co. building is an eight-story structure nearing completion. When the walls of the blazing establishment collapsed the firemen secured a better opportunity of playing upon the adjoining business houses and thus prevented the flames from attacking surrounding property.

By noon, the fire was under control. Small buildings in the rear of the furniture building and also to the west of the burned area were crushed by falling walls. The fronts of the stores on the south side of Market Street, opposite the fire, were all more or less damaged by the heat. Great tongues of flame, swept along by the northwest wind, shot across the broad thoroughfare, and for a time it looked as if the fire would spread to these buildings.

The loss is estimated at half a million dollars, most of which will fall on Hunt, Wilkinson & Co., whose loss is estimated at $250,000. Henry C. Lea’s loss on the building is about $150,000. William F. Potts & Son suffered a loss of $60,000, while other occupants of the Potts buildings and surrounding property owners suffered other losses aggregating $25,000. The Philadelphia firemen worked nobly and displayed the greatest heroism. Many of them received more or less serious hurts, among them Chief Baxter; but no lives were lost so far as concerned them. They have no fire-nets and so were obliged to extemporize some for the poor victims to jump into. Too many jumped unsuccessfully.

Selected quotes on the fire from other media sources in 1901:

“Never in its history has Philadelphia experienced a fire which spread with such great rapidity,” reported the Inquirer. Never before were so many victims “speeded through gates of eternity,” reported the Atlanta Constitution. “Rows of charred bodies at the morgue, a score of homes made desolate, a gaunt pile of twisted, steaming ruins on Market Street between Twelfth and Thirteenth, are monuments to a fire” that was “swift as a whirlwind, sickening in its horrors.”

First responders were quick, “but the flames were quicker.” The fire rose quickly “from cellar to roof, eating into adjoining buildings and hanging in a seething, spark-dotted canopy over Market street.”

Hell reigned outside and in: “Sixty or more men, women and children were at work on the upper floors of the building. The roaring flames and the suffocating smoke that cut off retreat were their first and only warnings. Madly they groped for windows and the fire escapes, many meeting death where they stood, others reaching the iron railed balconies, only to find themselves like rats in a trap, confronted with the alternative of being gridironed or the chance of being crushed on the stones below. Most of those killed were at work on the sixth floor, where women were engaged in sewing. It was reported that goods were stored against the windows, which prevented the women from getting out on the fire escapes, but this was positively denied by a member of the firm.”

“Thousands from the streets below witnessed tragedy upon tragedy, powerless to help. They saw women penned in by flame tearing out their hair in their frenzy. They saw men struggle on wires and gratings and burn as they hung between earth and sky. They saw others plunge from the windows or turn and stagger back into the pitiless cauldron. The stones of Commerce Street, the narrow highway at the rear of the building, rang the dirge of more than one victim who jumped blindly and missed the net.”

“Squares away the screams of the dying could be heard. Tongues cannot tell the horrors that eyes saw.”

At one point, “all eyes turned to the fire escapes” outside a seventh-story window, where upholsterers “were running down the escape pell-mell. The smoke ascending in their faces was growing blacker and blacker. A man appeared at the window with a woman. He put his arm around her waist. They began to climb down the escape and reached the sixth floor. He seemed to faint. They stopped to rest, and then made another struggle.”

“Cheer after cheer went up from the street at this. But the situation was growing more desperate every second. When the next wave of smoke passed, the woman was seen standing alone on the landing. It was impossible for her to get down through the flames beneath her. She heard the shouts and news the net had been spread below to catch her. She had one chance in a hundred to save her life by a leap. The firemen grabbed their net and looked up. They could not see her. The woman peered down. She could not see them. Persons father away tried to shout directions. It was a guess. It was her only chance. She leaped. Her form came straight through the air, feet foremost. She jumped well and clear. Thousands of eyes watched the flying form. They saw it strike the iron rail of the awning. She dropped a little to one side of the net outstretched to save her and struck the pavement. Such was the death of Susan Gormley, 42 years of age, of 1727 Filbert Street.”

A special jury of experts convened by the City Coroner collected evidence, reviewed testimony and found the structure in compliance with what safety codes existed. They couldn’t zero in on what started the fire, suggesting the deceased “could probably explain the direct cause.” And they recommended sweeping changes aimed at prevention, mitigation and “providing proper and sufficient means of escape.”

The site of the fatal fire is now occupied the large high-rise Marriott Philadelphia Downtown hotel. There is no memorial marker at the site.

Commentary:

The tragic fire at the Hunt, Wilkinson & Company furniture factory remains the deadliest fire in the history of the City of Philadelphia. The blaze started in the basement of the building and involved flammable solvents and lacquers. The uncontrolled fire roared up an open elevator shaft trapping dozens of workers on the upper floors. The unsprinklered brick and joist structure was equipped on the back side of the building with early style iron fire escapes that featured vertical ladders between the balconies. Many victims were trapped on the balconies as the vertical ladders slowed the descent of workers attempting to flee the burning structure. Shortly after the fire, the city recognized the inadequacies of these types of fire escapes and they were prohibited in new construction, yet many existing buildings equipped with them remained. It wasn’t until several more years that this type of dangerous fire escape was finally outlawed in the city.

This large loss of life fire has been generally overlooked by many fire historians and has largely been overshadowed by another factory fire that occurred ten years later in New York City at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company that killed 146 garment factory workers in 1911: [[https://www.facebook.com/.../permalink/938730834464485/](https://www.facebook.com/groups/192218352449074/permalink/938730834464485/?__cft__[0]=AZjP95yTjWpY7K4GBiHqXvBVG9MDzodxEfeQxvvUoBhnNSBD2QgP4o8YRU_SDYwN8JCJJUYfSOR9fjNLAeSgbCKnEHCszaRPpgZFxBhyPjGTKNu01ghCvVHmKqvSuSKKaCJwSRWtUm6y0jumvH-dYnr2Jm70R6L1ujDKYTTptLjWSimNCdVd44vWTDb0RbfI0V9i&__tn__=-UK-R)](https://www.facebook.com/groups/192218352449074/permalink/938730834464485/?__cft__[0]=AZjP95yTjWpY7K4GBiHqXvBVG9MDzodxEfeQxvvUoBhnNSBD2QgP4o8YRU_SDYwN8JCJJUYfSOR9fjNLAeSgbCKnEHCszaRPpgZFxBhyPjGTKNu01ghCvVHmKqvSuSKKaCJwSRWtUm6y0jumvH-dYnr2Jm70R6L1ujDKYTTptLjWSimNCdVd44vWTDb0RbfI0V9i&__tn__=-UK-R)

Despite the large loss of life in the Philadelphia fire, it is often not listed among the list of the deadliest fires in the United States.

# Industrial Modern @ Buggy Works

Share:
*   [Email](mailto:?subject=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works&body=I%20thought%20you%20might%20like%20this%20post%20from%20European%20Home%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)

*   [Houzz](http://www.houzz.com/imageClipperUpload?link=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F&imageUrl=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2017%2F08%2FLucius140-Steel-PS.jpg&title=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works)
*   [Twitter](https://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works&url=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)

There has been something of an industrial design Renaissance happening in the rust belt and across the nation. Recently, we discovered an old Buggy Works factory in Ohio that has been re-purposed and remodeled into modern condominiums. The residents here have embraced the historic nature of this old factory, while adding their own modern touches along the way.

First, a bit of history about the factory.

![Image 3](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/d503b24af1ea632e2acf57f2b26e9ef4-huntsville-buggy.jpg)
_The old Buggy Works Factory in the early 1900’s._

In 1904, the Columbus Buggy Company opened a new plant to accommodate for its growth. With the introduction of the automobile, buggy and carriage manufacturers faced serious competition. They began to produce automobiles, both electric and gas powered. Unfortunately, these changes weren’t enough as the company shut down in 1913 after going bankrupt.

After many years of vacancy, this warehouse has now been renovated into 68 urban lofts. The historic aspect combined with the modern sophistication create the foundation of a unique urban village, just steps away from all the city’s cultural and entertainment options.

![Image 4](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/outside-of-building-present.jpg)
_The newly remodeled Buggy Works Factory, that is now used as condominiums._

We sat down with one of the condo owners, Cyndi Collins, to talk about industrial modern design and the new Lucius 140, peninsula fireplace on which her entire design centers.

**What first inspired the design for this space?**

The overall design of the building was really what inspired us. The exposed brick, the wood beams… it already had such a rustic and unique look.

![Image 5](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-PS.jpg)
_The Lucius 140 is the focal point of this industrial modern space._

**Tell us about the fabrication of the fireplace hearth.**

We worked with a really skilled metal fabricator — [Fortin Ironworks](http://www.fortinironworks.com/). We have worked with them for years and years now. They do great ironwork and are very old school in their approach. The best part is, they truly love doing what they do. We actually had the fireplace shipped right to them so they could custom-create the hearth for us.

**A lot of the original industrial details from this space are still present and some new elements are added, such as that I-beam hearth. Why was it important for you to keep this industrial aesthetic?**

The building itself is what we originally fell in love with. It was so unique and we wanted to bring out its inner character. I’d say in general, I gravitate to more imaginative spaces.

![Image 6](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-2.jpg)
_“We use this space for everything- Living room, dining room, reading room. It’s our favorite place to be.”_

**What is your favorite design piece of the room?**

I would say the fireplace. I did a lot of searching to find the perfect fireplace. I started looking at 4-sided, peninsulas, room dividers… I can’t tell you how many hours I spent. It became my project every night before bed. I wanted it to be the heart of the home.

![Image 7](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-3.jpg)
The Grey Stones fire media complement the textures of the brick wall throughout the space.

**This is truly a beautiful space, thank you so much for your time.**

You’re welcome! I just love how you can move around the space and still see the Lucius from everywhere since it is so wide open. We’re all really happy with it. Our favorite thing to do as a family on a cold day is light up our fireplace and all huddle around.

**Citations:**

All photography by John Evans

Thank you to our friends at[Mid Ohio Hearth Products](http://www.columbusfireplaces.com/), of Columbus, OH for this beautiful installation.

![Image 8](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Jamie-Nickerson-150x150.jpg)**_Posted By: Jamie Nickerson_**

_Jamie is a Marketing Intern at European Home. She is pursuing her bachelor’s degree in Marketing at Endicott College.She loves how digital media connects us with so many great designs all across the globe. “I love finding our fireplaces in beautiful places such as Australia, Norway and NYC- all from the comfort of my desk chair!”_

# Industrial Modern @ Buggy Works

Share:
*   [Email](mailto:?subject=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works&body=I%20thought%20you%20might%20like%20this%20post%20from%20European%20Home%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)
*   [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)
*   [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/cws/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)
*   [Pinterest](http://pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F&description=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works)
*   [Houzz](http://www.houzz.com/imageClipperUpload?link=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F&imageUrl=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2017%2F08%2FLucius140-Steel-PS.jpg&title=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works)
*   [Twitter](https://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Industrial%20Modern%20%40%20Buggy%20Works&url=https%3A%2F%2Feuropeanhome.com%2Funcategorized%2Findustrial-modern-buggy-works%2F)

There has been something of an industrial design Renaissance happening in the rust belt and across the nation. Recently, we discovered an old Buggy Works factory in Ohio that has been re-purposed and remodeled into modern condominiums. The residents here have embraced the historic nature of this old factory, while adding their own modern touches along the way.

First, a bit of history about the factory.

![Image 3](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/d503b24af1ea632e2acf57f2b26e9ef4-huntsville-buggy.jpg)
_The old Buggy Works Factory in the early 1900’s._

In 1904, the Columbus Buggy Company opened a new plant to accommodate for its growth. With the introduction of the automobile, buggy and carriage manufacturers faced serious competition. They began to produce automobiles, both electric and gas powered. Unfortunately, these changes weren’t enough as the company shut down in 1913 after going bankrupt.

After many years of vacancy, this warehouse has now been renovated into 68 urban lofts. The historic aspect combined with the modern sophistication create the foundation of a unique urban village, just steps away from all the city’s cultural and entertainment options.

![Image 4](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/outside-of-building-present.jpg)
_The newly remodeled Buggy Works Factory, that is now used as condominiums._

We sat down with one of the condo owners, Cyndi Collins, to talk about industrial modern design and the new Lucius 140, peninsula fireplace on which her entire design centers.

**What first inspired the design for this space?**

The overall design of the building was really what inspired us. The exposed brick, the wood beams… it already had such a rustic and unique look.

![Image 5](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-PS.jpg)
_The Lucius 140 is the focal point of this industrial modern space._

**Tell us about the fabrication of the fireplace hearth.**

We worked with a really skilled metal fabricator — [Fortin Ironworks](http://www.fortinironworks.com/). We have worked with them for years and years now. They do great ironwork and are very old school in their approach. The best part is, they truly love doing what they do. We actually had the fireplace shipped right to them so they could custom-create the hearth for us.

**A lot of the original industrial details from this space are still present and some new elements are added, such as that I-beam hearth. Why was it important for you to keep this industrial aesthetic?**

The building itself is what we originally fell in love with. It was so unique and we wanted to bring out its inner character. I’d say in general, I gravitate to more imaginative spaces.

![Image 6](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-2.jpg)
_“We use this space for everything- Living room, dining room, reading room. It’s our favorite place to be.”_

**What is your favorite design piece of the room?**

I would say the fireplace. I did a lot of searching to find the perfect fireplace. I started looking at 4-sided, peninsulas, room dividers… I can’t tell you how many hours I spent. It became my project every night before bed. I wanted it to be the heart of the home.

![Image 7](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Lucius140-Steel-3.jpg)
The Grey Stones fire media complement the textures of the brick wall throughout the space.

**This is truly a beautiful space, thank you so much for your time.**

You’re welcome! I just love how you can move around the space and still see the Lucius from everywhere since it is so wide open. We’re all really happy with it. Our favorite thing to do as a family on a cold day is light up our fireplace and all huddle around.

**Citations:**

All photography by John Evans

Thank you to our friends at[Mid Ohio Hearth Products](http://www.columbusfireplaces.com/), of Columbus, OH for this beautiful installation.

![Image 8](https://europeanhome.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Jamie-Nickerson-150x150.jpg)**_Posted By: Jamie Nickerson_**

_Jamie is a Marketing Intern at European Home. She is pursuing her bachelor’s degree in Marketing at Endicott College.She loves how digital media connects us with so many great designs all across the globe. “I love finding our fireplaces in beautiful places such as Australia, Norway and NYC- all from the comfort of my desk chair!”_

The **Columbus Buggy Company** was an early [buggy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(automobile) "Buggy (automobile)") and [automotive manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_manufacturing "Automotive manufacturing") based in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), United States, from 1875 to 1913.

Begun by three business partners, the company set up its manufacturing facilities in what is today the [Arena District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_District "Arena District") producing inexpensive buggies and [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboards "Dashboards"), and quickly saw success. At its height it employed 1,200 people and was producing 100 buggies a day which were sold in every state in the United States. The company was one of the city's major employers and a significant portion of the city's buggy manufacturing economy. After the turn of the century it oriented itself toward production of electric vehicles and, later, of [automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles "Automobiles"). Crippled by the [Great Flood of 1913](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1913 "Great Flood of 1913") and unable to compete with cheaper alternatives like the [Model T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_T "Model T"), the company eventually went bankrupt in 1913, reorganized, and closed its doors a few years later.

It influenced the early automobile industry production methods and several notable employees, including [Eddie Rickenbacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rickenbacker "Eddie Rickenbacker") and [Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone"). The company buildings, after some time empty, have since been re-developed as office space in the Arena District.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg/250px-Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg)

First home of the Iron Buggy Co., the predecessor of the Columbus Buggy Co., at 180 N. High St. in Columbus

The Columbus Buggy Company was established by entrepreneur Clinton D. Firestone and brothers George and [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Glaze_Peters "Oscar Glaze Peters") Peters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892324-2) The three partners saw [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio") as a ripe location for a business thanks to cheap labor as well as the recent network of railroads created during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") reducing the costs of goods. The completion of the [Hocking Valley Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocking_Valley_Railway "Hocking Valley Railway") also granted them ample access to coal, wood and iron from [southeast Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Ohio "Southeast Ohio").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200385-3)

Before starting the company, the Peters brothers had worked in the leather trade,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200385-3) but had developed a process to produce cheap buggies for close to $150 apiece, using wood obtained from a company near the [Ohio Penitentiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Penitentiary "Ohio Penitentiary") and building using a specialized manufacturing system. Before 1870 they produced 100 and sold them successfully at auction, though their business partners refused further work, leaving them in debt.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4)[[Note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-6) In 1870, they were introduced to Firestone, a native of [Canton, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Ohio "Canton, Ohio") and who had operated a railroad business in [Cedar Rapids, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Rapids,_Iowa "Cedar Rapids, Iowa"), moved to Columbus and financed the business with $5,000. Their first venture, Iron Buggy Company, launched in 1870 in a shanty built for $100,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4) at 180 North High Street and focused it on selling cheap [buggies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(automobile) "Buggy (automobile)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200630-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012118-8) The business saw immediate success thanks to a design created by the Peters brothers and a system of labor that made production efficient, and it sold 237 buggies in its first year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978389-9) The building it was housed in burnt down on May 27, 1874, and was rebuilt.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892553-10) In 1875 its owners sold the business to another buggy producer, H. K. Tuller of Buckeye Buggy Company.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978389-9)

### Success

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Success")]

In 1875, the three formed the Columbus Buggy Company and Peters Dash Company,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200630-7) with $20,000 in capital.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4) Its first facility was locating at Wall and Locust streets near the modern day [One Nationwide Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Nationwide_Plaza "One Nationwide Plaza") building in the [Arena District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_District "Arena District"), immediately north of [downtown Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Columbus,_Ohio "Downtown Columbus, Ohio"), and near the Ohio Penitentiary and [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Columbus) "Union Station (Columbus)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11) His business specialized in making buggies that were affordable to people at all price ranges as well as [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboards "Dashboards"), carriage fenders, washes and straps for carriage dealers and manufacturers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892327-12) The company quickly saw success, drawing $50,000 in revenue in its first year, but sales quickly grew.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) By 1878 it had 250 employees and was making 100 buggies a week.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978391-13)

In 1883, the company had 1,000 employees and was producing 25,000 buggies a year. That year it was struck with a [patent infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") lawsuit from [Timken Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timken_Company "Timken Company"), alleging the company had stolen the idea for an "automatic" spring part used in its carriages, and seeking $50,000 in damages. Columbus Buggy Co. filed a [countersuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countersuit "Countersuit") and the two businesses traded barbs in [trade publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_publications "Trade publications") for two months before the courts decided in Studebaker's favor in December 1884.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199818-14) Columbus Buggy Co. was obliged to pay $3,000 in damages, though it began to use Timken springs in models starting in 1886, and the Timken and Firestone families maintained a friendly relationship during and after the litigation.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199819-15)

The company continued to add buildings as it continued to expand along High Street until it became the largest manufacturer of buggies in the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11) By 1888 it occupied an entire city block between High Street and Wall Street.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) In 1890 it pledged $5,000 to the creation of a [YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YMCA "YMCA") building in downtown Columbus.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892717-17) In the meantime, it began advertising its vehicles and dash products heavily in magazines.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978390-18)

At its height in 1892,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) the company employed 1,200 people and built 100 vehicles and 1,500 carriage [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboard "Dashboard") a day, with its products exported to other countries around the world. Its revenue grew to $2 million a year on an active capital of about $1 million and about $300,000 a month in payroll.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) The company had a presence at the [1893 Chicago World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1893_Chicago_World's_Fair "1893 Chicago World's Fair"), where it boasted that it had dealerships in every state and shipped overseas.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) By that year, though, its buggies, which sold for $110, were considered overpriced.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200235-19)

By 1900, about two dozen other buggy producers had formed around Columbus, with factories working day and night in the city, and an estimated one in six buggies in use around the world was built in Columbus.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) Some of these companies were older than Columbus Buggy Co,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892328-20) but the manufacturer remained one of the largest businesses in the city. Columbus Buggy Co. moved its production to a new plant at 400 Dublin Road in 1906 at Firestone's insistence.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11)

With the advent of the [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile "Automobile"), Columbus Buggy Co. found itself at a competitive disadvantage to companies in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), which had a greater access to steel.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) In 1903, though, it opted to produce an [electric vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") to compete with these new and increasingly popular vehicles.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21)

The 400 Dublin Road facility began producing its first electric [coupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupe "Coupe") in 1903, the Columbus Electric Model No. 1000. This would be one of several models of electric vehicle the company produced in larger scale beginning in 1905. The company advertised the vehicles as easy to operate, targeting women, and that they were quiet. But the vehicles were limited by a top speed of 20 miles per hour (32 km/h), limited range and a need to recharge batteries for several hours.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22) Powered by Willard batteries, this car sold for about $1,000.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) It produced several models including the No. 3003 Firestone Motor Buggy: a light motor buggy, which it also marketed to physicians as a medical [phaeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaeton_(carriage) "Phaeton (carriage)"), as well as the Columbus Station Wagon No. 1102, which was to be driven by a chauffeur while its passengers rode in an enclosed compartment.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21) In 1907, it bought the Springfield Automotive Company of [Springfield, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Ohio "Springfield, Ohio") which had been manufacturing the Bramwell, a [gasoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline "Gasoline") powered automobile.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)

In 1909, the company hired [Lee Frayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Frayer "Lee Frayer") to design a full-sized car, with [Eddie Rickenbacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rickenbacker "Eddie Rickenbacker") as his assistant.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) The Firestone-Columbus, a gasoline-powered car geared toward families, began production in 1909.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22) About 500 of the vehicles sold in the first year and it was generally well received in the market. Improvements were made to the vehicles continually as they were produced, as opposed to creating successive [model years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_year "Model year").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) There were a few different variations on the vehicle, including the model 76-A, an intermediate sized vehicle that could carry four passengers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21) The Columbus-Firestone was reported to be the first car with its [steering wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steering_wheel "Steering wheel") on the left side of the car.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25)

Introduced at the [1909 Chicago Auto Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1909_Chicago_Auto_Show "1909 Chicago Auto Show"), it became popular and sold 2,000 units a year, all made at the 400 Dublin Road plant. By 1912 there were more cars of this brand than any other in Columbus and the company was producing 2,000 a year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) But it also struggled to compete with cheaper competitors, notably the [Ford Model T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Model_T "Ford Model T").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22)

The company built a special [racing buggy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_car "Race car"), the Red Wing, which it entered into the [1911 Indianapolis 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Indianapolis_500 "1911 Indianapolis 500"), designed by Frayer and Rickenbacker and driven by Frayer. Though the car didn't finish the race, it was credited with finishing 13th in the race.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200714-26) They subsequently entered a car into the [1912 Indianapolis 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Indianapolis_500 "1912 Indianapolis 500"), this time driven by Rickenbacker. It finished 21st.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25)

### Decline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Decline")]

The business was affected by the severe flooding of local rivers during the [Great Flood of 1913](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1913 "Great Flood of 1913") and it this damaged the business sufficiently for it to declare [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) with the company $624,000 in debt. Initially it was offered for sale for 25 cents on the dollar, but received only one offer, for less than $100,000, prompting its interests, headed by Frank L. Chase, to withdraw the offer. Under an order from a federal judge, $273,000, or 44 percent of the debt, was eventually paid to creditors.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnonymous201236-27) In 1914, a new entity, named the New Columbus Buggy Co., was incorporated with $500,000 in capital under a new ownership group, including C. A. Finnegan and E. D. Hoefeller of [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnonymous201233-28) This entity, controlled by the company's creditors, continued production at the plant.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25) That same year, Firestone died.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) Both the Firestone Electric and the Columbus-Firestone vehicle lines were produced into 1915, when the company ceased operations, leaving an inventory of 35 new electric cars and 12 automobiles, as well as several used cars.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)

Following the closure of the Columbus Buggy Co. The [Allen Motor Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_(1913_Ohio_automobile) "Allen (1913 Ohio automobile)") of [Fostoria, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostoria,_Ohio "Fostoria, Ohio") leased the plant and built automobiles there before closing in 1923.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) The building itself was home to Janitrol Corp. before being redeveloped as the Buggyworks building in the 1990s.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002120-29)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg/250px-Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg)

[Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone") was a salesman for Columbus Buggy Co. before he launched his own company, [Firestone Tire & Rubber Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Tire_&_Rubber_Co. "Firestone Tire & Rubber Co."), in 1900.

The company played a key role in shaping the early history of the automobile.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) Its manufacturing processes for efficiently producing vehicles were notable and ahead of many companies of its time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978386-5) The success of the business brought attention to C. D. Firestone, who became a prominent figure in the carriage industry and he became president of the Carriage Builders National Association in 1888.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199818-14)[[Note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-32)

Several of the company's employees rose to great prominence in the industry. Clinton Firestone's cousin, [Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone"), was a salesmen for the company. During his time as a salesman, and racing buggies through the streets of [Detroit, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit,_Michigan "Detroit, Michigan"), Clinton Firestone met [Henry Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford "Henry Ford"), who helped him obtain tires for custom-built racing carriages.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200234-33) Firestone, seeing the advantage of the buggies' thick rubber tires, left the company and in 1900 founded the [Firestone Tire and Rubber Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Tire_and_Rubber_Company "Firestone Tire and Rubber Company") in [Akron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron,_Ohio "Akron, Ohio") to produce rubber tires for carriages and buggies. By 1904, it was the largest tire manufacturer in the world.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200235-19)

Eddie Rickenbacker joined the company at the age of 17, and he quickly became an engineer and troubleshooter, dispatched to help owners when they had problems with their vehicles, and his service increased the reputation of the business among its owners.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) It was during this assignment that Rickenbacker, while serving as a test driver for the vehicles, developed an affinity for driving fast cars.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed2003106-34)

Some of the original sales catalog promotional material of the company are still preserved in the [Henry Ford Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford_Museum "Henry Ford Museum").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-35)

### Buggyworks complex

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Buggyworks complex")]

The company's original buildings north of downtown Columbus were redeveloped as part of a larger revival of the industrial area north of Columbus — by then termed the Arena District — following the construction of [Nationwide Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_Arena "Nationwide Arena"). Nationwide Realty Investors, a development affiliate of [Nationwide Insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_Insurance "Nationwide Insurance"), acquired two of the production facilities at 390 and 400 W. Nationwide Blvd., termed the "Buggyworks", and redeveloped them into 145,000 square feet of office space.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-36) The development project cost $10.5 million.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-37) The office buildings attracted a number of tenants, the first being [Cameron Mitchell Restaurants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Mitchell_Restaurants "Cameron Mitchell Restaurants").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-38) Another portion of the complex at 440 W. Nationwide Blvd., was redeveloped into loft condominiums.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-39)

The **Columbus Buggy Company** was an early [buggy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(automobile) "Buggy (automobile)") and [automotive manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_manufacturing "Automotive manufacturing") based in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), United States, from 1875 to 1913.

Begun by three business partners, the company set up its manufacturing facilities in what is today the [Arena District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_District "Arena District") producing inexpensive buggies and [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboards "Dashboards"), and quickly saw success. At its height it employed 1,200 people and was producing 100 buggies a day which were sold in every state in the United States. The company was one of the city's major employers and a significant portion of the city's buggy manufacturing economy. After the turn of the century it oriented itself toward production of electric vehicles and, later, of [automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles "Automobiles"). Crippled by the [Great Flood of 1913](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1913 "Great Flood of 1913") and unable to compete with cheaper alternatives like the [Model T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_T "Model T"), the company eventually went bankrupt in 1913, reorganized, and closed its doors a few years later.

It influenced the early automobile industry production methods and several notable employees, including [Eddie Rickenbacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rickenbacker "Eddie Rickenbacker") and [Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone"). The company buildings, after some time empty, have since been re-developed as office space in the Arena District.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg/250px-Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iron_Buggy_Company_illustration.jpg)

First home of the Iron Buggy Co., the predecessor of the Columbus Buggy Co., at 180 N. High St. in Columbus

The Columbus Buggy Company was established by entrepreneur Clinton D. Firestone and brothers George and [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Glaze_Peters "Oscar Glaze Peters") Peters.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892324-2) The three partners saw [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio") as a ripe location for a business thanks to cheap labor as well as the recent network of railroads created during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") reducing the costs of goods. The completion of the [Hocking Valley Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocking_Valley_Railway "Hocking Valley Railway") also granted them ample access to coal, wood and iron from [southeast Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Ohio "Southeast Ohio").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200385-3)

Before starting the company, the Peters brothers had worked in the leather trade,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200385-3) but had developed a process to produce cheap buggies for close to $150 apiece, using wood obtained from a company near the [Ohio Penitentiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Penitentiary "Ohio Penitentiary") and building using a specialized manufacturing system. Before 1870 they produced 100 and sold them successfully at auction, though their business partners refused further work, leaving them in debt.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4)[[Note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-6) In 1870, they were introduced to Firestone, a native of [Canton, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Ohio "Canton, Ohio") and who had operated a railroad business in [Cedar Rapids, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Rapids,_Iowa "Cedar Rapids, Iowa"), moved to Columbus and financed the business with $5,000. Their first venture, Iron Buggy Company, launched in 1870 in a shanty built for $100,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4) at 180 North High Street and focused it on selling cheap [buggies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(automobile) "Buggy (automobile)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200630-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012118-8) The business saw immediate success thanks to a design created by the Peters brothers and a system of labor that made production efficient, and it sold 237 buggies in its first year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978389-9) The building it was housed in burnt down on May 27, 1874, and was rebuilt.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892553-10) In 1875 its owners sold the business to another buggy producer, H. K. Tuller of Buckeye Buggy Company.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978389-9)

### Success

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Success")]

In 1875, the three formed the Columbus Buggy Company and Peters Dash Company,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200630-7) with $20,000 in capital.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892326-4) Its first facility was locating at Wall and Locust streets near the modern day [One Nationwide Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Nationwide_Plaza "One Nationwide Plaza") building in the [Arena District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_District "Arena District"), immediately north of [downtown Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Columbus,_Ohio "Downtown Columbus, Ohio"), and near the Ohio Penitentiary and [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Columbus) "Union Station (Columbus)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11) His business specialized in making buggies that were affordable to people at all price ranges as well as [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboards "Dashboards"), carriage fenders, washes and straps for carriage dealers and manufacturers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892327-12) The company quickly saw success, drawing $50,000 in revenue in its first year, but sales quickly grew.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) By 1878 it had 250 employees and was making 100 buggies a week.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978391-13)

In 1883, the company had 1,000 employees and was producing 25,000 buggies a year. That year it was struck with a [patent infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") lawsuit from [Timken Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timken_Company "Timken Company"), alleging the company had stolen the idea for an "automatic" spring part used in its carriages, and seeking $50,000 in damages. Columbus Buggy Co. filed a [countersuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countersuit "Countersuit") and the two businesses traded barbs in [trade publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_publications "Trade publications") for two months before the courts decided in Studebaker's favor in December 1884.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199818-14) Columbus Buggy Co. was obliged to pay $3,000 in damages, though it began to use Timken springs in models starting in 1886, and the Timken and Firestone families maintained a friendly relationship during and after the litigation.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199819-15)

The company continued to add buildings as it continued to expand along High Street until it became the largest manufacturer of buggies in the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11) By 1888 it occupied an entire city block between High Street and Wall Street.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) In 1890 it pledged $5,000 to the creation of a [YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YMCA "YMCA") building in downtown Columbus.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892717-17) In the meantime, it began advertising its vehicles and dash products heavily in magazines.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978390-18)

At its height in 1892,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) the company employed 1,200 people and built 100 vehicles and 1,500 carriage [dashboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboard "Dashboard") a day, with its products exported to other countries around the world. Its revenue grew to $2 million a year on an active capital of about $1 million and about $300,000 a month in payroll.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) The company had a presence at the [1893 Chicago World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1893_Chicago_World's_Fair "1893 Chicago World's Fair"), where it boasted that it had dealerships in every state and shipped overseas.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200348-16) By that year, though, its buggies, which sold for $110, were considered overpriced.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200235-19)

By 1900, about two dozen other buggy producers had formed around Columbus, with factories working day and night in the city, and an estimated one in six buggies in use around the world was built in Columbus.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) Some of these companies were older than Columbus Buggy Co,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1892328-20) but the manufacturer remained one of the largest businesses in the city. Columbus Buggy Co. moved its production to a new plant at 400 Dublin Road in 1906 at Firestone's insistence.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012126%E2%80%93127-11)

With the advent of the [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile "Automobile"), Columbus Buggy Co. found itself at a competitive disadvantage to companies in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), which had a greater access to steel.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) In 1903, though, it opted to produce an [electric vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") to compete with these new and increasingly popular vehicles.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21)

The 400 Dublin Road facility began producing its first electric [coupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupe "Coupe") in 1903, the Columbus Electric Model No. 1000. This would be one of several models of electric vehicle the company produced in larger scale beginning in 1905. The company advertised the vehicles as easy to operate, targeting women, and that they were quiet. But the vehicles were limited by a top speed of 20 miles per hour (32 km/h), limited range and a need to recharge batteries for several hours.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22) Powered by Willard batteries, this car sold for about $1,000.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) It produced several models including the No. 3003 Firestone Motor Buggy: a light motor buggy, which it also marketed to physicians as a medical [phaeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaeton_(carriage) "Phaeton (carriage)"), as well as the Columbus Station Wagon No. 1102, which was to be driven by a chauffeur while its passengers rode in an enclosed compartment.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21) In 1907, it bought the Springfield Automotive Company of [Springfield, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Ohio "Springfield, Ohio") which had been manufacturing the Bramwell, a [gasoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline "Gasoline") powered automobile.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)

In 1909, the company hired [Lee Frayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Frayer "Lee Frayer") to design a full-sized car, with [Eddie Rickenbacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rickenbacker "Eddie Rickenbacker") as his assistant.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) The Firestone-Columbus, a gasoline-powered car geared toward families, began production in 1909.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22) About 500 of the vehicles sold in the first year and it was generally well received in the market. Improvements were made to the vehicles continually as they were produced, as opposed to creating successive [model years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_year "Model year").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) There were a few different variations on the vehicle, including the model 76-A, an intermediate sized vehicle that could carry four passengers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016156-21) The Columbus-Firestone was reported to be the first car with its [steering wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steering_wheel "Steering wheel") on the left side of the car.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25)

Introduced at the [1909 Chicago Auto Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1909_Chicago_Auto_Show "1909 Chicago Auto Show"), it became popular and sold 2,000 units a year, all made at the 400 Dublin Road plant. By 1912 there were more cars of this brand than any other in Columbus and the company was producing 2,000 a year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) But it also struggled to compete with cheaper competitors, notably the [Ford Model T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Model_T "Ford Model T").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002121-22)

The company built a special [racing buggy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_car "Race car"), the Red Wing, which it entered into the [1911 Indianapolis 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Indianapolis_500 "1911 Indianapolis 500"), designed by Frayer and Rickenbacker and driven by Frayer. Though the car didn't finish the race, it was credited with finishing 13th in the race.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett200714-26) They subsequently entered a car into the [1912 Indianapolis 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Indianapolis_500 "1912 Indianapolis 500"), this time driven by Rickenbacker. It finished 21st.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25)

### Decline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Decline")]

The business was affected by the severe flooding of local rivers during the [Great Flood of 1913](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1913 "Great Flood of 1913") and it this damaged the business sufficiently for it to declare [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) with the company $624,000 in debt. Initially it was offered for sale for 25 cents on the dollar, but received only one offer, for less than $100,000, prompting its interests, headed by Frank L. Chase, to withdraw the offer. Under an order from a federal judge, $273,000, or 44 percent of the debt, was eventually paid to creditors.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnonymous201236-27) In 1914, a new entity, named the New Columbus Buggy Co., was incorporated with $500,000 in capital under a new ownership group, including C. A. Finnegan and E. D. Hoefeller of [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnonymous201233-28) This entity, controlled by the company's creditors, continued production at the plant.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012108-25) That same year, Firestone died.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) Both the Firestone Electric and the Columbus-Firestone vehicle lines were produced into 1915, when the company ceased operations, leaving an inventory of 35 new electric cars and 12 automobiles, as well as several used cars.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23)

Following the closure of the Columbus Buggy Co. The [Allen Motor Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_(1913_Ohio_automobile) "Allen (1913 Ohio automobile)") of [Fostoria, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostoria,_Ohio "Fostoria, Ohio") leased the plant and built automobiles there before closing in 1923.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunter2012135-24) The building itself was home to Janitrol Corp. before being redeveloped as the Buggyworks building in the 1990s.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett2002120-29)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg/250px-Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvey_Samuel_Firestone_by_Underwood_c1910.jpeg)

[Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone") was a salesman for Columbus Buggy Co. before he launched his own company, [Firestone Tire & Rubber Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Tire_&_Rubber_Co. "Firestone Tire & Rubber Co."), in 1900.

The company played a key role in shaping the early history of the automobile.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed200386-1) Its manufacturing processes for efficiently producing vehicles were notable and ahead of many companies of its time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuttle1978386-5) The success of the business brought attention to C. D. Firestone, who became a prominent figure in the carriage industry and he became president of the Carriage Builders National Association in 1888.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPruitt199818-14)[[Note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-32)

Several of the company's employees rose to great prominence in the industry. Clinton Firestone's cousin, [Harvey S. Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_S._Firestone "Harvey S. Firestone"), was a salesmen for the company. During his time as a salesman, and racing buggies through the streets of [Detroit, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit,_Michigan "Detroit, Michigan"), Clinton Firestone met [Henry Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford "Henry Ford"), who helped him obtain tires for custom-built racing carriages.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200234-33) Firestone, seeing the advantage of the buggies' thick rubber tires, left the company and in 1900 founded the [Firestone Tire and Rubber Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Tire_and_Rubber_Company "Firestone Tire and Rubber Company") in [Akron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron,_Ohio "Akron, Ohio") to produce rubber tires for carriages and buggies. By 1904, it was the largest tire manufacturer in the world.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryan200235-19)

Eddie Rickenbacker joined the company at the age of 17, and he quickly became an engineer and troubleshooter, dispatched to help owners when they had problems with their vehicles, and his service increased the reputation of the business among its owners.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrenickWrenick2016158-23) It was during this assignment that Rickenbacker, while serving as a test driver for the vehicles, developed an affinity for driving fast cars.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTELentz,_Ed2003106-34)

Some of the original sales catalog promotional material of the company are still preserved in the [Henry Ford Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford_Museum "Henry Ford Museum").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-35)

### Buggyworks complex

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_Buggy_Company&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Buggyworks complex")]

The company's original buildings north of downtown Columbus were redeveloped as part of a larger revival of the industrial area north of Columbus — by then termed the Arena District — following the construction of [Nationwide Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_Arena "Nationwide Arena"). Nationwide Realty Investors, a development affiliate of [Nationwide Insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_Insurance "Nationwide Insurance"), acquired two of the production facilities at 390 and 400 W. Nationwide Blvd., termed the "Buggyworks", and redeveloped them into 145,000 square feet of office space.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-36) The development project cost $10.5 million.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-37) The office buildings attracted a number of tenants, the first being [Cameron Mitchell Restaurants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Mitchell_Restaurants "Cameron Mitchell Restaurants").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-38) Another portion of the complex at 440 W. Nationwide Blvd., was redeveloped into loft condominiums.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Buggy_Company#cite_note-39)
