# Timeline: Factory fires through history

Here’s a look at some of factory fires since the 1900s, and the impact (or lack thereof) they had on labor conditions.

[Agence France-Presse](https://theworld.org/categories/miscellaneous/agence-france-presse-2)

July 31, 2016

[MK Mariya Karimjee](https://theworld.org/contributors/mariya-karimjee)

Share

View Image: 151846022.jpg

Pakistani rescuers move the dead body of a garment factory worker.

Asif Hassan

Two separate factory fires, one in Lahore and the other in Karachi, have killed over 300 people in Pakistan, raising concerns about the government’s ability to safely regulate industrial environments.

However, factory fires aren’t uncommon, especially in the developing world where labor conditions are unregulated and often dangerous.

Here’s a look at some of factory fires since the 1900s, and the impact (or lack thereof) they had on labor conditions.

**March 20, 1905:**A boiler explosion at the Grover Shoe Factory in Brockton, Mass., causes a fire and building collapse that kills 58 people and injures 150 others.

**Impact:** After another fatal Massachusetts boiler explosion the following year in Lynn, Mass. — this time at a shoe factory — the American Society of Mechanical Engineers [helped to pass an act](http://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9E0DE3D9133AE733A25752C2A9659C946497D6CF) regulating the maintenance of steam boilers, passed in 1907, eventually resulting in a national safety code.

**March 25, 1911:** A fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City kills more than 100 garment workers, who died either because of the fire or by jumping to their death out of the burning building.

**Impact:**The fire helped the efforts of the International Ladies’ Garment Worker’s Union, which fought for better working conditions, and [helped improve factory safety standards](http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/triangle-shirtwaist-fire), leading to new laws and regulations throughout the United States.

**July 22, 1913:** A fire at the Binghamton clothing factory in New York State kills 100 people trapped inside.

**Impact:**George F. Johnson, an industrialist in the area, [installed automatic sprinkler systems](http://thedailystar.com/columns/x112901097/Binghamton-fire-spurred-improved-safety-laws) and other protective devices in every one of his vast array of shoe factories.

**November 18, 1968:** A fire at Stern's upholstery factory in Glasgow, Scotland, kills 24 people after spreading to a tobacco warehouse, an ice cream factory and the Harland and Wolff engine factory.

**Impact:** Politicians in Glasgow promised it would never happen again. But it wasn’t until multiple other tragedies had taken place that [fire regulations were actually changed](http://www.bbc.co.uk/scotland/history/articles/the_cheapside_fire/).

**May 10, 1993:** A fire at the Kader Toy Factory in Thailand kills 188 and injures 469 workers, most of them women. The tragedy occurred primarily because exit doors were locked and the stairwell collapsed.

**Impact:** The International Committee of the Fourth International (ICFI) dispatched a reporting team to Thailand to investigate the incident, revealing the extent of an initial cover-up by the Thai government. Analysts agree that the fire, which brought about local anger,[didn’t bring about any lasting change](http://www.wsws.org/articles/2003/may2003/kade-m16.shtml) — the conditions for workers in Thailand and other Asian countries have actually significantly worsened since then.

**February 1, 1997:** A fire breaks out at the Toyota subsidiary Aisin Seiki in Japan. There are no casualties.

**Impact:** Toyota [reduced the number of variations in its parts](http://www.rbbi.com/company/toyota/fire.htm) to ease production and reduce risk.

**November 22, 2006:** A fire at a leather factory in Kolkata, India kills at least 10 workers.

**Impact:** Fire safety licenses and insurance for leather factory workers[were made mandatory,](http://www.telegraphindia.com/1080617/jsp/calcutta/story_9422571.jsp) but according to reports, government officials do little to ensure those policies are followed by factories.

**February 1, 2008:** An explosion at an unlicensed fireworks factory in Istanbul kills 22 and injures 100.

**Impact:** Istanbul’s Mayor [urged citizens to report illegal factories](http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/7219381.stm) to authorities, as regulation is very difficult to maintain.

**April 25, 2008:**A fire spanning the four stories of Rosamor Furniture factory in Casablanca, Morocco, kills 55 workers.

**Impact:**The regional commander of Casablanca’s civil defense was fired and a new fire policy is enacted.

**December 2010:**A factory fire in Ashulia, Bangladesh kills 29 people.

**Impact:** The factory [continued to operate for US brands such as Tommy Hilfiger](http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/regions/asia-pacific/120430/bangladesh-garment-workers-brave-deadly-fires). Little international attention was given to the incident, and a prominent labor activist was murdered to remind the community that pushing for better labor standards can be lethal.

# Timeline: Factory fires through history

Here’s a look at some of factory fires since the 1900s, and the impact (or lack thereof) they had on labor conditions.

[Agence France-Presse](https://theworld.org/categories/miscellaneous/agence-france-presse-2)

July 31, 2016

[MK Mariya Karimjee](https://theworld.org/contributors/mariya-karimjee)

Share

View Image: 151846022.jpg

Pakistani rescuers move the dead body of a garment factory worker.

Asif Hassan

Two separate factory fires, one in Lahore and the other in Karachi, have killed over 300 people in Pakistan, raising concerns about the government’s ability to safely regulate industrial environments.

However, factory fires aren’t uncommon, especially in the developing world where labor conditions are unregulated and often dangerous.

Here’s a look at some of factory fires since the 1900s, and the impact (or lack thereof) they had on labor conditions.

**March 20, 1905:**A boiler explosion at the Grover Shoe Factory in Brockton, Mass., causes a fire and building collapse that kills 58 people and injures 150 others.

**Impact:** After another fatal Massachusetts boiler explosion the following year in Lynn, Mass. — this time at a shoe factory — the American Society of Mechanical Engineers [helped to pass an act](http://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9E0DE3D9133AE733A25752C2A9659C946497D6CF) regulating the maintenance of steam boilers, passed in 1907, eventually resulting in a national safety code.

**March 25, 1911:** A fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City kills more than 100 garment workers, who died either because of the fire or by jumping to their death out of the burning building.

**Impact:**The fire helped the efforts of the International Ladies’ Garment Worker’s Union, which fought for better working conditions, and [helped improve factory safety standards](http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/triangle-shirtwaist-fire), leading to new laws and regulations throughout the United States.

**July 22, 1913:** A fire at the Binghamton clothing factory in New York State kills 100 people trapped inside.

**Impact:**George F. Johnson, an industrialist in the area, [installed automatic sprinkler systems](http://thedailystar.com/columns/x112901097/Binghamton-fire-spurred-improved-safety-laws) and other protective devices in every one of his vast array of shoe factories.

**November 18, 1968:** A fire at Stern's upholstery factory in Glasgow, Scotland, kills 24 people after spreading to a tobacco warehouse, an ice cream factory and the Harland and Wolff engine factory.

**Impact:** Politicians in Glasgow promised it would never happen again. But it wasn’t until multiple other tragedies had taken place that [fire regulations were actually changed](http://www.bbc.co.uk/scotland/history/articles/the_cheapside_fire/).

**May 10, 1993:** A fire at the Kader Toy Factory in Thailand kills 188 and injures 469 workers, most of them women. The tragedy occurred primarily because exit doors were locked and the stairwell collapsed.

**Impact:** The International Committee of the Fourth International (ICFI) dispatched a reporting team to Thailand to investigate the incident, revealing the extent of an initial cover-up by the Thai government. Analysts agree that the fire, which brought about local anger,[didn’t bring about any lasting change](http://www.wsws.org/articles/2003/may2003/kade-m16.shtml) — the conditions for workers in Thailand and other Asian countries have actually significantly worsened since then.

**February 1, 1997:** A fire breaks out at the Toyota subsidiary Aisin Seiki in Japan. There are no casualties.

**Impact:** Toyota [reduced the number of variations in its parts](http://www.rbbi.com/company/toyota/fire.htm) to ease production and reduce risk.

**November 22, 2006:** A fire at a leather factory in Kolkata, India kills at least 10 workers.

**Impact:** Fire safety licenses and insurance for leather factory workers[were made mandatory,](http://www.telegraphindia.com/1080617/jsp/calcutta/story_9422571.jsp) but according to reports, government officials do little to ensure those policies are followed by factories.

**February 1, 2008:** An explosion at an unlicensed fireworks factory in Istanbul kills 22 and injures 100.

**Impact:** Istanbul’s Mayor [urged citizens to report illegal factories](http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/7219381.stm) to authorities, as regulation is very difficult to maintain.

**April 25, 2008:**A fire spanning the four stories of Rosamor Furniture factory in Casablanca, Morocco, kills 55 workers.

**Impact:**The regional commander of Casablanca’s civil defense was fired and a new fire policy is enacted.

**December 2010:**A factory fire in Ashulia, Bangladesh kills 29 people.

**Impact:** The factory [continued to operate for US brands such as Tommy Hilfiger](http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/regions/asia-pacific/120430/bangladesh-garment-workers-brave-deadly-fires). Little international attention was given to the incident, and a prominent labor activist was murdered to remind the community that pushing for better labor standards can be lethal.

[![Image 11: 🚂 Ruth, Michigan: Tracks, Faith, and Small-Town Life Before highways and chain stores, Ruth was a busy Thumb town with a railroad depot, creamery, livery, taverns, two hotels and a church steeple that could be seen for miles. Settled in the 1850s by German immigrants, first known as Adams Corners, Ruth became a flag stop on the Pere Marquette Railway in 1898 — complete with a 10-car siding and no regular station agent. Crops shipped out by rail. Travelers stepped off onto wooden platforms. And one dramatic train wreck near town briefly turned this quiet stop into headline news. **Columbus City Hall** was the city hall for [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), located on [Capitol Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Square "Capitol Square") in [the city's downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Columbus,_Ohio "Downtown Columbus, Ohio"). The building served the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Columbus,_Ohio "Mayor of Columbus, Ohio") and [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Council "Columbus City Council") from its construction in 1872 until its demolition in 1921. The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890. In 1928, the site became home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)"), and the current [Columbus City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(Ohio) "Columbus City Hall (Ohio)") opened nearby.

This city hall had three floors, including a post office and library space on the first floor, meeting rooms and offices on the second, and a large public hall on the third. The building housed Columbus's first public library, from 1873 until it expanded and moved in 1906.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Columbus municipal government established its first permanent offices at the [Central Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Market_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Central Market (Columbus, Ohio)"), operating from its second floor from 1850 to 1872. Construction for the Capitol Square-area building began in May 1869, and the building's opening ceremony was held on March 28, 1872. The total cost, including for the property, was $175,000 to $185,000.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2-1872-2)

During the building's operation, it hosted numerous galas and events. The opening ceremony was reportedly a success, with hundreds to thousands attending. Speeches were followed by dancing into the late night.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-3) The building also hosted [Benjamin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Butler "Benjamin Butler"), [Carl Schurz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Schurz "Carl Schurz"), and [Willie Redmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Redmond "Willie Redmond"). Governor [William Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Allen_(governor) "William Allen (governor)")'s inaugural ball was held there in 1874, as well as a reception for [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") in 1879. Numerous state conventions were held in the space, in addition to state and city meetings, gatherings honoring Civil War generals, legislative banquets, and election night gatherings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-events-4)

The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Lentz-5)

### Destruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Destruction")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg/250px-City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg)

City Hall one day after the fire

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg/250px-Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg)

Plaque at the Ohio Theatre commemorating the building

City Hall was demolished in a fire that began about 8 p.m. on January 12, 1921.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) At the time, about 100 people were attending a basketball practice inside, and others were attending a meeting of City Council at the same time. There were no injuries during the incident. [James Thurber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thurber "James Thurber"), later known for his cartoons, was covering the City Council meeting as a _Columbus Dispatch_ reporter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6) Sixteen engine companies and six truck companies arrived to fight the fire, setting numerous hoses onto the fire by 8:30 p.m. from multiple areas, including from atop the roof of the Grand Theater building.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Crowds witnessed the building fire, held back into the sloping Statehouse grounds.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-7) The crowds reportedly had few regrets or tears, and a general attitude of "good riddance" to its destruction among the public and city officials.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-8) Exterior walls remained standing, though seemingly about to topple. The entire roof burned away, and the second and third floor interiors were turned into a large pile of debris.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Property loss was estimated at about $75,000; like all city buildings at the time, it was not insured. It was the third public structure to burn in recent months, after the city prison and a more minor fire at the [Columbus State Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_State_Hospital "Columbus State Hospital").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Records lost in the building's fire reportedly included those on the [Franklin Park Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Park_Conservatory "Franklin Park Conservatory"), making much of its early history unknown.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-9) News from four days after the fire claimed all valuable documents and records were saved, though the Children's Playhouse Project was affected. About 5,000 costumes were lost, as well as four sets of scenery and several pageant lights. This combined loss was estimated at $6,300. In addition, thousands of city codes were lost, as well as all bound copies of city bulletins and annual reports for all departments; all these documents were said to be replaceable.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-10)

By the next day, city officials toured the burned building with the determination of making the site habitable within 30 days. Following their tour, they unanimously abandoned any proposals to rebuild City Hall on that site, with most council members indicating the new riverfront civic center as the most appropriate place to rebuild.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Though the origin of the fire was undetermined by this point, three theories existed: it could have been started from blowtorches left in the building's cupola by workers who were repairing the roof, one of which was found atop charred timber in the wreckage. Other ideas included defective wiring caused a spark, or that lit cigarette butts could have sparked the flames.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Two days after the fire, Columbus's library trustees offered the second floor of the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)") to the mayor and most city officials, which they promptly accepted.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-11)

The fire allowed city leaders to rebuild City Hall with a better structure and in the new [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Civic_Center_(Ohio) "Columbus Civic Center (Ohio)") site. Prominent citizens lauded the mayor, offering "congratulations on the successful fire". The site is now home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

## Attributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Attributes")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg/250px-City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall,_Columbus_illustration.jpg)

Original design for the building, including a clock tower

The building was 80 feet wide, 187.5 feet long, and 98 feet tall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was originally set to be 140 feet tall, though its clock tower was never built. The structure was designed by Detroit architect Robert T. Brookes, designer of Towers Hall at [Otterbein University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otterbein_University "Otterbein University") and the final architect for [St. Joseph Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Cathedral_(Columbus,_Ohio) "St. Joseph Cathedral (Columbus, Ohio)") in Columbus. The building utilized dark cream-colored Amherst sandstone for its exterior walls, and had a steep roof with two pitches, both covered in blue Vermont slate. The building's entranceway included seven [lancet archways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture#Pointed_arches "Gothic architecture"), separated by massive piers. A balcony existed above the central three arches, with additional balconies above the diagonal arches on the building's northeast and northwest corners. Upper windows matched the lower arches with their lancet heads. An iron water tank stood on the southeast corner of the building by the roof.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

Initially seen as a perfect example of Gothic Revival architecture, it later grew a reputation as unsatisfactory for a city hall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was described by the _Columbus Dispatch_ a day after the fire as "long an eyesore to Columbus",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) and in 2012 as a "Gothic nightmare of a building".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

### Interior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Interior")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg/250px-Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg)

Reading room

The building's first floor had an open [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_(architecture) "Arcade (architecture)") with a variegated marble floor along its north and west sides. A central lobby included a large staircase to the second floor, while to its rear was another lobby with stairs at the sides, leading to all upper floors. To the rear of that was the merchants' exchange.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

At its opening, the west side of the first floor also held the city's post office, a space including a separate fireproof room. The left or east side housed the city's first [public library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_library "Public library"), a glass-divided room which opened on March 4, 1873. The front section was a reading room, while the back was reserved for books and the librarian's desk.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-13) The collection contained 1,500 books.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) These included 1,200 from the Columbus Athenaeum (1853-1872),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-davies-15) 358 from Columbus's high school library, and 33 from its horticultural society.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-history-16) In 1906, the reading room moved to a separate building across from the [Ohio Statehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Statehouse "Ohio Statehouse"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) and by 1907 to the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)"), where it remains today.

On the second floor was another lobby with five rooms on either side, for city officials and committees.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12) To the rear was the council chamber, an elaborately decorated space with watercolor-frescoed walls.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-FLC-17) The third floor held the public hall, a multipurpose room of 140 by 74 feet, with a height of 53 feet. It was estimated to seat 3,200 people, or give standing room to almost 6,400. A stage stood at the south end of the hall, while a gallery stood at the north end.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Columbus City Hall** was the city hall for [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), located on [Capitol Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Square "Capitol Square") in [the city's downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Columbus,_Ohio "Downtown Columbus, Ohio"). The building served the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Columbus,_Ohio "Mayor of Columbus, Ohio") and [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Council "Columbus City Council") from its construction in 1872 until its demolition in 1921. The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890. In 1928, the site became home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)"), and the current [Columbus City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(Ohio) "Columbus City Hall (Ohio)") opened nearby.

This city hall had three floors, including a post office and library space on the first floor, meeting rooms and offices on the second, and a large public hall on the third. The building housed Columbus's first public library, from 1873 until it expanded and moved in 1906.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Columbus municipal government established its first permanent offices at the [Central Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Market_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Central Market (Columbus, Ohio)"), operating from its second floor from 1850 to 1872. Construction for the Capitol Square-area building began in May 1869, and the building's opening ceremony was held on March 28, 1872. The total cost, including for the property, was $175,000 to $185,000.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2-1872-2)

During the building's operation, it hosted numerous galas and events. The opening ceremony was reportedly a success, with hundreds to thousands attending. Speeches were followed by dancing into the late night.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-3) The building also hosted [Benjamin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Butler "Benjamin Butler"), [Carl Schurz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Schurz "Carl Schurz"), and [Willie Redmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Redmond "Willie Redmond"). Governor [William Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Allen_(governor) "William Allen (governor)")'s inaugural ball was held there in 1874, as well as a reception for [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") in 1879. Numerous state conventions were held in the space, in addition to state and city meetings, gatherings honoring Civil War generals, legislative banquets, and election night gatherings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-events-4)

The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Lentz-5)

### Destruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Destruction")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg/250px-City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg)

City Hall one day after the fire

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg/250px-Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg)

Plaque at the Ohio Theatre commemorating the building

City Hall was demolished in a fire that began about 8 p.m. on January 12, 1921.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) At the time, about 100 people were attending a basketball practice inside, and others were attending a meeting of City Council at the same time. There were no injuries during the incident. [James Thurber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thurber "James Thurber"), later known for his cartoons, was covering the City Council meeting as a _Columbus Dispatch_ reporter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6) Sixteen engine companies and six truck companies arrived to fight the fire, setting numerous hoses onto the fire by 8:30 p.m. from multiple areas, including from atop the roof of the Grand Theater building.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Crowds witnessed the building fire, held back into the sloping Statehouse grounds.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-7) The crowds reportedly had few regrets or tears, and a general attitude of "good riddance" to its destruction among the public and city officials.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-8) Exterior walls remained standing, though seemingly about to topple. The entire roof burned away, and the second and third floor interiors were turned into a large pile of debris.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Property loss was estimated at about $75,000; like all city buildings at the time, it was not insured. It was the third public structure to burn in recent months, after the city prison and a more minor fire at the [Columbus State Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_State_Hospital "Columbus State Hospital").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Records lost in the building's fire reportedly included those on the [Franklin Park Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Park_Conservatory "Franklin Park Conservatory"), making much of its early history unknown.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-9) News from four days after the fire claimed all valuable documents and records were saved, though the Children's Playhouse Project was affected. About 5,000 costumes were lost, as well as four sets of scenery and several pageant lights. This combined loss was estimated at $6,300. In addition, thousands of city codes were lost, as well as all bound copies of city bulletins and annual reports for all departments; all these documents were said to be replaceable.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-10)

By the next day, city officials toured the burned building with the determination of making the site habitable within 30 days. Following their tour, they unanimously abandoned any proposals to rebuild City Hall on that site, with most council members indicating the new riverfront civic center as the most appropriate place to rebuild.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Though the origin of the fire was undetermined by this point, three theories existed: it could have been started from blowtorches left in the building's cupola by workers who were repairing the roof, one of which was found atop charred timber in the wreckage. Other ideas included defective wiring caused a spark, or that lit cigarette butts could have sparked the flames.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Two days after the fire, Columbus's library trustees offered the second floor of the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)") to the mayor and most city officials, which they promptly accepted.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-11)

The fire allowed city leaders to rebuild City Hall with a better structure and in the new [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Civic_Center_(Ohio) "Columbus Civic Center (Ohio)") site. Prominent citizens lauded the mayor, offering "congratulations on the successful fire". The site is now home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

## Attributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Attributes")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg/250px-City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall,_Columbus_illustration.jpg)

Original design for the building, including a clock tower

The building was 80 feet wide, 187.5 feet long, and 98 feet tall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was originally set to be 140 feet tall, though its clock tower was never built. The structure was designed by Detroit architect Robert T. Brookes, designer of Towers Hall at [Otterbein University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otterbein_University "Otterbein University") and the final architect for [St. Joseph Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Cathedral_(Columbus,_Ohio) "St. Joseph Cathedral (Columbus, Ohio)") in Columbus. The building utilized dark cream-colored Amherst sandstone for its exterior walls, and had a steep roof with two pitches, both covered in blue Vermont slate. The building's entranceway included seven [lancet archways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture#Pointed_arches "Gothic architecture"), separated by massive piers. A balcony existed above the central three arches, with additional balconies above the diagonal arches on the building's northeast and northwest corners. Upper windows matched the lower arches with their lancet heads. An iron water tank stood on the southeast corner of the building by the roof.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

Initially seen as a perfect example of Gothic Revival architecture, it later grew a reputation as unsatisfactory for a city hall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was described by the _Columbus Dispatch_ a day after the fire as "long an eyesore to Columbus",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) and in 2012 as a "Gothic nightmare of a building".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

### Interior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Interior")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg/250px-Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg)

Reading room

The building's first floor had an open [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_(architecture) "Arcade (architecture)") with a variegated marble floor along its north and west sides. A central lobby included a large staircase to the second floor, while to its rear was another lobby with stairs at the sides, leading to all upper floors. To the rear of that was the merchants' exchange.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

At its opening, the west side of the first floor also held the city's post office, a space including a separate fireproof room. The left or east side housed the city's first [public library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_library "Public library"), a glass-divided room which opened on March 4, 1873. The front section was a reading room, while the back was reserved for books and the librarian's desk.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-13) The collection contained 1,500 books.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) These included 1,200 from the Columbus Athenaeum (1853-1872),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-davies-15) 358 from Columbus's high school library, and 33 from its horticultural society.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-history-16) In 1906, the reading room moved to a separate building across from the [Ohio Statehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Statehouse "Ohio Statehouse"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) and by 1907 to the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)"), where it remains today.

On the second floor was another lobby with five rooms on either side, for city officials and committees.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12) To the rear was the council chamber, an elaborately decorated space with watercolor-frescoed walls.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-FLC-17) The third floor held the public hall, a multipurpose room of 140 by 74 feet, with a height of 53 feet. It was estimated to seat 3,200 people, or give standing room to almost 6,400. A stage stood at the south end of the hall, while a gallery stood at the north end.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

On January 12, 1921, Columbus City Hall, the building in the middle of the block, suffered a massive fire that left its stone walls standing, but the interior gutted. Built in 1872, the building was an example of Gothic Revival architecture that was not well-loved amongst the citizens of Columbus by the early 20th century. 

After the fire, City Hall was considered a total loss, and plans were quickly made to build a new City Hall closer to the river. The remains of City Hall were demolished by September 1921, and in 1928 the [Ohio Theatre](https://www.facebook.com/ohiotheatrecolumbus?__cft__[0]=AZg7fCMnDrMiDpx_lYeKf9TOfhsbZtAO367VJMaVuK6hNF9XwvfQH22gnxnXI4iTbAKPjgIJgGTjQ_kC0crv2zP_86MJutkkQg3Gr0CEsDftwr1m0xIZKQT2aULSkqTSkdHjy-kkdRdWGDIF6iIMB11ilcVROiJ-&__tn__=-]K-R) opened on the same site. Other businesses on the same block in 1921 included the Capitol City Bank, the Milk Store, the Grand Theatre, and the Hartman Theatre, located in the Hartman Building.

On January 12, 1921, Columbus City Hall, the building in the middle of the block, suffered a massive fire that left its stone walls standing, but the interior gutted. Built in 1872, the building was an example of Gothic Revival architecture that was not well-loved amongst the citizens of Columbus by the early 20th century. 

After the fire, City Hall was considered a total loss, and plans were quickly made to build a new City Hall closer to the river. The remains of City Hall were demolished by September 1921, and in 1928 the [Ohio Theatre](https://www.facebook.com/ohiotheatrecolumbus?__cft__[0]=AZg7fCMnDrMiDpx_lYeKf9TOfhsbZtAO367VJMaVuK6hNF9XwvfQH22gnxnXI4iTbAKPjgIJgGTjQ_kC0crv2zP_86MJutkkQg3Gr0CEsDftwr1m0xIZKQT2aULSkqTSkdHjy-kkdRdWGDIF6iIMB11ilcVROiJ-&__tn__=-]K-R) opened on the same site. Other businesses on the same block in 1921 included the Capitol City Bank, the Milk Store, the Grand Theatre, and the Hartman Theatre, located in the Hartman Building.

# The 1921 Fire That Destroyed Columbus’s Original City Hall

[![Image 3: Chelsea Wiley](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/06a1199703abbfac2eb3b9fe7d0a9c3250d0ae259c07d7ae63227cc7ab372542?s=56&d=retro&r=g)By Chelsea Wiley](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/author/chelsea/)April 29, 2025[Follow us on Google Discover](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=columbusnavigator)

**Before Columbus had its current City Hall by the riverfront,** the city’s leaders worked out of a massive, Gothic-style building right on Capitol Square. And if you’ve never heard about it, you’re not alone.

Built in 1872, Columbus’s old City Hall was dramatic in every sense: towering stone archways, soaring ceilings, a library, a post office, a massive public hall that could fit thousands of people. It even helped launch the United Mine Workers of America in 1890.

![Image 4: original columbus city hall](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1548px-City_Hall_Columbus_illustration.jpg)

Original design for the building, including a clock tower.

Video 4

Video 5

Video 6

But for all its ambition, the building wasn’t exactly beloved. Over the years, it earned nicknames like a “Gothic nightmare” and an “eyesore.”

And by the 1920s, it wasn’t just outdated. It was doomed.

On a cold January night in 1921, while a city council meeting and a basketball practice were happening inside (because of course that’s how this goes), a fire broke out. It spread fast. Sixteen engine companies rushed in, but it was too late: the roof collapsed, the upper floors turned into a mountain of debris, and Columbus’s original City Hall was history.

![Image 5: columbus city hall fire](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1069px-City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg)

City Hall one day after the fire.

Miraculously, no one was hurt. Reporter James Thurber (yes, that James Thurber) was covering the city council meeting when the fire started. As he and everyone else fled, crowds gathered on the Statehouse lawn to watch it burn. Strangely enough, most people weren’t sad about it. If anything, it was kind of a relief. Even city officials were reportedly happy to say “good riddance” to the building.

It also wasn’t insured. And as if losing a whole city hall wasn’t enough, key historical documents burned with it, including early records for places like the Franklin Park Conservatory.

To top it off, it was the third major public building to catch fire in just a few months, after the city prison and part of the state hospital.

In the aftermath, leaders decided not to rebuild on the site.

![Image 6: columbus city hall](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1163px-Columbus_Ohio_JJ_52-crop.jpg)

City Hall at it’s current location at 90 W Broad Street. [Photo by Jsjessee,](https://www.flickr.com/photos/96853498@N02/50529142981/)[CC BY-SA 2.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=95720288)

Instead, they moved operations to a temporary space — and eventually to the Civic Center riverfront where City Hall stands today.

The site where the old City Hall once loomed? It’s now home to the Ohio Theatre. (Yep, the one with the sparkling chandeliers and the gorgeous marquee.)

# The 1921 Fire That Destroyed Columbus’s Original City Hall

[![Image 3: Chelsea Wiley](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/06a1199703abbfac2eb3b9fe7d0a9c3250d0ae259c07d7ae63227cc7ab372542?s=56&d=retro&r=g)By Chelsea Wiley](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/author/chelsea/)April 29, 2025[Follow us on Google Discover](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=columbusnavigator)

**Before Columbus had its current City Hall by the riverfront,** the city’s leaders worked out of a massive, Gothic-style building right on Capitol Square. And if you’ve never heard about it, you’re not alone.

Built in 1872, Columbus’s old City Hall was dramatic in every sense: towering stone archways, soaring ceilings, a library, a post office, a massive public hall that could fit thousands of people. It even helped launch the United Mine Workers of America in 1890.

![Image 4: original columbus city hall](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1548px-City_Hall_Columbus_illustration.jpg)

Original design for the building, including a clock tower.

Video 4

Video 5

Video 6

But for all its ambition, the building wasn’t exactly beloved. Over the years, it earned nicknames like a “Gothic nightmare” and an “eyesore.”

And by the 1920s, it wasn’t just outdated. It was doomed.

On a cold January night in 1921, while a city council meeting and a basketball practice were happening inside (because of course that’s how this goes), a fire broke out. It spread fast. Sixteen engine companies rushed in, but it was too late: the roof collapsed, the upper floors turned into a mountain of debris, and Columbus’s original City Hall was history.

![Image 5: columbus city hall fire](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1069px-City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg)

City Hall one day after the fire.

Miraculously, no one was hurt. Reporter James Thurber (yes, that James Thurber) was covering the city council meeting when the fire started. As he and everyone else fled, crowds gathered on the Statehouse lawn to watch it burn. Strangely enough, most people weren’t sad about it. If anything, it was kind of a relief. Even city officials were reportedly happy to say “good riddance” to the building.

It also wasn’t insured. And as if losing a whole city hall wasn’t enough, key historical documents burned with it, including early records for places like the Franklin Park Conservatory.

To top it off, it was the third major public building to catch fire in just a few months, after the city prison and part of the state hospital.

In the aftermath, leaders decided not to rebuild on the site.

![Image 6: columbus city hall](https://www.columbusnavigator.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/1163px-Columbus_Ohio_JJ_52-crop.jpg)

City Hall at it’s current location at 90 W Broad Street. [Photo by Jsjessee,](https://www.flickr.com/photos/96853498@N02/50529142981/)[CC BY-SA 2.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=95720288)

Instead, they moved operations to a temporary space — and eventually to the Civic Center riverfront where City Hall stands today.

The site where the old City Hall once loomed? It’s now home to the Ohio Theatre. (Yep, the one with the sparkling chandeliers and the gorgeous marquee.)

On January 12, 1921, Columbus City Hall, the building in the middle of the block, suffered a massive fire that left its stone walls standing, but the interior gutted. Built in 1872, the building was an example of Gothic Revival architecture that was not well-loved amongst the citizens of Columbus by the early 20th century. 

After the fire, City Hall was considered a total loss, and plans were quickly made to build a new City Hall closer to the river. The remains of City Hall were demolished by September 1921, and in 1928 the Ohio Theatre opened on the same site. Other businesses on the same block in 1921 included the Capitol City Bank, the Milk Store, the Grand Theatre, and the Hartman Theatre, located in the Hartman Building."

On January 12, 1921, Columbus City Hall, the building in the middle of the block, suffered a massive fire that left its stone walls standing, but the interior gutted. Built in 1872, the building was an example of Gothic Revival architecture that was not well-loved amongst the citizens of Columbus by the early 20th century.   
  
After the fire, City Hall was considered a total loss, and plans were quickly made to build a new City Hall closer to the river. The remains of City Hall were demolished by September 1921, and in 1928 the Ohio Theatre opened on the same site. Other businesses on the same block in 1921 included the Capitol City Bank, the Milk Store, the Grand Theatre, and the Hartman Theatre, located in the Hartman Building.

# Central Ohio Fire Museum

**For generations, firefighters have risked their lives to help their communities in the time of need. Some have paid the ultimate price by dying in the line of duty.**

## Central Ohio Fire Museum

**_"Learning from the past to save the future"_**

The Central Ohio Fire Museum & Learning Center pays tribute to our firefighters, past present and future, and the rich legacy they have left us. Through a collection of hand-drawn, horse-drawn and motorized fire apparatus, visitors can retrace the steps of firefighters and learn about their day-to-day lives in the engine house.

Set in an authentically restored 1908 Columbus Engine House (No.16) our building is on the National Register of Historic Places. Nearly $700,000 was raised from Firefighters, corporate and community sponsors to restore the front facade in 1990 and the journey to educate the public began.

![Image 2](https://www.columbus.gov/files/sharedassets/city/v/1/public-safety/fire/museum.jpg?w=400&h=314)

The Museum opened in October 2002, and hosts nearly 4,000 visitors each year, the vast majority being children in grades K - 2nd. However, people of all ages enjoy the diversity and history offered in this interactive Museum setting.

The Museum's mission is to teach fire safety, education, prevention, and life saving procedures to all people in age -appropriate settings. Personalized individual tours are offered as well as classroom style settings for those who are looking for a more formal session.

Come visit "Fire Safety Way", where our qualified fire safety instructors will educate using hands-on, interactive, informational, and fun displays emphasizing the importance of Fire prevention.

# Central Ohio Fire Museum

**For generations, firefighters have risked their lives to help their communities in the time of need. Some have paid the ultimate price by dying in the line of duty.**

## Central Ohio Fire Museum

**_"Learning from the past to save the future"_**

The Central Ohio Fire Museum & Learning Center pays tribute to our firefighters, past present and future, and the rich legacy they have left us. Through a collection of hand-drawn, horse-drawn and motorized fire apparatus, visitors can retrace the steps of firefighters and learn about their day-to-day lives in the engine house.

Set in an authentically restored 1908 Columbus Engine House (No.16) our building is on the National Register of Historic Places. Nearly $700,000 was raised from Firefighters, corporate and community sponsors to restore the front facade in 1990 and the journey to educate the public began.

![Image 2](https://www.columbus.gov/files/sharedassets/city/v/1/public-safety/fire/museum.jpg?w=400&h=314)

The Museum opened in October 2002, and hosts nearly 4,000 visitors each year, the vast majority being children in grades K - 2nd. However, people of all ages enjoy the diversity and history offered in this interactive Museum setting.

The Museum's mission is to teach fire safety, education, prevention, and life saving procedures to all people in age -appropriate settings. Personalized individual tours are offered as well as classroom style settings for those who are looking for a more formal session.

Come visit "Fire Safety Way", where our qualified fire safety instructors will educate using hands-on, interactive, informational, and fun displays emphasizing the importance of Fire prevention.

# 1908 City Hall Fire

## 

On January 24, 1908, at 2:23 am, a fire was discovered on the 3rd-floor of City Hall. The air temperature was 17 degrees and falling, with a steady, brisk wind blowing.

The building housed City and County offices, Police headquarters and the jail. Also, the City Electrician's Office and Fire Alarm system were located on the 3rd-floor.

Because of the fire, the fire alarm system became inoperable, and was reported by citizens to Central Fire Station. The fire spread rapidly and extended into the dome.

A General alarm was soon sounded, with mutual aid requested from Auburn, Augusta, Bath, Biddeford, Lewiston, Saco, South Portland, and as far away as Portsmouth, NH.

The Chestnut Street church and Union Mutual buildings sustained fire damage, and dozens of small fires were set from flying brands, as far away as Maple Street.

Early in the fire, City Clerk A.L.T. Cummings ran from his home to City Hall, and with assistance, nearly all records in the Clerk's and Mayor's offices were saved, as far back as when Portland was the Town of Falmouth in the 1700's. County records were mostly saved, except the records in the Register of Probate office were destroyed.

A number of firefighters were injured. The most serious was Chief Engineer Melville N Eldridge, injuring both feet by stepping on hot embers with nails. Later, he was struck and thrown to the ground by the ladder pipe of Ladder 5, when the wooden aerial broke apart. He was carried across the street to his office in the Central Fire Station, and commanded the fire from his second-floor front windows.

Portland's Bravest "answering the bell" Since 1768.

## City Hall Fire - Highlights

*   City Hall destroyed, only walls left standing - Total Loss, approximately $600,000.
*   Insurance, $80,000.
*   Second time City Hall burned down, July 4, 1866. The walls are all that was left from the 1858 building.
*   Fire discovered at 2:23 am, Alarm system not working because of the fire.
*   1,000 Western Maine Jubilee Knights of Pythians in City Hall ordered to leave building.
*   Severe weather conditions, Temperatures between 10 to 14-Degrees, winds up to 26 MPH.
*   Chestnut Street Church and Union Mutual buildings damaged.
*   Dozens of other fires started by flying cinders and brands, as far away as Maple Street.
*   Mutual Aid summoned from Auburn, Augusta, Bath, Biddeford, Lewiston, Saco, South Portland, and Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
*   Several Injured, including Chief Engineer Melville Eldridge, who was injured seriously twice.
*   Chief Eldridge carried to his 2nd-floor office in Central Station and commanded fire from his front windows, and relayed orders to Assistant Engineer Thomas Payne in front of City Hall.
*   Portland's only ladder truck with an aerial ladder (Ladder 5) broke when it was being moved.
*   Third-floor City Electrician's Office and fire alarm system destroyed.
*   Fire alarm system out of order, Chief tells citizens to call 395-1 by phone for a fire.
*   City Clerk and other city officials did heroic work in saving city and county records.
*   Cumberland County Register of Probates office records destroyed.
*   All City Hall offices destroyed and were temporarily relocated to other city buildings.
*   City Hall's Police headquarters and jail destroyed, prisoners were relocated or released.
*   Congress Street electric car service out of commission.

# 1908 City Hall Fire

## 

On January 24, 1908, at 2:23 am, a fire was discovered on the 3rd-floor of City Hall. The air temperature was 17 degrees and falling, with a steady, brisk wind blowing.

The building housed City and County offices, Police headquarters and the jail. Also, the City Electrician's Office and Fire Alarm system were located on the 3rd-floor.

Because of the fire, the fire alarm system became inoperable, and was reported by citizens to Central Fire Station. The fire spread rapidly and extended into the dome.

A General alarm was soon sounded, with mutual aid requested from Auburn, Augusta, Bath, Biddeford, Lewiston, Saco, South Portland, and as far away as Portsmouth, NH.

The Chestnut Street church and Union Mutual buildings sustained fire damage, and dozens of small fires were set from flying brands, as far away as Maple Street.

Early in the fire, City Clerk A.L.T. Cummings ran from his home to City Hall, and with assistance, nearly all records in the Clerk's and Mayor's offices were saved, as far back as when Portland was the Town of Falmouth in the 1700's. County records were mostly saved, except the records in the Register of Probate office were destroyed.

A number of firefighters were injured. The most serious was Chief Engineer Melville N Eldridge, injuring both feet by stepping on hot embers with nails. Later, he was struck and thrown to the ground by the ladder pipe of Ladder 5, when the wooden aerial broke apart. He was carried across the street to his office in the Central Fire Station, and commanded the fire from his second-floor front windows.

Portland's Bravest "answering the bell" Since 1768.

## City Hall Fire - Highlights

*   City Hall destroyed, only walls left standing - Total Loss, approximately $600,000.
*   Insurance, $80,000.
*   Second time City Hall burned down, July 4, 1866. The walls are all that was left from the 1858 building.
*   Fire discovered at 2:23 am, Alarm system not working because of the fire.
*   1,000 Western Maine Jubilee Knights of Pythians in City Hall ordered to leave building.
*   Severe weather conditions, Temperatures between 10 to 14-Degrees, winds up to 26 MPH.
*   Chestnut Street Church and Union Mutual buildings damaged.
*   Dozens of other fires started by flying cinders and brands, as far away as Maple Street.
*   Mutual Aid summoned from Auburn, Augusta, Bath, Biddeford, Lewiston, Saco, South Portland, and Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
*   Several Injured, including Chief Engineer Melville Eldridge, who was injured seriously twice.
*   Chief Eldridge carried to his 2nd-floor office in Central Station and commanded fire from his front windows, and relayed orders to Assistant Engineer Thomas Payne in front of City Hall.
*   Portland's only ladder truck with an aerial ladder (Ladder 5) broke when it was being moved.
*   Third-floor City Electrician's Office and fire alarm system destroyed.
*   Fire alarm system out of order, Chief tells citizens to call 395-1 by phone for a fire.
*   City Clerk and other city officials did heroic work in saving city and county records.
*   Cumberland County Register of Probates office records destroyed.
*   All City Hall offices destroyed and were temporarily relocated to other city buildings.
*   City Hall's Police headquarters and jail destroyed, prisoners were relocated or released.
*   Congress Street electric car service out of commission.

# Columbus City Hall

## 1872

[![Image 1: Columbus City Hall Marker image. Click for full size.](https://www.hmdb.org/Photos2/296/Photo296912.jpg?1231201463600PM)](https://www.hmdb.org/PhotoFullSize.asp?PhotoID=296912)

Photographed by William Fischer, Jr., May 28, 2012

1. Columbus City Hall Marker

Inscription. 

Columbus City Hall. Construction of old City Hall on this site was begun in 1869 and completed in 1872 at a cost of $175,000. The 140-foot high building of Gothic design contained dark cream Amherst stone and was one of the prominent landmarks of its day. First floor was occupied by the U.S. Post Office, the Columbus Public Library and the City Board of Trade. City Council Chamber and office rooms were located on the second floor and a public auditorium seating 3000 persons occupied the third floor. The building was destroyed by a $75,000 fire the night of January 21, 1921. Construction of the present Loew's Ohio Theater building was completed March 17, 1928. On opening night Mayor James J. Thomas delivered the dedicatory address. This marker sponsored by , the City of Columbus , and , Loew's Theaters , Dedicated April, 1964. . This historical marker was erected in 1964 by Franklin County Historical Society. It is in Uptown District in Columbus in Franklin County Ohio

# Columbus City Hall

## 1872

[![Image 1: Columbus City Hall Marker image. Click for full size.](https://www.hmdb.org/Photos2/296/Photo296912.jpg?1231201463600PM)](https://www.hmdb.org/PhotoFullSize.asp?PhotoID=296912)

Photographed by William Fischer, Jr., May 28, 2012

1. Columbus City Hall Marker

Inscription. 

Columbus City Hall. Construction of old City Hall on this site was begun in 1869 and completed in 1872 at a cost of $175,000. The 140-foot high building of Gothic design contained dark cream Amherst stone and was one of the prominent landmarks of its day. First floor was occupied by the U.S. Post Office, the Columbus Public Library and the City Board of Trade. City Council Chamber and office rooms were located on the second floor and a public auditorium seating 3000 persons occupied the third floor. The building was destroyed by a $75,000 fire the night of January 21, 1921. Construction of the present Loew's Ohio Theater building was completed March 17, 1928. On opening night Mayor James J. Thomas delivered the dedicatory address. This marker sponsored by , the City of Columbus , and , Loew's Theaters , Dedicated April, 1964. . This historical marker was erected in 1964 by Franklin County Historical Society. It is in Uptown District in Columbus in Franklin County Ohio

**Columbus City Hall** was the city hall for [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), located on [Capitol Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Square "Capitol Square") in [the city's downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Columbus,_Ohio "Downtown Columbus, Ohio"). The building served the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Columbus,_Ohio "Mayor of Columbus, Ohio") and [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Council "Columbus City Council") from its construction in 1872 until its demolition in 1921. The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890. In 1928, the site became home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)"), and the current [Columbus City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(Ohio) "Columbus City Hall (Ohio)") opened nearby.

This city hall had three floors, including a post office and library space on the first floor, meeting rooms and offices on the second, and a large public hall on the third. The building housed Columbus's first public library, from 1873 until it expanded and moved in 1906.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Columbus municipal government established its first permanent offices at the [Central Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Market_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Central Market (Columbus, Ohio)"), operating from its second floor from 1850 to 1872. Construction for the Capitol Square-area building began in May 1869, and the building's opening ceremony was held on March 28, 1872. The total cost, including for the property, was $175,000 to $185,000.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2-1872-2)

During the building's operation, it hosted numerous galas and events. The opening ceremony was reportedly a success, with hundreds to thousands attending. Speeches were followed by dancing into the late night.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-3) The building also hosted [Benjamin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Butler "Benjamin Butler"), [Carl Schurz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Schurz "Carl Schurz"), and [Willie Redmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Redmond "Willie Redmond"). Governor [William Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Allen_(governor) "William Allen (governor)")'s inaugural ball was held there in 1874, as well as a reception for [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") in 1879. Numerous state conventions were held in the space, in addition to state and city meetings, gatherings honoring Civil War generals, legislative banquets, and election night gatherings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-events-4)

The building was the founding site for the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") in 1890.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Lentz-5)

### Destruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Destruction")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg/250px-City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall_after_the_fire_photograph.jpg)

City Hall one day after the fire

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg/250px-Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ohio_Theatre_City_Hall_plaque.jpg)

Plaque at the Ohio Theatre commemorating the building

City Hall was demolished in a fire that began about 8 p.m. on January 12, 1921.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) At the time, about 100 people were attending a basketball practice inside, and others were attending a meeting of City Council at the same time. There were no injuries during the incident. [James Thurber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thurber "James Thurber"), later known for his cartoons, was covering the City Council meeting as a _Columbus Dispatch_ reporter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6) Sixteen engine companies and six truck companies arrived to fight the fire, setting numerous hoses onto the fire by 8:30 p.m. from multiple areas, including from atop the roof of the Grand Theater building.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Crowds witnessed the building fire, held back into the sloping Statehouse grounds.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-7) The crowds reportedly had few regrets or tears, and a general attitude of "good riddance" to its destruction among the public and city officials.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-8) Exterior walls remained standing, though seemingly about to topple. The entire roof burned away, and the second and third floor interiors were turned into a large pile of debris.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Property loss was estimated at about $75,000; like all city buildings at the time, it was not insured. It was the third public structure to burn in recent months, after the city prison and a more minor fire at the [Columbus State Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_State_Hospital "Columbus State Hospital").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Records lost in the building's fire reportedly included those on the [Franklin Park Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Park_Conservatory "Franklin Park Conservatory"), making much of its early history unknown.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-9) News from four days after the fire claimed all valuable documents and records were saved, though the Children's Playhouse Project was affected. About 5,000 costumes were lost, as well as four sets of scenery and several pageant lights. This combined loss was estimated at $6,300. In addition, thousands of city codes were lost, as well as all bound copies of city bulletins and annual reports for all departments; all these documents were said to be replaceable.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-10)

By the next day, city officials toured the burned building with the determination of making the site habitable within 30 days. Following their tour, they unanimously abandoned any proposals to rebuild City Hall on that site, with most council members indicating the new riverfront civic center as the most appropriate place to rebuild.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) Though the origin of the fire was undetermined by this point, three theories existed: it could have been started from blowtorches left in the building's cupola by workers who were repairing the roof, one of which was found atop charred timber in the wreckage. Other ideas included defective wiring caused a spark, or that lit cigarette butts could have sparked the flames.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1)

Two days after the fire, Columbus's library trustees offered the second floor of the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)") to the mayor and most city officials, which they promptly accepted.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-11)

The fire allowed city leaders to rebuild City Hall with a better structure and in the new [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Civic_Center_(Ohio) "Columbus Civic Center (Ohio)") site. Prominent citizens lauded the mayor, offering "congratulations on the successful fire". The site is now home to the [Ohio Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Theatre_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Ohio Theatre (Columbus, Ohio)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

## Attributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Attributes")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg/250px-City_Hall%2C_Columbus_illustration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_Hall,_Columbus_illustration.jpg)

Original design for the building, including a clock tower

The building was 80 feet wide, 187.5 feet long, and 98 feet tall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was originally set to be 140 feet tall, though its clock tower was never built. The structure was designed by Detroit architect Robert T. Brookes, designer of Towers Hall at [Otterbein University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otterbein_University "Otterbein University") and the final architect for [St. Joseph Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Cathedral_(Columbus,_Ohio) "St. Joseph Cathedral (Columbus, Ohio)") in Columbus. The building utilized dark cream-colored Amherst sandstone for its exterior walls, and had a steep roof with two pitches, both covered in blue Vermont slate. The building's entranceway included seven [lancet archways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture#Pointed_arches "Gothic architecture"), separated by massive piers. A balcony existed above the central three arches, with additional balconies above the diagonal arches on the building's northeast and northwest corners. Upper windows matched the lower arches with their lancet heads. An iron water tank stood on the southeast corner of the building by the roof.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

Initially seen as a perfect example of Gothic Revival architecture, it later grew a reputation as unsatisfactory for a city hall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) It was described by the _Columbus Dispatch_ a day after the fire as "long an eyesore to Columbus",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Dispatch_Jan_13-1) and in 2012 as a "Gothic nightmare of a building".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-2012_Dispatch-6)

### Interior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Interior")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg/250px-Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Columbus_Reading_Room.jpg)

Reading room

The building's first floor had an open [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_(architecture) "Arcade (architecture)") with a variegated marble floor along its north and west sides. A central lobby included a large staircase to the second floor, while to its rear was another lobby with stairs at the sides, leading to all upper floors. To the rear of that was the merchants' exchange.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)

At its opening, the west side of the first floor also held the city's post office, a space including a separate fireproof room. The left or east side housed the city's first [public library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_library "Public library"), a glass-divided room which opened on March 4, 1873. The front section was a reading room, while the back was reserved for books and the librarian's desk.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-13) The collection contained 1,500 books.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) These included 1,200 from the Columbus Athenaeum (1853-1872),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-davies-15) 358 from Columbus's high school library, and 33 from its horticultural society.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-history-16) In 1906, the reading room moved to a separate building across from the [Ohio Statehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Statehouse "Ohio Statehouse"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-Mileposts-14) and by 1907 to the [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(Columbus,_Ohio) "Main Library (Columbus, Ohio)"), where it remains today.

On the second floor was another lobby with five rooms on either side, for city officials and committees.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12) To the rear was the council chamber, an elaborately decorated space with watercolor-frescoed walls.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-FLC-17) The third floor held the public hall, a multipurpose room of 140 by 74 feet, with a height of 53 feet. It was estimated to seat 3,200 people, or give standing room to almost 6,400. A stage stood at the south end of the hall, while a gallery stood at the north end.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_City_Hall_(1872%E2%80%931921)#cite_note-07-1871-12)
